en: Preface to the Newly Compiled Biographies and Eulogies of the Portraits of the Eighty-Eight Patriarchs The portraits of the eighty-eight patriarchs were originally transcribed from the Imperial Palace at the beginning of the dynasty and enshrined in the Patriarchs’ Hall at Jinling.
In the Jia-shen year of the Wanli era, the Great Master Zibo obtained Ding Nan-yu of Xin’an to produce faithful copies for the three halls.
These were distributed among famous mountains. In the year Yimao (1635), Master Hanshan further inscribed small volumes for each, providing biographies and eulogies to follow them.
In the year Renshen of the Chongzhen era (1632), Qian Xian of Jiahe carved woodblocks for their publication. As for the texts of these biographies and eulogies:

It originally consisted of seventy-seven [chapters], with eleven missing. In the year Jiashen, my fellow student, the retired official Li Gao (style name Yugong), who holds the rank of Yubu, composed eleven supplementary chapters to fill the gaps.
He further augmented it with the works of the three great masters Yunqi, Zibo, and Hanshan.
Just as plans were being made for its carving and distribution, the project was interrupted by the upheavals of the times. This autumn, together with Yugong’s eldest son, Nianzu—
We met again in Guangling, where he presented his manuscript to me, desiring to have it carved into printing blocks to fulfill his late father’s aspirations.
I earnestly encouraged his resolve. As for Zunu’s request for a single word from me:

the origins of this compilation and the benefits it shall bring to the world have already been explained in detail by the various gentlemen; what more could I possibly add? Nevertheless, I have heard that regarding the ancient sages and worthies...
That which has been transmitted as instruction to the world consists of words, mind, and further, the body. Words belong to the written teachings;
the mind belongs to the Way as the fundamental principle. If one does not read those writings, the Way cannot be heard. Even if one reads all those writings to the end...

The Way is not necessarily realized through hearing. If one seeks the Way in words, you yourself have already stated the principle that "I desire there to be no speaking," which means words are not to be relied upon.
If one seeks the Way in the mind, the Buddhist scriptures further state that "when seeking the mind, it is ultimately unattainable," meaning the mind is likewise not easily relied upon.

Thus, the Buddhist's aspiration to advance toward Buddhahood and the Confucian's aspiration to advance [toward sagehood]— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
As for the sages and worthies, what could one possibly do? It is sufficient to seek them within one’s own person.

That which is transmitted is the conduct of those individuals, preserved in order to maintain the Way of those individuals. Confucius said, "There is no aspect of my conduct that I have not shared with you, my disciples.
Mencius said, "Wear the robes of Yao, recite the words of Yao, and practice the conduct of Yao..."

conduct. It was simply Yao. Now, the ancient sages have long passed away; yet the traces of their personal experiences, as well as the means by which they entered the Way and advanced in virtue, do not perish along with them.
Thus, by reading the "Xiangdang" (On Demeanor) chapter, one can take as a teacher the way in which Confucius attained his sagehood.
By reading the Seven Chapters of Mencius, one [can likewise understand] the Master of Ziyu’s...

This is why the worthy may be taken as teachers. Extending this principle to the great Confucian scholars such as Shao, Zhou, Cheng, Zhang, Zhu, and Lu—if one truly examines their writings, scrutinizes their words, and investigates their conduct, those individuals who do not fall short of the sages and worthies may likewise be taken as teachers.
Now, among these eighty-eight patriarchs, there are the ancestral masters of the Western Heaven and the East...

The teaching of the Land of the East features a separate transmission outside the scriptures. From Caoxi downward, the lamp of the five schools has been passed on, with various lineages branching out from among them:
whether Chan masters, founders of sects, those of the Vinaya, or Pure Land, extending even to the various schools of Ci'en, Xianshou, Tiantai, and Yogācāra.
Nevertheless, regarding their transmission of the mind and succession of the Dharma, as well as their preeminent practice and realization, they remain truly outstanding.
This account is thus complete. Indeed, by tracing and investigating it through these various biographies, one observes their ways of transcending the world;

therein, those who have achieved transcendence may be taken as teachers. One observes their ways of cultivating the mind; therein, those who have attained purity and refinement are sufficient to serve as models.

Now, there are those with the ferocity to wear stones around their waists for the sake of mortars or to sever their arms with sharp blades; if they seek a teacher, there is none toward whom they would not be sincere.
He possessed the diligence of ascending Mount Touzi three times and visiting Master Dongshan nine times; in terms of refining his learning, there was nothing he did not master.

He possessed the stillness of Zhiyi’s five years of seclusion under snow-covered peaks and upon ice-bound rafts; in terms of dwelling in the mountains, there was no place that did not bring him peace.

He possessed the tranquility of the ninety-day retreat at Tiantai, where birds nested in his robes and folds; in terms of practicing dhyāna, there was nothing he neglected. There was Lin... [text truncated]
Jizhou’s fist-shattering of cliffs and seizing of the fly-whisk—when applied to the immediate occasion, there is nothing that is not transcended.
There is Lianchi and Hanshan, who maintained a daily recitation of sixty thousand Buddha-names; and Yongming, who chanted the Lotus Sūtra thirteen thousand times.
When one cultivates the practice of Pure Land, there is nothing that is not accomplished. There is the "bird-nest" pine of Daolin and Xuefeng’s...

thus, there was nothing they did not penetrate. Students simply fail to establish their resolve.
If one aspires to the lofty traces and transcendent paths, there is nothing to be grasped, yet this very non-grasping is itself sufficient.

As for those who awaken to the nature of life by fanning away the fire, or whose doubts are dispelled by contemplating a shadow—whether they completely discard words and phrases, or whether both mind and dharmas are simultaneously extinguished.

The Master Ba’s citations are incisive and thorough, never wearying of detailed analysis. His primary intent lies in breaking down the barriers between the various schools so that all may return together to the perfectly penetrating ocean of Dharma.
His arguments are established with the utmost impartiality and correctness.

He often reflects upon how the Sage of Mount Ni and the Ascetic of Ku County were both praised as "dragons," and how Huiyuan’s quiet cultivation at Tiger Creek surpassed the ancients; his vision is vast and his mind is empty of self. How extraordinary!

The paths are identical and their destination the same; there is no distinction between them at all. Those with views of extreme divergence in later generations fail to examine the original source and merely cling to their own sectarian gateways.

Not only do Confucianism and Buddhism divide their territories as if they were hostile nations, but even those such as Zhu Xi and Lu Xiangshan—who shared the same lineage as Kongzi and Mengzi—have fallen into such divisions.

Yet, criticisms and attacks have been hurled at one another; though both Dongji and Caoqi emerged from the same source, the fact that they set up arms against each other reveals the shallowness and narrowness of their insight.
By attaining the discourse of Master Gao and his son, one may return to a state of serene detachment.
Preface to the Biographical Eulogies for the Eighty-Eight Patriarchs’ Portraits by Grand Master Han, Compiled by Director of the Imperial Library Yu Gong:
When the Tathāgata appeared in the world, he first turned the Dharma wheel of the Four Noble Truths and finally transmitted the wondrous mind of the separate lineage.

His teachings were divided into five periods, and his precepts were integrated for the seven classes of practitioners. Yet, when it comes to the single gate of the Pure Land, the Buddha-dharma has already declined; nevertheless, it shall still endure for a thousand years.

Those who are able to recognize the four characters of "Amitābha Buddha" shall all occupy high seats. This is because [the Buddhas] compassionately pity sentient beings and skillfully manifest expedient means.

However, if one discusses this matter, there is not even the space of a hair between [right and wrong]. The discourse on the moon at Vulture Peak and the pointing at the moon at Caoxi are both merely adding feet to a body;
they represent the total functioning of all the spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) under heaven, yet none have ever struck the mark directly.
How could one further distinguish between high and low within phenomena that are like dreams and illusions?

The authentic portraits of the eighty-eight patriarchs originated from the Imperial Palace and were enshrined in the Patriarchs’ Hall; they were expanded upon by the Venerable Zibo and eulogized by the Great Master Hanshan.
The late Master Yupeng,虞部 (Yubu) Buzhi, was fully equipped in all the various gateways of Chan, Teaching, Vinaya, Esoteric, and Pure Land.

Out of the Bodhisattva’s protective mindfulness for the sake of sentient beings, he opened every door rather than specializing in a single path. While there may have been aspects yet to be fully perfected within each individual gateway, he provided whatever imagery was necessary;

his compositions were formed spontaneously according to occasion. Where no imagery existed, he did not leave it unfulfilled, yet this was never a matter of forced fabrication. He attained the very essence of the truth.
This is the sublime essence of the surging waves of the Dharma-ocean. While visiting Lingjiang, the honorable Mr. Ning’s son, Nianzu, presented this work for my inspection;
thus, I was able to read it through from beginning to end and compose these reflections on its meaning. The Nianzu family lineage has served as a golden fortress for the dissemination of our Dharma.
This book serves to manifest the vast and great power of aspiration of his ancestors. As the Tathāgata said: "To be born into the family of Bodhisattvas is the most difficult thing in the world."

Thus, regarding his place within the family of Bodhisattvas, he succeeded to their aspirations and carried out their deeds; through the convergence of past causes, there occurred that which happened spontaneously without being expected.
Regarding the Gao family, I cannot help but feel profound admiration and veneration.

Postscript to the Portraits of the Various Patriarchs The various patriarchs were the masters who transmitted the Buddha’s mind-seal. I recall that in the past, when the World-Honored One preached the Dharma on Vulture Peak, he was constantly accompanied by one thousand two hundred and fifty disciples.
Furthermore, at the end of the Buddha’s life, when he held up a flower, Kāśyapa broke into a subtle smile.
He smiled and subsequently transmitted the mind-seal, establishing the principle of the "separate transmission outside the teachings. This is the Zen school (Chánzōng).

why not carve the portraits as well and publish them together? This would cause all who see or hear of them to give rise to joy.

The Venerable Cunda transmitted [the teaching] to the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya. "Ājñāta" is his name; it means "understood. "Kauṇḍinya," or alternatively "Cunda," means "fire-vessel";
this is his clan name (gotra), which became his surname because his ancestors were engaged in that occupation. He was a member of the Buddha’s maternal clan.
When the Buddha first left the royal palace and entered the mountains, there were five men who attended upon him; Dignāga was one of them.

Later, while the Buddha was practicing in the mountains, the five men departed from him and each pursued a different path. When the Buddha had completed his six years of asceticism and first attained enlightenment, he went to the Deer Park.
Hearing of this, the five men all assembled together. There, the Buddha first preached the Four Noble Truths in their three turnings.
Turning the Wheel of the Dharma, the Buddha asked the five men, "Do you understand? The Venerable One was the first to answer, saying, "I have understood.

Therefore, the Buddha confirmed it, saying, "Ājñāta-Kauṇḍinya," by which he received that name. Among the one thousand two hundred and fifty disciples who constantly followed the Buddha, Kauṇḍinya was foremost because he was the first to awaken;
thus he led the way in being the first to receive ordination, owing to his past merit.
Regarding the cause: according to the *Kāraṇa-puṇya-sūtra*, in the past the Buddha was a rishi named Kṣāntivādin who practiced the Way in the mountains.
King Candra (known as King Kali) was of an extremely violent and wicked nature. One day, he took his court ladies into the mountains for a hunt.

The king grew weary and fell into a brief sleep, while the ladies entered the forest to gather flowers. Upon reaching the hermitage of the rishi, the rishi preached the Dharma to them for a long time.
The king awoke; not seeing the women, he took his sword and searched for them. He found them at the place of the seer. The king asked in anger, "Who are you?
He replied, "I am the Seer of Forbearance. The king asked, "Have you attained the meditative concentrations of the higher stages? He replied, "Not yet. The king said:
Since he had not yet attained meditative concentration, he was but an ordinary person. He then drew his sword and cut off the hands and feet of the rishi.
The rishi’s countenance remained unmoved. The king asked, "Do you resent me? The rishi replied, "I do not resent you. May I attain Buddhahood and be the first to deliver you.
It was this very person who was later delivered first—namely, King Kali. Eulogy:
When the elephant king wanders, the elephant calf follows; they seek one another through sound and scent, gathering together when conditions meet.
Even those who were the greatest enemies become the closest of kin through the Way, just as two chariots follow the same ruts—there must surely be a cause.
Transmitted by the First Patriarch, Venerable Kāśyapa.
The First Patriarch of the Western Heaven was the Venerable Mahākāśyapa. He was a native of Magadha and belonged to the Brahmin caste.
*Mahā* is a Sanskrit term meaning "Great"; *Kāśyapa* means "Drinking Light," which is his name. His father’s name was Yinze (Drinking Moisture), and his mother’s was Xiangzhi (Fragrant Will).
The teacher and disciple were born with golden complexions because, in a former life, they were goldsmiths who possessed a profound understanding of the nature of gold.

In the past, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin who entered parinirvāṇa, and a stūpa was erected for him. When the image within the stūpa became damaged, there was a poor woman who took a gold bead to the goldsmith’s workshop and exchanged it for gold to repair the image.
She then offered it as a gift. Consequently, the two of them made a vow to become husband and wife; through these causes and conditions, [they were born with golden complexions].
It was felt that for ninety-one kalpas his body had been entirely golden, and he had long dwelt in the heavens;

subsequently, he was born in the kingdom of Magadha with a body of radiant golden hue, and was therefore called Kāśyapa (The Radiant One). Upon seeing the Buddha, he resolved to seek renunciation. The Buddha said, "Welcome, Bhikṣu."
His beard and hair fell away naturally, and the *kāṣāya* robe clung to his body. He was constantly praised as the foremost among the assembly for practicing the *dhūta* austerities;

thus he was known as the *dhūta* Master Suvarṇavarṇa. When the Buddha was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, he held up a flower and showed it to the assembly. The assembly remained bewildered, but only the Venerable One broke into a smile.
The Buddha said, "I possess the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate of the reality-mark (*bhūtanimitta*) which is signless (*animitta*)."
"I entrust to you this wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa*. Guard and uphold it well. Then he spoke in verse:
"The Dharma is originally no-dharma; no-dharma is also dharma. Now I transmit this dharma at the time of no-dharma. As for dharma, when has it ever been dharma? This is the Zen school."
The Founder’s Eulogy states:
A form of golden hue with a vajra for a heart, Upholding the life of wisdom, he constantly turns the Wheel of Dharma.
When the World-Honored One held up the flower, he broke into a smile; To this day, it leaves people beyond the reach of thought.
The Second Patriarch, Venerable Ānanda, was transmitted [the Dharma] by the Second Patriarch.
He was a native of Rājagṛha; his clan name was Kṣatriya, and his father was King Droṇodana. He was, in fact, the younger cousin of the Buddha.
In the Sanskrit language he is called Ānanda; this is translated here as "Joyous Celebration" (Qingxi) or also as "Rejoicing" (Huanxi). When the Tathāgata attained...

He was born at night, and thus he was named Ananda. He was widely learned and profoundly erudite, possessing unimpeded wisdom; the World-Honored One declared him foremost among those who possess *dhāraṇī*.
Throughout his successive past lives, he had served various Buddhas and upheld the treasury of the Dharma; therefore, he now left the household life under the Buddha to serve as his attendant.
Not a single word of the Dharma preached by the Buddha did he omit, and thus, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, he compiled the treasury of the Dharma.
All were proclaimed from his mouth. Kāśyapa asked the great assembly, "Is what Ānanda has spoken free from error?
They all replied, "It is no different from what the World-Honored One has taught. Kāśyapa then said, "I am Ānanda. My life will not remain much longer;
I now entrust the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma to you. You must protect and uphold it well. Listen to my verse: 'The nature of each and every dharma is originally...'"
"Dharma. There is neither dharma nor non-dharma. How could there be both dharma and non-dharma within a single dharma?
Having spoken this verse, Kāśyapa took up his saṃghāṭī robe and entered Mount Kukkuṭapāda to enter meditative absorption, awaiting the descent of Maitreya.
Ānanda was thus the Second Patriarch. The eulogy says:
His vast learning is like the ocean, drinking in and containing the flowing currents of the Dharma;
the appearance and disappearance of all Buddhas do not depart from his tongue, which beats the bellows of the Dharma-transformation, setting the rhythm of its transformation.
Therefore, my teacher was one who attained the Center through the Particulars—the transmission of the Third Patriarch, the Venerable Śaṇakavāsin.
The Third Patriarch, Venerable Śaṇakavāsin, was a native of the kingdom of Mathurā. His clan name was Viśākha; his father was Vanavāsin and his mother was Kauśeya.
He was born after being in the womb for six years. In the Sanskrit language he is called Śaṇaka, which here means "naturally clothed";
this refers to the name of a nine-jointed, exquisite grass found in the Western Regions. Whenever a sage is born, this grass grows [spontaneously].
In this pure and clean place, such auspicious grasses appeared as a response when the Venerable One was born.

Formerly, when the Tathāgata was traveling to convert beings, he arrived at the kingdom of Mathurā and saw a grove of green trees with lush branches and leaves. He said to Ānanda: "One hundred years after my parinirvāṇa..."
There was a bhikṣu named Śāṇakavāsin who turned the sublime Wheel of Dharma within this forest. Later, Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa was born;
having received the Dharma-eye from the Venerable Ānanda, he resided in this forest and subdued two fire-dragons. The dragons offered him the land, and he established a Brahma-palace there.
After the Venerable One had long fulfilled his transformative conditions, he thought of entrusting the True Dharma [to a successor] and traveled to the country of Tāḍita, where Upagupta [resided].
Many came to seek refuge with him and serve as his attendants. He asked Ghosaka, "How old are you? He replied, "I am seventeen years old.
The master said, "Is it your body that is seventeen, or is your nature seventeen? He replied, "My teacher’s hair has turned white; is it the hair that has turned white, or is the mind white?
The master said, "It is my hair that has turned white, not my mind. [Ghosaka] said, "My body is seventeen, but not..."

This was the seventeenth [succession] in the lineage. The Venerable One recognized that he was a vessel for the Dharma; three years later, he shaved his head and conferred the full precepts upon him. He then addressed him, saying:
"In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the True Dharma Eye and the unsurpassed wondrous Dharma to Kāśyapa. It was passed down in succession until it reached me, and I now entrust it to you.
Do not allow it to be severed. Listen to my verse: 'Neither dharma nor mind; no mind...'"
Nor is there any dharma. When these so-called mental dharmas are spoken of, these dharmas are not mental dharmas. This is the Third Patriarch. He praised [the teaching], saying:
"The numinous root of Prajñā was already realized in previous lives; Thus, as the Master was about to emerge, the auspicious grass first responded.
To seal mind with mind is like casting fire into fire; Meeting on a narrow path, there is no place to hide."
The Biography of the Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta.
The Fourth Patriarch, Venerable Upagupta, was a native of the country of Tāla. His clan name was Śūdra; his father’s name was Kalyāṇamati.

He left home at the age of seventeen and, at twenty, received the mind-seal of the Third Patriarch. He traveled through various regions to transform beings, and those he delivered were exceedingly numerous. By...
The palace of Māra shook violently, and Pāpīyān was filled with grief and fear. He then exhausted all his demonic power to harm the Venerable One.

While the Venerable One was absorbed in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), Māra took a necklace and fastened it around his neck. Upon emerging from concentration, the Venerable One took the corpses of a human, a dog, and a snake, and transformed them into flower garlands.
He addressed Māra with gentle words, and Māra joyfully accepted and tied them on; immediately they became putrid corpses, ruined by maggots.
It became putrid; he loathed it so much that he could not endure it. He exhausted all his magical powers, yet in the end, he could not remove it. Thereupon, he entreated the Venerable One for mercy.

The Venerable One instructed the Māra to take refuge in the Triple Gem and to repent and reform his transgressions, whereby he attained liberation. For every person the Venerable One saved, he placed a tally-stick in a stone chamber.
The chamber, though only one *zhang* square, eventually became filled with them. Later, there was the son of an elder named Ghoṣila who came.

He requested ordination. The Venerable One asked, "Do you seek ordination with your body, or do you seek ordination with your mind? He replied, "I have come for ordination, not for the sake of body or mind.
The Venerable One said, "If it is neither for the sake of body nor mind, who then is it that seeks ordination? He replied, "As for one who seeks ordination..."
Because there is no self and no notion of self; because there is no self and no notion of self, the mind neither arises nor ceases. That the mind neither arises nor ceases is the eternal Way.

The Buddhas are also eternal, for the mind has no form or characteristics, and its essence is likewise so. [The Master] said: "You shall attain great enlightenment; the mind will naturally penetrate through itself.
He then performed the tonsure and conferred the full precepts upon him, further declaring: "In your father's dream, a golden sun appeared..."
“Śāṇakavāsin, you may be named Diṭṭhagāmaṇi (Ditoka). He said: ‘The Tathāgata entrusted the treasury of the Great Dharma-Eye to me in succession;
I now entrust it to you. Do not let it be severed. Guard and uphold it well. Listen to my verse: ‘The mind is itself the original mind;

The original mind is not a dharma that exists. If there were a dharma that existed, there would be an original mind; But since it is neither mind nor a fundamental dharma, He is the Fourth Patriarch.’”
The Eulogy says:
When one person’s mind becomes empty, the palace of Māra trembles; who would dare lightly handle the vajra-blade?
If one is willing to turn the light back upon itself, the wild mind is instantly stilled; through prostration and taking refuge, all transgressions are extinguished.
The Fifth Patriarch, Venerable Diṭṭhagga:
The lineage of the Fifth Patriarch, Venerable Diṭṭhagga, was passed down from him. He was a native of the kingdom of Magadha. In the Sanskrit language he is called Diṭṭhagga;
in this [Chinese] language it means "Measure of Penetrating Reality. When he was first born, his father dreamed that a golden sun emerged from the house, illuminating heaven and earth. Before him...
There was a great mountain, adorned with various jewels; from its summit, springs gushed forth, flowing in torrents in all four directions.
Later, he encountered the Venerable Kūṭadanta, who explained it for him, saying: "The jewel mountain is my own body. The gushing springs represent the inexhaustibility of the Dharma.
The sun emerging from the house is a sign that you have now entered the Path. Its illuminating of heaven and earth signifies that your wisdom transcends all."
Upon hearing these words, the Venerable One rejoiced and proclaimed: "The majestic mountain of the seven treasures constantly wells forth the spring of wisdom;

transformed into a hymn of the True Dharma, it can deliver all who possess the karmic affinity. The Venerable Kūṭadanta also spoke a verse: "I transmit my Dharma to you; you shall manifest great wisdom.
Like the golden sun rising from its chamber, it shall illuminate heaven and earth. Having heard this, the Venerable One...
Having offered verses of homage and respectfully received [the teachings], he later traveled to the kingdom of Central India. There were eight thousand great rishis there, with Mīḍhaka at their head.
Hearing that the Venerable One had arrived, they led their assembly to pay him homage and said: "In the past, we were born together in the Brahma Heaven.

I encountered a rishi who bestowed the methods of the rishis upon me, while you, Master, met a son of the Buddha and practiced *dhyāna*. Since then, our karmic destinies have followed divergent paths."

After six kalpas had passed, [the Buddha] said, "That you have endured through successive kalpas is indeed true and not in vain. You may now abandon heterodoxy and return to the orthodox, so as to enter the Buddha-vehicle.
Mīchaka said, "It is fortunate that we have met today; is this not due to past affinities? I pray that the Master, out of compassion, will grant me liberation.
The Venerable One immediately ordained him, conferred full ordination upon him, and then said, "In the past, the Tathāgata, with the Great Dharma..."
[The Dharma] was secretly entrusted to Kāśyapa and passed down in succession until it reached me. I now entrust it to you; you must protect and cherish it. Then he spoke this verse:
"Penetrating the mind of the fundamental Dharma, there is neither dharma nor non-dharma. Awakening is the same as non-awakening; without mind, there is also no dharma.
This was the Fifth Patriarch. The eulogy says:
Having already awakened to the original mind, which shines like the sun day and night, He reveals that the dream of birth and death is transcended by the light;
the Master’s Dharma is fundamentally without self, and dharmas do not exist. Uniting emptiness with emptiness, his tongue does not leave his mouth.
—The Transmission of the Venerable Sixth Patriarch Mīzhājiā.
The Sixth Patriarch, Venerable Mīchaka, was a native of Central India.

Having transmitted the Dharma, he traveled to the kingdom of Northern India and saw auspicious golden clouds above the city battlements. He sighed and said, "This is the breath of a person on the Way;
there must surely be my successor here. He then entered the city. Amidst the bustling market stalls, he saw a man holding a wine vessel who came forward to ask him:
"From where have you come, Master? Where do you wish to go? The Patriarch said, "I have come from my own mind; I wish to go nowhere.
[The monk] asked, "Do you recognize the object in my hand? The Patriarch said, "This is a vessel for contact, yet it carries purity. [The monk] asked, "Do you recognize me, Master?"
The Patriarch said, "I do not recognize it; that which is recognized is not me. He then said to him, "Try to state your own name and lineage, and I shall show you your original cause.
That man spoke a verse, saying: "From immeasurable kalpas past, until my birth in this land, My original surname was Bharadvāja, and my given name was Vāsukī.
The Patriarch said, "My teacher, Diṭṭhaga, said... [The text continues: "...the world..."
In the past, when the World-Honored One was traveling through Northern India, he said to Ānanda: "Three hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, a holy man shall appear in this land.
His clan name will be Bharadvāja and his personal name will be Vasumitra. He shall be the seventh in the lineage of the patriarchs of dhyāna.
The World-Honored One has prophesied you; you ought to leave the household life. Thereupon, Vasumitra set down his bowl, prostrated before the Master, and standing to one side, spoke thus:
"I reflect upon past kalpas when I once acted as a *dānapati* and offered a precious throne to a Tathāgata. That Buddha bestowed a prediction upon me, saying:
'In the present Bhadrakalpa, within the Dharma of Śākyamuni, you shall propagate the ultimate teaching. This now accords with the Master’s words; I pray that you grant me liberation.
The Patriarch then shaved his head and conferred the full precepts upon him, and said to him: "The Treasury of the True Dharma-Eye transmitted by the World-Honored One, I now..."
I entrust this to you; do not let it be severed. Then he spoke in verse: "No mind can be apprehended; What is spoken of cannot be called a dharma.
If one realizes that the mind is no-mind, Only then does one understand the mind and its dharmas. He was thus the Sixth Patriarch. The eulogy says:
All comes from this; it is not for any other purpose. Meeting in the bustling marketplace, he spontaneously reveals his vessel.
Seeing clearly what was yet to come, he knew today beforehand. When conducting business, one does not concern oneself with the price.
The Seventh Patriarch, Venerable Vasumitra’s Transmission.
The Seventh Patriarch, Vāsūmitra, was a native of Northern India. His family name was Bharadvāja, which in this language means "swift and sharp-witted.
He constantly wore pure garments and carried a vessel for wine as he wandered through the streets and neighborhoods, sometimes chanting and sometimes whistling; people regarded him as mad.
Upon meeting the Venerable Miśraka, who proclaimed the Tathāgata’s past prophecy, he reflected upon his own prior karmic conditions and cast away his vessel.

Having left the household life to receive the Dharma, he traveled to the kingdom of Kāmarūpa to propagate the teachings and extensively perform Buddhist rites. Before his Dharma seat, there suddenly appeared a man of wisdom who declared, "My name is Buddhanandi;
I shall now debate the meaning of the Dharma with you, Master. The Patriarch said, "O worthy one, where there is debate, there is no true meaning; where there is true meaning, there is no debate.
If you intend to debate the meaning, it will ultimately not be a discussion of the true meaning. Nandi understood the Master’s intent.
Yi-sheng was deeply impressed and said with reverence, "I vow to seek the Way and partake of the flavor of the nectar.
The Patriarch then shaved his head for him and conferred the full precepts upon him, saying, "The Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, I now entrust to you; you must uphold and protect it."

Then he spoke in verse: "The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; It manifests dharmas equal to empty space. When the realization of empty space is attained, There is neither 'is' nor 'non-is'.
Having thus transmitted the Dharma, he immediately entered the Samādhi of Compassionate Mind. At that time, Brahmā, Śakra, and all the devas...
They all came forward to pay their respects and spoke in verse: "O Ancestor of the Sages of the Bhadrakalpa, you shall occupy the seventh position.
Venerable One, we cherish you; please proclaim for us the stage of the Buddha. The Venerable One arose from samādhi and addressed the assembly, saying: "The Dharma I have attained is not existent;
if one recognizes the stage of the Buddha, it is because it is free from existence and non-existence. Having spoken these words, he returned to samādhi. This is [the account].
He became the Seventh Patriarch. The eulogy says:
Coming from a familiar path, one suddenly meets a close friend; A single word of discussion instantly reveals what is innately present.
Begging for the flavor of nectar, he was shown the Dharma of space; If one claims there is something attained, one falls into the seventh or eighth stage.
The Transmission of the Eighth Patriarch, Venerable Buddhanandi.

The Eighth Patriarch, Venerable Buddhanandi, was a native of the kingdom of Kāmarūpa. His clan name was Gautama. He possessed a fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) upon his crown and was endowed with swift and unimpeded eloquence.
Initially, he encountered Vasumitra, from whom he left the household life and received instruction. Subsequently, leading a group of disciples, he arrived at...
In the kingdom of Tiṅga, at the house of Viśāla, he saw a white light ascending from the dwelling.

He said to his disciples, "There is a sage in this house who does not speak with his mouth; he is a true vessel for the Mahāyāna. He does not walk along the four crossroads, for he knows that contact is defiling."
When he had finished speaking, the elder came out to pay his respects and asked, "What do you require? The Patriarch said, "I am seeking an attendant.
The elder said, "I have a son named Buddhabhadra; he is already fifty years old, yet he has never spoken a word nor ever set foot upon the ground.
The Patriarch said, "If it is as you describe, he is truly my disciple. Upon hearing this, Buddhabhadra rose immediately and prostrated himself.
He spoke in verse: "Parents are not my kin; who is the most intimate kin?
The Buddhas are not my Way; who is the supreme Way? The Patriarch answered in verse: "What you say is intimate with the mind—parents cannot be compared to it.
Your practice accords with the Way—the mind of all Buddhas is precisely this. To seek outwardly for a Buddha with form is not like you; if you wish to recognize [the Buddha]..."

"Your original mind is neither joined nor separated. Upon hearing this, Bodhidharma took seven steps. The Patriarch said, "This child has encountered Buddhas in the past and possesses vast compassionate vows.
Fearing that his parents' affection would make it difficult for him to renounce them, he did not speak of his sandals."
The elder then renounced his home to enter the monastic life. His grandfather soon conferred upon him the full precepts (*upasampadā*) and further addressed him, saying:
"I now entrust to you the Tathāgata’s Treasury of the True Dharma Eye (*saddharmapuṇḍarīka-dharmanetra*). Do not allow it to be severed. He then spoke this verse:
"Space has neither interior nor exterior; The nature of mind is likewise so. If one realizes space as it is, One penetrates the principle of *tathatā* (Suchness). This was the Eighth Patriarch.
The Eulogy says:
It is not that there is nothing to say, for words cannot reach it; it is not that there is no practice, for originally there are no traces.
Now that one meets such a person, one may finally open one’s mouth; from this point on, one acts accordingly, never falling into the pitfalls of conventional patterns.
The Biography of the Ninth Patriarch, Vajramitra:
The Ninth Patriarch, Vajramitra, was a native of the country of Ti-ga. His secular surname was Viśāla.

Having received the entrustment of the Eighth Patriarch, he later traveled to Central India to propagate the Dharma. At that time, there was an elder named Gandhacchattra who brought his son with him...
He came to pay his respects to the Patriarch and said, "This child remained in the womb for sixty years; therefore, he is named Nansheng (Difficult to Be Born).

He once met an immortal who told me that this boy was no ordinary person and would surely become a vessel of the Dharma. Now that he has encountered you, O Venerable One, you may allow him to leave the household life.

The Patriarch immediately shaved his head. At the moment of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of ordination), auspicious light illuminated the seat, and thirty-seven *śarīra* relics were manifested.
[The Dharma] was manifested before him. From then on, he practiced with diligence, forgetting all fatigue. Eventually, the Patriarch said to him:
"The Tathāgata entrusted the treasury of the Great Dharma-Eye to me through successive transmission. I now entrust it to you; you must cherish and protect it so that it does not come to an end.

He then spoke this verse: "The True Principle is originally nameless; It is because of names that the True Principle is revealed. Having received the true and real Dharma, It is neither true nor false."
False. These constitute the nine patriarchs. The eulogy says:
Dwelling within the mother’s womb for sixty years, He waited only for the Master’s arrival to fulfill his prior karmic conditions.
The radiance upon his crown was originally inherent; A single stroke of realization pierced through it like the roar of a lion.
The Biography of the Tenth Patriarch, Master Xié.
The Tenth Patriarch, Master Xié, was a native of Central India. His original name was Nansheng.

When he was about to be born, his father dreamed of a white elephant with a precious throne upon its back, on which was placed a bright pearl. It entered through the gate, and its light illuminated the four quarters.
The assembly, having awakened, subsequently met the Ninth Patriarch. He attended at his side and never slept; because his side never touched the mat, he was thus titled the Venerable Pārśva.
When he first arrived in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra, he rested beneath a tree and pointed to the ground with his right hand, telling the assembly:
"When this ground turns golden in color, a sage shall enter this assembly. Having finished speaking, it immediately turned [golden].
At that time, there was a son of an elder named Pūrṇayaśas, who stood before him with palms joined. The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from?
He replied, "My mind does not go anywhere. The Patriarch said, "Where do you dwell? He replied, "My mind does not abide anywhere."
The Patriarch said, "Are you not settled? He replied, "All Buddhas are likewise. The Patriarch said, "You are not the Buddhas.
He replied, "The Buddhas are also not the Patriarch. Thereupon he spoke a verse, saying: "This ground turns golden, Foretelling the arrival of a Sage.
He shall sit beneath the Bodhi tree, And having perfected the Flower of Enlightenment. Yaśas then spoke another verse, saying: "The Master sits upon the golden ground, Constantly preaching..."
The true meaning turned its light back to illuminate me, causing me to enter samādhi. The Patriarch, knowing his intent, immediately ordained him as a monk and conferred the full precepts upon him.
He then addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury is now entrusted to you;
you must cherish and protect it. He then spoke this verse: "The true essence is naturally true; Because of the truth, there is a principle of explanation. If one can grasp the truth,"
The True Dharma has neither movement nor stillness; this constitutes the ten patriarchs. The eulogy says:
Pointing at the ground, it turns to gold, appearing with the mere movement of the hand. The Sage arrives immediately—how marvelous!
It is like calling out into a valley and receiving an echo in response. Thus one knows that the nature of my mind is fundamentally without coming or going.
The Transmission of the Eleventh Patriarch, Venerable Pūrṇāśaya.
The Eleventh Patriarch, Venerable Pūrṇāśaya, was a native of the city of Pāṭaliputra. His clan name was Gautama, and his father was Ratnagātra.
Having received the Dharma from the Venerable Pārśva, he traveled to seek out the Mahāsattva Aśvaghoṣa in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, where he was welcomed by him.
He prostrated and asked, "I wish to recognize the Buddha. Which one is he? The Patriarch said, "If you wish to recognize the Buddha, it is that which you do not recognize.
He asked, "Since I do not recognize the Buddha, how can I know it is him? The Patriarch said, "Since you do not recognize the Buddha, how can you know it is not him?
He said, "This is the meaning of the saw. The Patriarch said, "That is the meaning of the wood. He asked, "What is the meaning of the saw? The Patriarch said, "... [The text ends here].
He emerged from the retreat together with his teacher. Aśvaghoṣa then asked, "What is the meaning of 'wood'? The Patriarch replied, "You have been liberated by me. Aśvaghoṣa was suddenly enlightened;
he prostrated himself in refuge and subsequently requested ordination. The Patriarch said to the assembly, "This is a Great Being."
In the past, he was the King of Vaiśālī. In that kingdom, there was a class of people who were like naked horses.
The king exercised his supernatural power and divided his body into silkworms, whereby they obtained clothing. Later, the king was reborn as a "horse-person" in Central India;
out of longing and grief, he neighed, and for this reason he was called Aśvaghoṣa (Horse-Neigh). The Tathāgata prophesied, saying: "Six hundred years after my parinirvāṇa, there shall be..."
The wise Aśvaghoṣa subdued the heretics in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī and delivered immeasurable people.

He shall succeed me in transmitting the transformation [of the Dharma]. Now is precisely the time. He then addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata’s Great Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma is now entrusted to you.

He then spoke a verse: "Delusion and awakening are like concealment and manifestation; clarity and darkness are not separate from one another. Now I entrust to you this dharma of concealment and manifestation, which is not merely one."
Nor is it two. This is the eleventh patriarch.
The eulogy says: The Buddha does not recognize the Buddha; the eye does not see the eye. Seeking elsewhere, he meets with censure.
Believing himself whole and complete, he has already been exposed and shattered. Only upon a sudden awakening does one realize that the talk has fallen away.
The Transmission of the Twelfth Patriarch, the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa:
The Great Being Aśvaghoṣa, the Twelfth Patriarch, was a native of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

Having received the Dharma from the Venerable Vasubandhu (Yaśas), he later turned the subtle wheel of the Dharma in the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra. Suddenly, a golden man emerged from the earth. Furthermore...
She transformed herself into a woman, pointed her right hand toward the Patriarch, and spoke this verse: "I bow my head to the Venerable Elder;
you shall receive the prediction of the Tathāgata. Now, upon this very ground, you proclaim the ultimate truth. Having finished speaking, she vanished instantly. The Patriarch said:
"Māra is about to come. After a short while, wind and rain arrived suddenly; heaven and earth were shrouded in darkness. The Patriarch said, "It is true that Māra has come. I shall eliminate him.
He then pointed into the air, and a great golden dragon appeared, manifesting fierce and powerful energy that shook the mountains and peaks.
The Patriarch remained solemn upon his seat, and the Māra could not move him. The Patriarch addressed him, saying, "You need only take refuge in the Triple Gem."
He immediately attained supernatural powers and restored his original form. He prostrated and repented. The Patriarch asked, "What is your name?

How many followers do you have? He replied, "My name is Kambala; I have three thousand followers. The Patriarch said, "Exerting all your supernatural powers, what kind of transformations can you perform?
He replied, "I could transform the vast ocean; that would be a very minor feat. The Patriarch said, "Then transform the ocean of nature (dharmatā-samudra)."
He asked, "Is it so? [The Master] replied, "What is meant by the 'Ocean of Nature' (*dharmadhātu*)? I have never known it. The Patriarch then explained the Ocean of Nature for him, saying:
"Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all established upon it; the three samādhis and the six supernormal powers manifest from it. Upon hearing these words, Kāpimāra was enlightened.
He then gave rise to faith in the Dharma and, together with three thousand followers, sought ordination. The Patriarch summoned five hundred arhats and conferred the full precepts upon him.
He further addressed him, saying: "The Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury is now to be entrusted to you.

Listen to these verses: 'Manifestation and concealment are the fundamental Dharma; light and darkness are originally not two. Now I entrust to you the Dharma of realization, which is neither grasped nor abandoned.'"
It is not separate; this constitutes the Twelfth Patriarch. The eulogy says:
The horse’s mournful neigh surely has its own cause; The woman who sprang from the earth was originally no such person.
Demons are fundamentally not demons, and Buddhas are likewise not Buddhas; Viewed with the correct eye, what thing is there at all?
The Biography of the Thirteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kāpimāra.
The Thirteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kāpimāra, was a native of the country of Pāṭaliputra. Initially, he was a non-Buddhist practitioner with three thousand disciples;
he was proficient in various heterodox doctrines and possessed great supernormal powers. Later, he received the Dharma from the Venerable Aśvaghoṣa and led his followers.

Upon arriving in Western India, there was a crown prince there named Meghasvāmin (Yún Zìzài). Having heard the name of the Venerable One with reverence, he invited him to the palace to provide offerings.
The Patriarch said, "The Tathāgata has taught that śramaṇas must not draw near kings or princes.
The Prince asked, "To the north of this city there is a mountain; on the mountain is a stone cave. May you practice meditative seclusion there? The Patriarch replied, "I agree," and entered.
After traveling several li through the mountains, he encountered a large python. The Master conferred upon it the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts; having listened, the python departed.
When the Master reached a stone cave, an old man dressed in plain white garments came forward and paid his respects. The Master asked, "Where do you reside? The man replied:
"In the past, I was a bhikṣu who practiced meditation here. At that time, there were novice bhikṣus who frequently came to request instruction;
I grew weary of answering them and gave rise to thoughts of resentment. When my life ended, I consequently fell into the body of a python and have dwelt in this cave for a thousand years.
Fortunately, I have now met the Venerable One and been able to hear the Dharma of the precepts. Having already attained liberation from suffering, I have come to express my gratitude. — Master Zhiyi.
Question: Who else dwells on this mountain? Answer: Ten *li* from here, there is a great tree whose shade covers five hundred great dragons.

This king of trees is named Nāgārjuna, who constantly preaches the Dharma for the assembly of dragons. The Patriarch then proceeded with his disciples to that place. Nāgārjuna came out to meet him and said:
"This deep mountain is desolate and solitary, a dwelling place for dragons and pythons. How is it that you, O Most Virtuous and Honored One, have come here?"
He manifested his supernatural powers. The Patriarch said, "I am not a supreme deity; I have come to visit you, a worthy one.

Nāgārjuna thought silently to himself, "Has this master attained the nature of certainty and clarified the eye of the Way? The Patriarch said, "Though you speak with your mind, I already know it with my mind.

Simply prepare yourself for the renunciation of the household life; why worry that I am not a sage? Nāgārjuna repented and apologized. The Patriarch immediately ordained him and five hundred nāgas as well.
The assembly together received the full precepts. [Bodhidharma] addressed them, saying: "The Tathāgata’s Great Dharma-Eye Treasury is entrusted to you.

Listen to my verse: 'Neither hidden nor manifest is the Dharma; this is called the true limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi). To awaken to this Dharma of the hidden and the manifest is neither folly nor wisdom.
This was the Thirteenth Patriarch. The eulogy says:
Attaining right knowledge and vision from amidst diversity, Encountering a venomous snake on the road, his heart of compassion arose;
He further inquired about the poisonous dragon, intending to subdue it all; Seeing with the eyes and knowing with the mind, like an echo emerging from a valley.
The Biography of the Fourteenth Patriarch, Venerable Nāgārjuna.
The Fourteenth Patriarch, Venerable Nāgārjuna, was a native of Western India. He first received the Dharma from Venerable Māra.
Later, he traveled to South India, where the people were largely devoted to meritorious works. The Patriarch preached the Dharma for them, revealing the Buddha-nature;
those who heard him all returned to their original resolve. The Patriarch then sat upon his seat and manifested a body of sovereign mastery, like the orb of the full moon.
The great assembly heard only the sound of the Dharma, but did not see his physical form.
Among the assembly was the son of an elder named Kanadeva, who said to the group, "Do you recognize this sign? The assembly replied, "We have never beheld it with our eyes; how can we identify it?
Kanadeva said, "This is the Venerable One manifesting the essence and characteristics of the Buddha-nature to show us. How do we know this? It is because there is no..."
The Samādhi of Marks: its form is like the full moon. The meaning of Buddha-nature is vast, empty, and luminous.

Having finished speaking, the wheel-mark vanished, and he returned to his original seat, where he spoke this verse: "The body manifests the mark of the full moon, To represent the essence of all Buddhas.

In teaching the Dharma, there is no fixed form, Employing means that transcend sound and color. Upon hearing this verse, the assembly suddenly realized non-arising and all vowed to leave the household life.

He went home to seek liberation. The Patriarch immediately shaved his head and conferred the full precepts upon him. In that country, there were previously more than five thousand followers of non-Buddhist paths who practiced great sorcery;
the Patriarch converted them all and caused them to take refuge in the Triple Gem. He then composed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
Having transmitted the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* and the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* to future generations, he then addressed his chief disciple, Kāṇadeva, saying:
"The Tathāgata’s treasury of the true Dharma-eye is now to be entrusted to you. Listen to my verse, which clarifies the principles of concealment and manifestation."
While he was explaining the principle of liberation, his mind did not grasp at phenomena; he felt neither anger nor joy. He is the Fourteenth Patriarch.
The eulogy says:
"Among dragons, he transformed into a dragon to use poison to counteract poison; the Venerable One, with a single word from his wondrous hand, subdued him."
The essence of the Buddha-nature samādhi is like empty space; hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates all enter therein.
The Biography of the Fifteenth Patriarch, Venerable Gaṇapati:
The Fifteenth Patriarch, Venerable Gaṇapati, was a native of South India. His secular surname was Viśrāva. Initially...
Seeking the karma of merit, he was also fond of debate. Later, he went to visit the Great Being Nāgārjuna.
As he was about to reach the gate, Nāgārjuna, knowing him to be a man of wisdom, first sent an attendant to place a bowl filled with water before his seat.

Upon seeing it, the Venerable One immediately cast a single needle into it and proceeded forward. They were delighted by their mutual accord. Nāgārjuna then preached the Dharma for him without rising from his seat.

A lunar disc appeared; one could hear its sound but not see its form. The Patriarch said to the assembly, "This auspicious omen signifies that the Master has manifested his Buddha-nature, indicating that the preaching of the Dharma transcends both sound and form.
Having received the Dharma, the Patriarch proceeded to the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
There was a householder named Brahmāyuṣmat. One day, mushrooms grew upon the trees in his garden; they were exceedingly sweet in flavor.
Only the householder and his second son, Rāhula, took them and ate them. Having eaten them, they both subsequently grew tall.
When the mushrooms had been exhausted, they grew again, yet no one else knew the reason. The Patriarch, knowing their past causes, went to their home.
The elder asked for the cause, and the Patriarch said: "In the past, your family once provided alms to a bhikṣu whose 'path-eye' was not yet clear;

because he had received the offerings in vain, his retribution was these wooden mushrooms. Only you and your son were sincere and earnest, so you alone were able to enjoy them, while the others were not."
He then asked the elder how old he was. The elder replied, "I am seventy-nine. The Master then spoke a verse:
"If one enters the Way without penetrating its principle, one returns to this body to consume the faithful's offerings. At eighty-one, the elder [will find that] his tree will no longer grow.

Having heard this, the elder was even more deeply moved by admiration and served. He immediately gave up his second son to follow the Master and leave the household life. The Venerable One then shaved his head.
Having conferred the full ordination, he then entrusted him with the Dharma-eye. A verse says: "I have explained the principle of liberation For the sake of one who transmits the Dharma;
In reality, there is nothing realized within the Dharma, Neither end nor beginning. This was the Fifteenth Patriarch. The eulogy says:
Casting the needle into the bowl, he attained a wondrous realization beyond words; demonstrating the meaning of Buddha-nature, the full moon appeared before him.
Arriving at the house of the elder, he used the needle to guide the thread, employing the conditions of another as his own expedient means.
The Transmission of the Sixteenth Patriarch, Venerable Rāhulabhadra.
The sixteenth patriarch, Venerable Rāhulata, was a native of Kapilavastu. Having attained the Dharma, he traveled to Śrāvastī to propagate the teachings.
There was a river there named Suvarṇodaka (Golden Water), whose taste was exceptionally fine; in its current, the reflections of five Buddhas appeared.
The Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying: "At the source of this river, five hundred *li* away, there is a holy one named Saṃghanandi."
He resided there. The Buddha prophesied that one thousand years hence, he would succeed to the holy position.

Having spoken thus, he led his assembly upstream until they reached that place, where they saw Saṃghanandin sitting peacefully in meditative absorption. The Patriarch and the multitude waited for him there.

After twenty-one days, he finally arose from his meditative absorption. The Patriarch asked him, "Is your body in samādhi, or is your mind in samādhi? Daiten replied, "Both body and mind are in samādhi.
The Patriarch said, "If both body and mind are in samādhi, how can there be entering and exiting? Daiten replied, "Although there is entering and exiting,"

Without losing his meditative composure, he engaged in such questions, answers, and cross-examinations for six or seven turns of speech. The Patriarch then explained the meaning of non-self (*anātman*) to him.
Nandī asked, "Whom did your worthy teacher study under to attain this non-self? The Patriarch replied, "My teacher was Kāṇadeva;
from him I realized this non-self. Nandī praised him with a verse: "I bow my head to Teacher Kāṇadeva, From whom you, O worthy one, have emerged. O worthy one..."
"Because there is no self. I wish to take you, Venerable One, as my teacher. The Patriarch replied in verse: "I have already attained non-self; You must see my 'self.
If you would take me as your teacher, Know that my 'self' is not a self. Nandimitra’s mind was suddenly enlightened, and he immediately sought ordination and liberation.
The Patriarch said, "Your mind is autonomous; it is not bound by me. The Patriarch then held up his alms bowl with his right hand and reached—
In the Brahma palace, he took fragrant food and shared his seat with Nandi to eat it. He then addressed the assembly, saying, "The one who shared my seat was the Tathāgata Śālarāja of the past.
Out of compassion for sentient beings, he descended to manifest his traces here. Nandi [performed] this by means of his supernormal power.
He extended his right hand to the adamantine foundation of the earth, took up the water of ambrosia in a lapis lazuli vessel, and offered it for the assembly to drink;

there was none among them who did not look up to him with reverence. The Patriarch transmitted the Dharma-eye, saying in verse: "In the Dharma, truly there is nothing realized; Neither grasped nor abandoned."
The Dharma has no marks of existence or non-existence; how could it arise internally or externally? This was the sixteenth patriarch. The eulogy says:
Seeking the current, one finds the source; water is exhausted and mountains are reached. Suddenly one beholds this man and knows him to be a sage.
Fragrant rice is brought forth, and he shares his seat to eat together. The great assembly drinks the nectar of immortality, as sweet as honey.
The Transmission of the Seventeenth Patriarch, Venerable Saṃghanandin.
The Seventeenth Patriarch, Venerable Saṃghanandin, was the prince of Ratnavyūha in the city of Śrāvastī.
From birth he was able to speak and constantly praised the Buddha’s deeds. At the age of seven, he grew weary of worldly pleasures and informed his parents, requesting to leave the home life.

At home, his parents firmly opposed him. He consequently went without food for an entire day. They finally permitted him to leave the household life while remaining at home, and he was named Saṃghanandi.
After nineteen years had passed, he would often think to himself, "I dwell in a royal palace; why have I left the household life?
One night, as a divine light shone down upon him, he saw a path that was level and smooth. Without realizing it, he walked slowly along it for about ten *li* until he reached a great [monastery].
Before the cliff was a stone cave, where he dwelt in tranquil seclusion. His parents searched for him but could not find him;
ten years passed until they encountered the Venerable Rāhulabhadra, who gave him instruction. Having attained the Dharma, he traveled to the kingdom of Mathurā to propagate the teachings.

Suddenly, a cool breeze swept over the assembly, bringing an extraordinary sense of joy and well-being to both body and mind. The Patriarch said, "This is the wind of the Way and its Virtue. There shall surely be..."

The Sage appeared in the world to succeed to the ancestral lamp. While traveling with his assembly through the mountains and valleys, he arrived at the foot of a peak and said to them, "There is purple cloud upon this peak, shaped like a canopy; a sage dwells there.

After they had lingered for a long time, they saw a young boy at a mountain cottage holding a round mirror, who went straight before the Patriarch. The Patriarch asked, "How old are you? He replied, "One hundred years. The Patriarch—

The Master said, "Your years are still few; why do you speak of a hundred years? The boy said, "I do not understand the principle; I am simply a hundred years old. The Master asked, "Are you skilled in the pivot [of the Dharma]?
The boy replied, "The Buddha said: 'If a person lives for a hundred years, yet does not understand the pivot of all Buddhas, it is better to live for a single day and attain such understanding.'"
If one were born for only a single day, one could attain definitive realization. When the parents heard their son’s words, they immediately renounced the world to follow him.
The Patriarch conferred full ordination upon him, naming him Gayāśata. Later, hearing the wind blowing the temple bells, the Patriarch asked, "Are the bells ringing, or is it the wind?
Śata replied, "It is neither the wind nor the bells; it is my own heart that is ringing. The Patriarch said, "Excellent! and immediately entrusted him with the Dharma.
Fayan. The verse says: "The ground of the mind is fundamentally unborn; the causal ground arises from conditions. Conditions and seeds do not obstruct one another;
so too it is with flowers and fruit. This was the seventeenth patriarch. The eulogy says:
Disliking the royal palace, Heaven opened a path for him; He traveled straight to the ultimate source, unaware of the reason why.
Beneath purple clouds, the Sage took his abode; He indeed met the young boy who understood the mechanism of all Buddhas.
The Eighteenth Patriarch, Venerable Gayasata, transmits [the Dharma].
The eighteenth patriarch, Venerable Gayasata, was a native of the kingdom of Mathura. His clan name was Udraka; his father was Devaśara and his mother was Bhadra.
She once dreamed that a great deity held up a mirror, and consequently she became pregnant. He was born after exactly seven days;
his body was as translucent as lapis lazuli, and though he never bathed, he remained naturally fragrant and pure. From childhood, he delighted in solitude and his speech was extraordinary.

As a youth, Bodhidharma went out for a stroll carrying a mirror and encountered Venerable Nandī, from whom he received ordination. Later, leading his disciples, he arrived at the kingdom of Greater Bactria (Mahāśakasthāna).
Seeing an unusual aura over a Brahmin’s house, the Patriarch was about to enter when the master of the house, Kumāralata, asked, "Who are these followers?
The Patriarch replied, "We are disciples of the Buddha. Upon hearing the name of the Buddha, Kumāralata’s mind and spirit were struck with awe.
He immediately closed the door. After a long while, Bodhidharma knocked on the door. Puṇyamitra said, "There is no one in this house. Bodhidharma said, "Who is it that says there is no one?

Upon hearing these words, Puṇyamitra realized he was an extraordinary person. He hurriedly opened the bolt and invited him inside. Bodhidharma said, "In the past, the World-Honored One made a prophecy, saying:
'One thousand years after my parinirvāṇa, a Great Being shall appear in the kingdom of Mo-ti (Mūlasthāna) to propagate and sustain [the Dharma]...'"

The Mysterious Transformation: Now you have encountered me; this is your response to this auspicious destiny. Thereupon, Kumārajīva awakened to the wisdom of his past lives and cast himself with sincerity into the monastic life.
His grandfather (the patriarch) performed the tonsure and ordination for him, conferring upon him the full precepts and the transmission of the Dharma.

He spoke this verse: "When there is the seed and the ground of the mind, Through causes and conditions, the sprout can emerge. If one does not obstruct these conditions, Then birth after birth shall be non-birth. This was the eighteenth patriarch. [End of] Praise.
It is said:
Born after seven days, yet not falling into the various aggregates; its substance is fragrant and pure, fundamentally pristine.
Who is it that, when the door is knocked, answers with silence? Suddenly awakened, one realizes the place of return in this very moment.
The Biography of the Nineteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kumāralāta.
The Nineteenth Patriarch, Venerable Kumāralāta, was the son of a Brahmin from the kingdom of Greater Yuezhi (Mahāśaka). In a former life, he was a celestial being of the Īśvara Heaven.

Upon seeing the jeweled ornaments (*ratnāvalī*) of a Bodhisattva, he suddenly conceived a heart of attachment and fell to be reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. There, he heard the [voice of] the Emperor...

He preached the Prajñāpāramitā and thus ascended to the Brahma Heaven. Because of his sharp faculties, he skillfully expounded the essential points of the Dharma, and all the devas honored him as their teacher.
When the time arrived to succeed to the Patriarchal lineage, he was consequently born in the country of Mo-zhi (Yuezhi), where he obtained the *śamatha* mind-seal.
Later, he traveled to the kingdom of Central India, where there was a Great Being named Śāyatā who asked: "In my family, my parents have long been faithful in the Three [Jewels]..."
Although he treasures [the Dharma], he is constantly afflicted by illness; his endeavors often do not accord with his wishes.

His neighbor is a *caṇḍāla* who makes a living through killing, yet his body is always robust and healthy, and his undertakings meet with success. "How fortunate is he, and what crime have I committed? Zu said: "Why is there need for such doubt?
Furthermore, the retribution for good and evil occurs across three periods of time. Ordinary people see only that the benevolent die young while the violent live long lives."
"Rebellion brings good fortune while righteousness brings misfortune. He then claimed that cause and effect do not exist and that sin and merit are empty.

Little did he know that shadows follow forms and that even a hair’s breadth of difference never fails; even after passing through hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, nothing is ever lost. Having heard these words, Śreṇika—

His doubts were instantly dispelled. The Patriarch said: "Although you have already gained faith in the three karmas, you have not yet clarified that karma arises from delusion, delusion exists dependent on consciousness, and consciousness depends upon non-awakening (avidyā).
Non-awakening depends upon the mind; the mind is fundamentally pure, without birth or extinction, and without fabrication."
There is no retribution; there is no victory or defeat. It is profoundly still and luminously aware. If you enter this Dharma-gate, you may be equal to all Buddhas.
All things—good and evil, conditioned and unconditioned—are like dreams and illusions. Śāyatā (Shenxiu) received these words and grasped their essential meaning;
he immediately awakened to his past wisdom and earnestly sought ordination. The Patriarch shaved his head and conferred upon him the full precepts, and then transmitted the Dharma to him.
The Eye. The verse says: "In its essential nature, there is fundamentally no arising; it is for the sake of those seeking [the truth] that the Dharma is taught.
Since nothing can be attained therein, why harbor doubts about what is or is not resolved? This is the nineteenth patriarch. The eulogy says:
Having been born in the heavens, one should not give rise to craving. If even a single thought is not forgotten, one will lack self-mastery;
it is through the power of Prajñā that one attains rebirth in the Brahma world. Thus, coming here to transmit the lamp is his family duty.
This concludes the transmission of the twenty-first patriarch, Venerable Śānavāsa.
The twentieth patriarch, Venerable Śāṇakavāsa, was a native of Northern India. His wisdom was profound and deep, and he transformed and guided immeasurable beings.
Later, he arrived at the city of Rājagṛha to propagate the teachings of the sudden enlightenment (Sudden Vehicle). There was a community of students there who valued debate above all else;

their leader was named Bhāṣu-paṇḍita, which translates as "Pervasive Practice" (Viśvabhu). He always ate only one meal a day and never lay down to sleep, performing prostrations during the six periods of the day.
The Buddha is pure and free from desire; he is the one to whom all beings turn. Before the Patriarch intended to save him, he first asked the assembly:
"This ascetic Pūrṇa is capable of practicing the Brahma-faring; can he attain the Way of the Buddha? The assembly replied, "Our teacher is diligent and persevering;

why should he not be able to do so? The Patriarch said, "Your teacher is far removed from the Way. Even if he were to practice austerities for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, it would all be the root of delusion."
The assembly asked, "Venerable sir, what virtues and practices do you possess that you should disparage our Master? The Patriarch replied, "I do not seek the Way, yet I am not inverted.
I do not prostrate to the Buddha, yet I do not treat him with contempt. I do not sit in perpetual meditation, yet I am not indolent.
I do not eat only once a day, yet I do not eat at improper times. I am not content, yet I have no greed. To have no expectations in the mind is what is called [the Way]."

He replied, "The Way. Having heard this, Viśvāmitra attained untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*), and with joy he offered praise. Upagupta said, "I have just now, before the assembly, humiliated you, my worthy friend. Are you not troubled by this?
Viśvāmitra replied, "I recall that for seven kalpas I was born in the Land of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).
The Teacher and the wise Moon-Pure (*Candraprabha*) prophesied to me that before long I would realize the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin. Since then, whenever I have heard [the Dharma]..."
"Various evil words are like the wind or an echo; how much more so now that you have obtained the drinking of the unsurpassed nectar—how could you instead give rise to feverish affliction?
I only pray that, out of great compassion, you will instruct me with the wondrous Way. The Patriarch said: "You have long planted manifold virtues and shall succeed to my lineage.
He then entrusted him with the Great Dharma-Eye, saying in verse: "When in accord with non-arising beneath a word, It is identical to the nature of the Dharma-realm. If one can..."
Thus is the understanding. Having completed the thorough penetration of phenomena and principle, this constitutes the twenty patriarchs.
The eulogy says: Non-arising is inherently present; there is no need to seek the truth. It manifests upon meeting conditions, like flowers blooming in spring.
To seek it with excessive urgency is to distance oneself further from the Way. Know the homecoming in the present moment and return by way of the path.
The Transmission of the Twenty-first Patriarch, Vairocana (Poxiandou).
The Twenty-first Patriarch, Vairocana, was a native of Rājagṛha. His clan name was Viśākha; his father was named Jyotiṣka and his mother was named Śuddhā.
The family was wealthy but childless, so the parents prayed at a Buddhist stūpa to seek an heir. One day—

One evening, his mother dreamed that she swallowed two pearls, one bright and one dark; upon waking, she found herself pregnant. After seven days had passed, an arhat named Xianzhong arrived at her home.

Guanggai presented him with the pearls and performed a ritual of homage. Xianzhong sat upright and accepted them, while Yan stepped forward to prostrate himself, whereupon Xianzhong rose from his seat to avoid him.
Guanggai could not fathom the reason for this and, unable to restrain himself, asked: "I am a man."

"Though he offered his respects, he did not look at me. What virtue does my wife possess that the Venerable One avoided her? The Worthy Second Brother replied, "I accepted his prostration and received the pearl;
it was only to bestow blessings upon you. Your wife carries a holy child who, when born, shall become a lamp for the world and a sun of wisdom. That is why I avoided her."
It was not that he held women in high regard; rather, he said, "Your wife shall give birth to two sons.
One shall be named Vasiṣṭha, whom I shall honor; the other shall be named Cūḍapanthaka. Long ago, when the Tathāgata was practicing the Way on Mount Himavat, a cūḍa-bird nested upon his head.
When the Buddha attained enlightenment, he prophesied: "In the second five-hundred-year period, you shall be born in the city of Rājagṛha as a Vaiśya..."
The Kāśyapa family were kinsmen of the Sage; now they have not failed him. Later, two sons were indeed born:

Vasiṣṭha-Panthaka was fifteen years old when he took ordination under the Arhat Prabhāsa, practicing the dhūta austerities. Subsequently, he received the Dharma-eye from Śayata and traveled to the kingdom of Nādikā to propagate the teachings.
The king of that country was named Nitya-Īśvara. When the Venerable One saw him, he said, "The Buddha prophesied—"
"In the second five-hundred-year period, there will be two great beings of supernormal power who will leave the household life to succeed the Sage;
one of them will be the king’s second son, Maṇḍara. Although my virtue is meager, I dare to take on his role.
The king said, "It is truly as the Venerable One has said. I shall renounce this son to become a śramaṇa. Thereupon, the king immediately renounced his second son, Maṇḍara.
The Venerable One immediately shaved his head, conferred the full precepts upon him, and entrusted him with the Great Dharma-Eye. He spoke in verse: "Bubbles and shadows are equally unimpeded;
why do you not awaken to this? To realize the Dharma within it—this is neither of the present nor of antiquity.
He was thus the twenty-first patriarch. The eulogy says:
Light and darkness share the same substance; the path of sages and ordinary beings is one and the same. The place of origin is profound and subtle, its cause unknown.
What is familiar is difficult to forget, so one seeks a companion. Suddenly meeting [him], the sincere mind grants its own assent.
(This name, Chuni, refers to the wild magpie; Xianzhong [is found] as "Zhong" in the Southern Canon.)
The Biography of the Twenty-second Patriarch, Venerable Maṇḍara:
The twenty-second patriarch, Venerable Maṇḍara, was the second son of King Nitya-vaśavartin of the country of Naṭika.
At the age of thirty, he encountered the Venerable Vasubandhu, left the household life, and received the transmission of the Dharma. He traveled to Western India, where the king was named Śatavāhana.

Upon seeing and paying homage to the Venerable, the king was moved to realization upon hearing the Dharma; he immediately abdicated the throne to his crown prince and entered the monastic order under the Patriarch.
After seven days, he realized the fruit of Arhatship. The Patriarch consoled him, saying: "You shall remain in this country and skillfully deliver others. Now, as for other regions..."
"There is a person of great Dharma-capacity; I shall go to transform him. Thereupon, the Patriarch burned incense and spoke from afar to the Bhikṣu Hui-le-na of the country of Mo-ti (Mūlasthāna):
"While you are in that country, instructing the flock of cranes, you are about to realize the fruit of the Path; you should know this for yourself."
At that time, Kṣānti was preaching a sūtra for the king of that country when he suddenly beheld a wondrous fragrance forming into tassels.
The king asked, "What omen is this? He replied, "This is the fragrant token sent in advance by the patriarch Mañjuśrī, who is coming from Western India to transmit the Buddha’s mind-seal.
The king asked, "How great is this master’s spiritual power? He replied, "This master has received the Buddha’s prophecy from afar."
While he was extensively proclaiming the profound transformation in this land, King [Kaniṣka] and Ratnamati both paid him homage from afar.
Knowing this, the Patriarch immediately departed for the country of Mo-ti (Yuezhi). The King and Ratnamati went out to welcome and invite him, providing offerings.
Ratnamati asked, "I have resided in the forest for nine white years; by what cause have I been moved by this flock of cranes? The Patriarch replied, "In a previous kalpa, you..."
Once, when you were a bhikṣu, you were about to go to the Dragon Palace for a meal offering.

Your disciples all wished to accompany you there, yet among those five hundred followers, you observed that not a single person was fit to serve as an attendant. You granted them permission to go on this journey.

Since then, as you have abandoned one life and entered another, you have constantly traveled through various kingdoms to transform beings. Because their merit is meager, those disciples have been born [into such states].
The feathered species, now moved by his kindness, followed him in a flock of cranes. Le-na asked, "By what skillful means can you cause them to attain liberation?
The Patriarch said, "I possess the unsurpassed Dharma-treasure; I shall entrust it to you. You must listen and receive this transformation for as long as the future endures.

Then he spoke this verse: "The mind turns following the myriad objects; where it turns, it is truly profound. If, while following the current, one recognizes one's own nature, there is no more sorrow."
There was also no sorrow. Upon hearing the verse, the flock of cranes flew away, crying out. This was the twenty-second patriarch. The eulogy says:
From the time he received the prediction, he did not engage in any other affairs; Those of a similar kind followed one another, and when conditions converged, they inevitably met.
Alas for that flock of cranes, who had been flying and crying for so long; Under a single word, they suddenly realized their inherent nature.
(One Indian year constitutes one *śveta*).
The Transmission of the Twenty-third Patriarch, Venerable Huike Na (Hulena). (*Hulena* is the Sanskrit term; in the language of China, it means "crane").
The Twenty-third Patriarch, Venerable Hulena, was a native of the country of Yuezhi. His clan was Brahmin. His father was Qian...
The Holy Mother, Jinguang, having no offspring, prayed before the Golden Pillars of the Seven Buddhas.
She then dreamed of a divine youth atop Mount Sumeru holding a golden ring who said, "I have come. Upon waking, she conceived.

When she gave birth and the child was seven years old, he wandered through the villages and, seeing a vulgar shrine among the common folk, entered the temple and rebuked it, saying, "You falsely conjure calamity and fortune to delude and mislead people..."

People annually expended livestock for sacrifices, causing immense injury and harm. As soon as he finished speaking, the temple structure suddenly collapsed. Consequently, the local community called him "The Holy Son.
At the age of twenty-two, he left the household life; at thirty, he met the Venerable Maṇiratha, who transmitted to him the treasury of the Dharma-eye.
He traveled to Central India to propagate the Unsurpassed Way, delivering those with karmic affinity and establishing them as his foremost disciples.
