Longzi died young. He had an elder brother, Simha, who was widely learned and possessed a powerful memory.
He served a Brahmin, but when his teacher passed away and his younger brother subsequently died, he took refuge with the Venerable One. He asked, "I wish to seek the Way; how should I apply my mind?

The Patriarch said, "If you wish to seek the Way, there is no place for the mind to be applied. He asked, "If there is no application of the mind, who performs the work of a Buddha? The Patriarch said:
"If you have any purposeful action, it is not merit. If you are without activity, that is itself the work of the Buddha.
The Sūtra says: "The merit I have performed is devoid of 'mine-ness' (mama-kāra). Having heard these words, Śiṃha immediately entered the wisdom of the Buddha.
At that time, the Patriarch pointed toward the northeast and asked, "What kind of phenomenon is this? Śiṃha replied, "I see a vapor like a white rainbow piercing through [the sky]."
"Furthermore, there are five paths of black vapor stretching horizontally across the heavens and the earth. The Patriarch asked, "What does this omen portend?
He replied, "It cannot be known. The Patriarch said, "Fifty years after my passing, a calamity shall arise in the kingdom of Northern India."
"Ying is within your body; I am about to pass away. Now, I entrust the Dharma-eye to you. Guard and uphold it well. Listen to my verse:
'When the nature of mind is recognized, it may be called inconceivable. It is clearly present yet cannot be grasped;
when attained, one does not speak of knowing. This was the twenty-third patriarch. The eulogy states:
From the summit of Mount Sumeru, he came bearing a golden ring; alas for that flock of cranes, their plight is pitiable.
Having obtained a lion cub, it let out a great roar; with a vital breath piercing the heavens, its lineage was tested.
Thus was transmitted the twenty-fourth patriarch, the Venerable Siṃha.
The twenty-fourth patriarch, Bhikṣu Siṃha, was a native of Central India. A Brahmin by birth, he attained the Dharma and traveled abroad.
Upon reaching the kingdom of Kaśmīra, he sought a successor for the Dharma. There he encountered an elder who led his son forward and addressed the patriarch, saying:
"This child’s name is Sīta. At birth, he clenched his left hand in a fist; now that he has grown, he is still unable to open it.
I pray that the Venerable One will reveal the karmic cause from his past life. The Patriarch looked at him and, reaching out his hand, said, "Give me back my pearl.
The boy immediately opened his hand and presented the pearl. The assembly was all struck with wonder. The Patriarch said, "In my previous existence, I was a monk. There was a boy named..."
“Vaspa. I once attended a vegetarian feast at the Western Sea and received this pearl as an offering (*dakṣiṇā*), which I entrusted to you. It is only natural that you now return my pearl.
The elder then relinquished his son, and the Patriarch immediately conferred full ordination upon him. Because of these prior conditions, he was named Vasubandhu (Vaspa-siddha).
The Patriarch then said to him, “My master had a secret prophetic prediction: you will encounter hardship before long. Regarding the Tathāgata’s True Dharma...”
"The Eye-Treasury is now transmitted to you; you should protect it so that it universally moistens all future ages. A verse says:

"When correctly explaining knowing and seeing, both knowing and seeing are the mind. When the mind is present, there is knowing and seeing; knowing and seeing are right here and now. Having spoken this verse, the Patriarch said:
He secretly entrusted his *saṃghāṭī* robe to Sthavira, instructing him to go to another country and transform beings according to their capacities.
Having received these instructions, Sthavira traveled directly to South India. The Patriarch said, "It is impossible to evade destiny. He then remained in Kaśmīra.

In his own country, two non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) plotted a rebellion using sorcery; they disguised themselves as monks and secretly entered the royal palace, intending to bring about disaster. The rebellion—
When this was done, King Gopa said in anger, "I have long since placed my heart's devotion in the Triple Gem; why then do you plot such harm?

He immediately ordered the destruction of the saṃghārāma and the expulsion of the Śākya community. The king himself took up his sword and went to the Venerable One’s dwelling, asking, "Has the Master realized the emptiness of the aggregates?"
The Patriarch said, "I have already attained it. The King said, "You may give me your head. The Patriarch said, "My body is not mine; why should I begrudge my head? The King then beheaded him.
White milk gushed forth to a height of several feet, and the King’s arm also fell off. He died seven days later. The eulogy says:
Upon meeting, he asked for the pearl; as soon as the hand was opened, it was there.

Because he knew that a debt from former times remained unpaid not long after their last parting, he had come specifically to repay it. When he placed his head before the blade, white milk flowed profusely.
This is the transmission of the twenty-fifth patriarch, Venerable Vasishṭha.
The twenty-fifth patriarch, Vasiṣṭha, was a native of Kaśmīra. His clan was Brahmin; his father was named Śāntacaryā and his mother, Nityasukhā.
Initially, his mother dreamed that she obtained a divine sword and subsequently conceived. When he was born, his left hand remained clenched in a fist.
He encountered the Venerable Siṃha, who revealed his past causes and secretly transmitted the Heart-Seal (cittamudrā) to him.

He then departed for South India, where the king, named Devaśrī, welcomed and made offerings to him. The king had two sons: the first was named Guṇottara, who was fierce and violent yet possessed great physical vigor;
the second was named Ratnamitra, who was gentle and mild but had suffered from chronic illness since childhood. The Patriarch then explained [the matter] to them.

Regarding cause and effect, the King immediately resolved his doubts. Later, when De-sheng ascended the throne, he again believed in non-Buddhist paths (tīrthikas) and posed difficult challenges to the Patriarch.

When he failed to respond as expected, Mi-dui offered counsel, whereupon he was imprisoned. The King suddenly questioned the Patriarch, saying, "My kingdom has long been free from such demonic deceptions."
The King asked, "What school of thought does that which you have transmitted belong to? The Patriarch replied, "In this kingdom, there has never been any heterodox teaching.
That which I have attained is precisely the Buddha’s school. The King said, "It has been twelve hundred years since the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa; from whom did you receive it?"
The Patriarch said, "The Mahāsattva Kāśyapa personally received the Buddha’s seal; it was transmitted successively down to the twenty-fourth generation, the Venerable Siṃha, from whom I received it.
The King asked, "I have heard that the Bhikṣu Siṃha could not escape execution;
how, then, could he transmit the Dharma to future generations? The Patriarch replied, "When my teacher faced danger, he secretly bestowed upon me the robe of faith and the Dharma verses."
To manifest his lineage, the King asked, "Where is that robe? The Patriarch immediately took the robe out from within his bag and showed it to the King. The King ordered it to be burned;
though the five colors remained vividly distinct, the robe was as it was before the wood had been consumed. The King then felt remorse and paid him homage.

Since it was now clear that Siṃha was the true successor, he pardoned Guptadatta. Guptadatta subsequently requested ordination; the Patriarch shaved his head, conferred the full precepts (*upasampadā*), and performed the *karmavācanā*.
At that moment, the earth shook violently. The Patriarch said, "I am already worn out by age; I now entrust the treasury of the Great Dharma Eye to you.
You must protect and cherish it. He then spoke this verse for me to hear: "The Sages speak of knowledge and vision, Yet within the objective realm there is neither right nor wrong.
I have now realized the true nature: There is neither the Way, nor is there principle. Thus he became the twenty-fifth patriarch. The eulogy says:
Wielding the sword of Prajñā and grasping the wish-fulfilling jewel, though it is said he has only arrived here for a brief moment, his practice is not in vain.
Even if he encounters an evil person, he finds a fine companion; by using the crooked to strike the straight, both find their advantage.
This is the transmission of the twenty-sixth patriarch, Venerable Ratnamitra.
The twenty-sixth patriarch, Venerable Ratnamitra, was the second son of King Devaśrī of South India.
Having received the Dharma-seal from Venerable Vāsava, he traveled to East India. There, the king was named Sthira and followed the non-Buddhist teacher, the Brahmin Dīrghanakha.
When the Venerable Patriarch was about to arrive, the Brahmin foresaw his entry and feared that the king would change his convictions.

He immediately gathered his disciples, intending to defeat [the Master] with incantations. When the Venerable One arrived, he went straight to the King’s residence. The King asked, "For what purpose has the Master come?
The Patriarch replied, "I have come to deliver sentient beings. The King asked, "By what dharma do you deliver them? The Patriarch replied, "I deliver them according to their kind.
Upon hearing these words, the Brahmin could not contain his rage; he immediately employed illusory arts (*māyā*) to conjure a great mountain upon the Patriarch's head.
[The Master] pointed upward. Suddenly, it crushed the assembly. The Brahmans and others, struck with fear, threw themselves at the Master for refuge.

Out of pity for their ignorance and delusion, the Master pointed upward once more; the mountain was transformed and vanished accordingly. He then expounded the essentials of the Dharma for the King, leading him toward the True Vehicle.
Thereupon, he said to the King: "In this country, there shall be a sage who will succeed me. At that time, there was the son of a Brahman, [who was] of such an age...

He was about twenty years old when he lost his parents at a young age; their names were unknown. He sometimes called himself "Yingluo" (Adorned with Necklaces), so people referred to him as the "Yingluo Boy.
He wandered through the streets and neighborhoods, begging for his daily sustenance.

Later, when the King and the Venerable One were traveling out together in the same carriage, they saw the Yingluo Boy bowing his head before them. The Master asked, "Do you remember past events? The boy replied, "I..."
He recalled that in the distant past, he had lived together with his teacher. While the teacher expounded the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, he himself had recited profound *sūtras*.
Today’s events were clearly in accord with their long-standing karmic affinity. The Patriarch said to the King, "This boy is no other than the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
After this boy, two more shall appear: one will transform the southern region of India, and the other..."
In China, because of his past causes, he was named Prajñātāra. He then entrusted him with the Great Dharma-Eye Treasury, saying in verse:
"The treasury of the true nature of the mind-ground has neither head nor tail; responding to conditions to transform beings, it is expediently called 'wisdom.
He was thus the twenty-sixth patriarch. The eulogy says:
The lineage was transmitted from the Kṣatriya caste like the succession of a lamp’s flame; because the true heir was not clearly identified, it nearly fell into ruin.
Suddenly, amidst the clamor of the marketplace, he heard of an old friend; when the container and its lid met, he finally attained the truth.
This is the transmission of the twenty-seventh patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra.
The twenty-seventh patriarch, Venerable Prajñātāra, was a native of Eastern India. Having attained the Dharma, he traveled to South India to propagate the teachings.
There, the king, named Gandhāra, venerated the Buddha-vehicle and honored him with offerings that surpassed those of all others.
He also bestowed upon him a priceless jewel. At that time, the king had three sons: Candravairocana, Śrīcandra, and [the third].

Dharmatara—his name means "Dharma-Extensive"—was the youngest of the bodhisattvas. His grandfather wished to test what he had attained, so he took the pearls that had been bestowed upon him and asked the three princes:
"These pearls are perfectly round and luminous; is there anyone who can equal them?

The first and second sons both replied, "Among the seven treasures, these pearls are the most honored; certainly nothing surpasses them. Were it not for the power of your majesty's Way, who could [do otherwise]?"
He accepted it. Jizi said, "This is a worldly treasure, but it is not the supreme one. Among all treasures, the Treasure of Dharma is supreme.
This is a worldly light, but it is not the supreme one. Among all lights, the Light of Wisdom is supreme.
This is a worldly clarity, but it is not the supreme one. Among all clarities, the Clarity of Mind is supreme. The radiance of this pearl cannot [illuminate itself]."
Zhao remarked, "One must rely on the light of wisdom to be able to discern this. The Patriarch marveled at his eloquence and wisdom and knew him to be his Dharma heir;

however, as the time was not yet ripe, he remained silent and kept him among the common monks. When King Xiang reached the end of his life and passed away, the entire assembly wailed and fainted with grief.

Only Dharmatrāta entered into meditative absorption before the coffin and emerged after seven days, whereupon he requested ordination. Only then did the Patriarch grant him the tonsure and full ordination.
He conferred the full precepts upon him and said: "In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa;
thus it was passed down in succession until it reached me. I now entrust it to you. Listen to my verse: 'The mind-ground gives rise to all seeds;
from conditions, the principle is further produced. When the fruit is full, Bodhi is perfected; when the flower opens, the world arises. This is the twenty-seventh patriarch. (Praise)
It is said:
Do not say that meeting by chance is without cause; the place of origin is natural and requires no expedient means.
Now, because of this pearl, one finds the person; when the pond is opened, the moon is found; when the stone is purchased, the clouds abound.
Biographies and Eulogies of the Eighty-Eight Patriarchs, Volume One;
Biographies and Eulogies of the Eighty-Eight Patriarchs, Volume Two.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Deqing of Mount Huánglú (Kāṅ-lu).
Recorded by Gao Chengshan, retired official of Xiushui;
supplemented by Qian Yingjin, superior scholar of Jiaxing;
compared with the *Biography of the Venerable Kangju*.
Kang Senghui was the son of the Grand Chancellor of the kingdom of Kangju. Having renounced the world in that country, he possessed divine and extraordinary powers.
He once gazed toward the land of Zhendan and saw a light illuminating the heavens, saying, "This is the radiance of the Buddha’s *śarīra*. Thereupon, he followed the light and arrived in Wu.
In the fourth year of the Chihu era, he reached Jinling and stayed in Changzhu Li, where he built a thatched hut and established an image of the Buddha.
He was walking along the road. When the people of the country first saw the śramaṇa, they regarded him as strange and reported it to the authorities.

Emperor Sun Quan of Wu said, "Is this the lingering influence of the Buddha's Way, of which Emperor Ming of Han dreamed? He issued an edict for [Kāśyapa] Mātaṅga to come and questioned him regarding his circumstances.

Mātaṅga replied, "The Great Master Tathāgata entered parinirvāṇa more than a thousand years ago. Nevertheless, his sacred relics and śarīras manifest divine responses in manifold ways. Formerly, King Aśoka..."

The King honored this and constructed eighty-four thousand stupas; this was the legacy of his transformative influence. Sun Quan, wishing to boast of his own prowess, said, "If the śarīra can be obtained, I shall have stupas built for them.
If it proves otherwise, there shall be the state's regular punishment. Zhihui requested that an altar be established to seek them, setting a seven-day deadline.
When there was no result after seven days, he extended the period by another fourteen days. Still there was no result. Sun Quan said, "Go ahead and boil them. Zhihui remained silent.
"Reciting the Buddha’s name is true compassion; how could it contravene my vow? Please grant me another seven days. At the fifth watch of the night, he heard a resonant sound.
Rising to look into the jar, he saw light flashing forth in various colors. At dawn, he presented it, and Quan, along with the high officials, gathered to observe it.

They sighed in admiration, saying, "This is an auspicious omen rarely seen in the world. Hui then further remarked, "The majestic spiritual power of the śarīra [relics] transcends all in the world..."
In the meantime, there was no one able to damage it. Even when a strong man used a hammer to strike it on an anvil, its radiance remained as it was.
Thereupon, a stupa was erected for it in the Fotuo Ward of Jianye, and a monastery was also built where it was enshrined; it was named Jianchu Monastery.
This is the present-day Dabaoen Temple, which marks the beginning of pagoda-temples in the region south of the Yangtze River. The eulogy states:
The *dharmakāya* relics pervade the entire earth; Their radiance shines everywhere, leaving no place untouched.
A supreme being followed this light and arrived, Earnestly entreating its manifestation; thus the Buddhist monastery was first opened.
The Biography of the Meditation Master Fotudeng of the Buddha Temple.
The Indian monk Fotudeng arrived at Luoyang and claimed to be over one hundred years old. He often went for many days without eating and was skilled in reciting incantations.
He could command spirits and deities; there was a hole by his side which he plugged with cotton wool, and at night he would pull out the wool, from which light emerged.
He illuminated his chamber. Whenever he went to the stream, he would take out his intestines and stomach to wash them, then return them to his belly.

He could hear the sound of bells and speak of good or ill fortune; there was nothing that did not prove wondrously accurate. During the rebellion in Luoyang, he hid among the weeds to observe the changing times.

At that time, Shi Le was stationed at Gepo and was committing many acts of slaughter. Fo Tucheng went to visit Le with his staff and almsbowl. Le tested him with his supernatural arts; Tucheng took a full—
He consecrated the water in his alms bowl with a mantra, whereupon a blue lotus flower suddenly sprang up within it, its radiance outshining the sun.
Shi Le, moved by this divine reverence, invited him into his military camp. When Shi Le assumed the title of King of Zhao and acted as the Emperor, his devotion to Fotudeng became even more profound.

After Shi Le passed away, his younger brother Shijia Jilong succeeded him on the throne and moved the capital to Ye City; he devoted himself even more earnestly to Fotudeng, ordering him to ride in an ornate palanquin during court assemblies.

He was led for an audience. The Attendant Censor and others all assisted in lifting the palanquin as he ascended the hall. The Crown Prince and the various dukes supported him from the sides as he moved forward. Those seated all rose.
An edict was issued for the Minister of Works, Li Nong, to inquire after his health every morning and evening. At that time, Zhi Daolin heard of this and said:
"Does Master Cheng consider Shi Jilong to be a sea gull? Jilong then asked, "The Buddha-dharma prohibits killing, yet I, Your Majesty, preside over life and death for the empire.
I fear I may be violating the Buddha's precepts. Cheng replied, "When a sovereign serves the Buddha, it lies in being reverent, frugal, compassionate, and patient;
in manifesting and praising the Way of the Buddha; in not committing acts of cruelty, and in not harming innocent people. If there are those who do evil, transform them through instruction."

"How could one who has repented not be punished? However, executions must not be indiscriminate, and punishments must be tempered with compassion. When he was about to depart from this world, he went to take his leave.
Shi Jilong said in astonishment, "Does the Great Monk suddenly wish to abandon me? Fotudeng replied, "To be born is to enter death."

"This is the constant nature of the Way. Longevity and brevity are fixed by destiny; there is no way to increase or diminish them. However, the Way prizes the completion of practice, and virtue prizes lack of indolence.
If one's virtue is without blemish, though one dies, it is as if one lives. If [the body] possesses none of this, what benefit is there in ten thousand years?
Having finished speaking, he sat upright and passed away. Later, a monk came from Yongzhou and reported that Fotudeng had entered the Guanzhong region. Shi Jilong then opened the tomb.
Upon looking, there was found only a block of stone. The eulogy says:
The actions of the Perfect Man, whether hidden or manifest, cannot be fathomed. His entire being is luminous, yet his function remains distinct.
Entering and exiting the Imperial Court like a bird familiar with seagulls, He departs freely and returns as he came, following the Way.
The Biography of Chan Master Huiyuan of Donglin.
Chan Master Huiyuan of Donglin, whose name was Huìyuǎn, was a native of Lóufán in Yànmén. His surname was Jiǎ. In his youth, he studied as a Confucian scholar;
he read widely across all books and was particularly profound in his mastery of the *Zhouyi*, *Laozi*, and *Zhuangzi*. He once accompanied his younger brother, Huìchí, to visit Dharma Master Dào’ān.
Upon hearing a lecture on the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he attained sudden enlightenment. He sighed in admiration, saying, "The divergent theories of the nine schools are nothing more than mere chaff.
Thereupon, he and his younger brother Huichi cast off their hairpins [to leave secular life] and studied under Master Dao’an. Among the several thousand disciples, he occupied the foremost seat.
Master Dao’an once remarked to the assembly, "As for making the Way flow to the eastern lands, it must be due to Huiyuan. Later, the Master followed Master Dao’an.
He traveled to Xiangyang. Encountering times of turmoil, Master Dao’an’s disciples were scattered as they parted ways at the crossroads;

all received his instruction and benefit, yet the Master alone did not hear a single word from him. He immediately knelt and requested, saying, "If I am alone without your exhortation, I fear I am no longer human.
Master Dao’an said, "As for one such as you, what more is there to worry about? The Master then traveled east to Jin, reaching Xunyang, where he beheld Mount Lu and took a liking to it. Thereupon—
Stop. Huìyǒng of Lóngquán Jīngshè previously resided at Xīlín; the Master then established a monastery to the east, which was called Dōnglín.

During the period of its construction, a mountain deity manifested his spirit. That evening there was heavy rain and thunder; when dawn broke, fine timbers and rare materials were arrayed in that place.
He then constructed the main hall, naming it Shényùn (Divine Transport). At that time, many of the world’s most talented men under the Jin dynasty...
Living in seclusion and refusing office, he heard of the Way of Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu, and all came to follow him.
The Master said to Liu Chengzhi and the others, "If you gentlemen should have a journey to the Pure Land, you must exert yourselves with diligence.

Thereupon, they collectively resolved their wills and made a vow before Amitābha Buddha, aspiring to be born in the Pure Land. Consequently, they gathered eighteen eminent worthies to form a society for the practice of *nianfo* (Buddha-recitation).
The total number of followers reached one hundred and twenty-three. They formed an alliance to devote their minds to pure practice (*śukla-karma*).
Only Tao Yuanming was addicted to wine; hearing that there was no wine in the mountains, he knit his brows and departed. Xie Lingyun excavated two ponds to plant lotuses.
The monk Huiyao carved twelve leaves of lotus flowers to float upon the water in order to determine the passage of time; this was called the "Lotus Water-Clock" (Lianlou).
To this day, the Pure Land school has seven patriarchs, and Master Huiyuan of Donglin is considered the first patriarch. The eulogy says:
With vast aspirations and lofty intent, his mind roamed through the Pure Land; he first established the tradition in the Eastern Land as its inaugural step.
The clear sounds of the lotus-hour bell and its flowing melodies continue to this day; among all who hear them, there are none whose hearts do not turn in devotion. Appendix:

Eulogies for the Ten Patriarchs of the Lotus School by Yu Chunchi of Qiantang (Formerly there were only seven patriarchs; with the enshrinement of three more at this time, they are called the Ten Patriarchs).
The First Patriarch of Mount Lu, Master Bianjue Zhengjue Yuanwu (Master Huiyuan, disciple of Master Dao’an):
The Venerable Yuan opened the school and first clarified the essentials of the mind; his image floated as his spirit moved, gathering the worthy and harmonizing with the subtle;
his dream divided the ocean of Dharma into ten branches, bringing pure illumination; the fame of the Lotus Society shall endure forever for a thousand autumns.
The Second Patriarch, Dharma Master Guangming of Chang’an (whom Shandao said was an emanation of Amitābha), manifested a body of weariness as a guide for beings.
When his strength failed and sweat flowed, he abandoned sleep and left his mat;
from his mouth issued billions of rays of light that welcomed people according to their voices. His lamp continued for immeasurable ages, carrying forward the causes of his practice.
The Third Patriarch, Master Banzhou (Chengyuan) of Mount Nanyue:
His disciples served emperors by prostrating from afar; he accepted coarse food and discarded money and grain upon the grass and soil;

through diligent exhortation, he led others to single-minded recitation as a preeminent teacher of universal salvation; wearing humble robes, he attended the Buddha, opening the way for the vast realm.
The Fourth Patriarch, Dharma Master Wuhui of Chang’an (the reincarnation of Fazhao and Shandao; his lineage from Huiyuan is recorded below).

Master Fazhao was the founder of the teaching who relied upon the Seven Buddhas as his teachers. He divided the lamp of the *Avataṃsaka* and transmitted its resonance both within and without the imperial palace.
His vows for the Five Assemblies were inconceivable; having realized supreme enlightenment, he suddenly returned to the Western Pond.
The Fifth Patriarch newly established Master Tairan (Shao Kang):
Master Tairan, Lord Kang, comes from An-yang; Qian Yu leads a thousand children, their mouths spitting forth ten thousand phenomena.
He emits light as he departs toward the West; one ray of light is not two. Born, he has long been born; departing, he truly does not depart.
The Sixth Patriarch, Chan Master Yongming Yanshou (Biography by Yan Shou, appearing below):
Yongming’s spirit dwells in the precious realm of the boundless; The myriad virtues all return to the One. In seven lifetimes he followed favorable conditions;

The Mirror of the Source (Zongjing) subsumes all forms. With robes tucked in his armpits, he sat in meditation; Ding Guang testified to him with his own mouth: "You are a Buddha. He entered the marketplace to dwell among the common people.
The Seventh Patriarch, Dharma Master Zhaoking Yuanjing (Shengchang), was born in Qiantang;
his subtle essence dwelt at West Lake’s Furi Temple. His pure conduct and companions were honored by high officials, ministers, and provincial governors.
Far-reaching, he was likened to Mount Kuang; yet who in recent times has truly entered his chamber? His returning radiance and intersecting light are neither two nor one.
The Eighth Patriarch, Zen Master Tianmu Zhongfeng (Mingben; biography follows):
Zhongfeng stood upon the earth as Amitābha, Praising his own original nature as the Buddha of Infinite Light.
Having realized the half-verse, he further expounded a hundred chapters; His radiance soared through Nanzhao, returning to preside over the Land of Bliss.
The Ninth Patriarch, Chan Master Chushi (Fanqi) of Tianning:
His literary prowess was renowned within the imperial palace; The Three Contemplations and a hundred poems reached all quarters.
With eyes beholding the sublime lotus, his pure light spread far and wide; Whether in the East or West, amidst existence or non-existence, he let out a single shout as he departed.
The Tenth Patriarch, Master Yunqi Lianchi (Zhu Hong; biography follows):
Lianchi proclaimed the principle early on, protecting the Muni’s secrets; He manifested as an ordinary person with conduct like that of an infant.

Turning his thoughts back to his own nature, he then composed verses in response to me; His commentaries and sub-commentaries are like a double-mandorla, their radiance shining from the setting sun in the west.
The Biography of the Chan Master Baozhi Gong Dashi:

The Great Being Baozhi Gong was originally a commoner from Dongyang in Jinling. He was the son of a woman of the Zhu family who, on the Shangsi festival day, heard the crying of a child within an eagle’s nest.
She climbed the tree and retrieved him, raising him as her own son. At the age of seven, he entered the service of a śramaṇa at Mount Zhongshan.
Sengjian left the household life and later manifested his spiritual traces. He hung a pair of scissors, a ruler, and a whisk upon the tip of his staff and traveled while carrying it.
Thus he came and went beneath Mount Xuan and the Jian River, with hair unshorn and walking barefoot, wearing a brocade robe; the common people called him Zhigong.
His face was square and as clear and translucent as a mirror; his hands and feet both had bird-like talons. As he walked through the villages, the children...
The crowd clamored and pursued him. At times he would secretly seek wine; at other times he would not eat for several days. Once, encountering someone eating minced fish, he asked for some.
The eater shared some with him, but with a frivolous mind, Zhì immediately spat it into the water, where it all became live fish.

From time to time he composed poems that were initially unintelligible, yet later they all came true. Emperor Wu of the Qi dynasty, enraged that the Great Being was deluding the masses, had him arrested.
He was taken into custody. On that day, the people of the country all saw the Great Being wandering through the marketplace;

yet upon investigation, he was still within the prison. Thereafter, there were many such miraculous occurrences. In the early years of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, an edict was issued for the Great Being Baozhi:

"His traces are constrained by dust and grime, yet his spirit wanders in profound stillness. Fire and water cannot scorch or moisten him; snakes and tigers cannot harm or frighten him. Regarding his speech—
Regarding Buddhist principles, they pertain to those above the level of the Śrāvakas; regarding the discourse on their reclusion, it concerns those who have transcended as high-ranking immortals.

How can one harbor groundless suspicions and inhibitions based on worldly laws and ordinary sentiments? From this day forward, both within and outside [the court], you are permitted to propagate the teachings as you see fit. The Emperor then commanded Zhang Sengyou—
When he was painting an image of Mahāsattva, his hand would not find its mark as soon as he took up the brush. Zhi himself used his finger to scratch a division across his face;
from it emerged the twelve faces of Avalokiteśvara, their wondrous features exceptionally beautiful, yet he ultimately could not paint them.

One day, while with the Emperor, they gazed out over the river. An object was coming upstream; the Master drew it toward them with his staff until it arrived—it was a piece of purple sandalwood. He then...
He was entrusted with the task of carving a portrait statue, which he completed in an instant; its divine spirit appeared as if alive.

Whenever the Emperor questioned him about matters of state, he would provide predictions in advance that no one could understand. When the Emperor asked whether his reign would encounter difficulties, the Master pointed to his own neck.
His intention was aimed at Hou Jing. He had previously selected his own burial site on Mount Zhong. Zhan said:
"The traces of the Perfected One are hidden and cannot be known; From where did he come? He became the offspring of a hawk.
Wandering through the world, no one can fathom him. He has torn away the mask of the face—what further need is there to speak?"
The Supplement to the Biography of National Teacher Huiyue of Zhiyi:
National Teacher Huiyue of Zhiyi, whose courtesy name was Desu, was surnamed Lou and was a native of Wushang in Dongyang.

His mother, Lady Liu, dreamed of a tall man holding a golden image and making her swallow it; she also saw purple flowers encircling her body, and from this she became pregnant. She then became aware [of the pregnancy].
His spirit was refreshed and his intellect became clear and enlightened. On the day of his birth, light and fragrance filled the air. From childhood, he took Buddhist rites as his play.
Seeing the local custom of raising silkworms, he refused to wear silk or floss. His paternal uncle was fond of hunting; although [the boy] repeatedly exhorted him to change, the uncle did not do so.
Consequently, [the boy] completely renounced meat and pungent flavors. One night, his uncle dreamed of a messenger in red robes holding a spear and halberd, who said to him:

He said, "You have been killing living beings all day long. When the Bodhisattva tried to convert you, you would not comply; he seized you to bring you to your death, which so startled you that sweat poured from you.
Because of this, you changed your occupation. Later, you wished to leave secular life but did not know where to go. Suddenly you saw a monk and questioned him;

the monk pointed eastward and said, 'The Buddha-dharma is very flourishing in Shan. You then lost sight of him and realized it was a divine manifestation. At the age of seventeen, he finally received the tonsure.

He shaved his hair at Dongshan Temple in Shangyu and served the śramaṇa Huìjìng of Nanlin. When Huìjìng passed away, [Huishou] dwelt in mountain caves and abstained from grain, subsisting only on pine and yu-she (dipsacus).
Zhōu Yōng, the Palace Secretary of the Qi dynasty, established Cǎotáng Temple for him to reside in.
The Grand Chancellor Chù Yuǎn and the Grand Marshal Wáng Jiǎn both requested that he expound the Dharma. Once, while Yuǎn was suffering from an illness, he saw a foreign monk who said: "Bodhi..."
Sengzang was about to arrive. Before long, the Master arrived, and the illness suddenly cleared up. Sengzang immediately requested to receive the five precepts.
The room where the Master resided was often filled with a wondrous fragrance, and fierce beasts would tread familiarly upon his steps; such spiritual wonders cannot be fully recounted.

When Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty greatly promoted the Dharma of the Precepts, he invited the Master to serve as his *ācārya* (preceptor), honoring him with the title "The Wise One" (*Zhìzhě*). The Crown Prince, various princes, high officials, and the monastic and lay communities all followed him.

The Master’s recipients of the precepts numbered forty-eight thousand. At the time of the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), there were once two male magpies and two peacocks that would come together to listen.
When the Emperor personally received the Bodhisattva Great Precepts, from then on, whenever he entered the hall for an audience, a separate lacquered couch was prepared;

the Emperor would first perform a prostration and only then take his seat. As the Master was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, fragrant incense filled the entire Dharma-realm. Having finished exhorting the assembly, the Master [passed away]. The [text] concludes.
He transformed [the cow] with his palm. The Emperor came in person to bid him farewell and wept bitterly for him. He decreed that [Baizigong] be buried to the left of the Baizigong Stūpa.
The green ox he had ridden bellowed and shed tears without ceasing. At the beginning of the stūpa’s construction, a pair of white cranes circled the stūpa, crying mournfully;
they did not depart until after the burial. The eulogy says:

This Great Bodhisattva manifested in the form of a bhikṣu; His precepts arose from his very nature—how could his supernormal powers not be perfected through cultivation? Acting as a teacher to emperors and a master of transformation, Master Zhigong was his neighbor, while the white crane soared and danced. The twenty-eighth patriarch, the Great Master Bodhidharma, was the third son of King Xiangzhi of South India.
After Prajñātāra had transmitted the Dharma to him, he said to him: "Wait sixty-seven years after my passing."

"You must go to China to administer the great medicine of the Dharma, directly reaching those of the highest faculties. Be careful not to travel too hastily; you would suffer decline under the sun [of that land].
While the Master was propagating the teachings in the kingdom, after a long time he felt that the conditions for China had ripened. He then went to the seashore and boarded a merchant vessel."

In the first year of the Datong era of the Liang dynasty, he arrived at the South Sea. The Regional Inspector Xiao Ang submitted a memorial reporting his arrival, and an imperial decree was issued for him to have an audience.
The Emperor asked, "I have built temples, transcribed scriptures, and ordained monks; what merit do these acts possess? The Master replied, "They possess no merit whatsoever. The Emperor said:
"Why do they lack merit? The Master said, "These are merely the minor fruits of humans and devas; they are causes of outflow (āsrava). The Emperor asked, "What is true merit?
The Master said, "Pure wisdom is wondrously perfect; its essence is inherently empty and quiescent.
Such merit is not to be sought through worldly means. The Emperor asked, "What is the primary meaning of the Noble Truths? The Master said, "It is vast emptiness, devoid of anything at all."
The Emperor said, "Who is it that stands before me? The Master replied, "I do not know. The Emperor did not realize the truth.

Knowing his opportunity was not yet ripe for harmony, the Master crossed the river and entered Wei, staying at Shaolin Temple on Mount Song. There he sat in wall-gazing all day long. At that time, there was a monk named Shen Guang who heard of the Master and went to him.
He attended upon him morning and evening. It happened that a great snow fell; Guang stood firm and unmoving until dawn, when the accumulated snow reached his knees.
It reached past his knees. The Master, moved by compassion, asked him, "What do you seek? Huiguan wept bitterly and made a piteous plea. The Master rebuked him for his arrogance.

Huiguan secretly took a sharp blade and severed his own left arm, placing it before the Master. The Master, knowing him to be a vessel for the Dharma, said, "Now that you have severed your arm to seek the Dharma, this may be permitted.
He then changed his name to Huike. Huike said, "The Dharma of all Buddhas..."
"May I hear about the Dharma-seal? Mazu said, "The Dharma-seal of all Buddhas is not obtained from another. Huik'e said, "My mind is not yet at peace.
Mazu said, "Bring forth your mind, and I will set it at peace for you. Huik'e said, "When I search for my mind, it is utterly unobtainable. Mazu said, "I have finished setting your mind at peace.
At this, Huik'e attained great enlightenment and declared, "In the past, the Tathāgata entrusted the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye to Kāśyapa."
Passing down through successive generations, it has now reached me; I now entrust it to you. You should uphold and protect it, along with this *kāṣāya* robe as a token of the Dharma.
Furthermore, the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* may serve as the seal of the mind. As the verse says: "I have come to this land To transmit the Dharma and save deluded beings."
One flower opens into five petals; the fruit ripens spontaneously. Thus he was the First Patriarch of this land.
The eulogy says: "The Master’s mind was too urgent; his arrival was too early. A single word did not meet [his expectation], and this mind remained unresolved.
He sat coldly at Shaolin until fortunately meeting Shen Guang. When one arm was severed, his Way flourished greatly."
The Biography of the Twenty-ninth Patriarch, the Great Master of the First Ancestor, Huikē.
The Great Master Huikē, the Second Ancestor, was a native of Wulao. His surname was Jī, and his father’s name was Jì. Initially, the family had no son;

after praying for a long time, one night they were moved by a supernatural light that illuminated the room. Consequently, the mother became pregnant, and the child was born with the auspicious sign of the light illuminating the chamber.

He was subsequently named Shenguang. From his youth, his aspirations were extraordinary. He first relied upon Chan Master Baoli of Mount Xiangshan, where he left the household life and received full ordination.
After traveling among lecture halls for thirty years, he returned to spend his days in constant seated meditation.

While in stillness, he beheld a divine being who informed him of the conditions for receiving the Way and instructed him to exchange his skull. Hearing that Master Bodhidharma was sitting in silence at Shaolin, he went straight there.

[The preceding account] concluded. Having attained the Seal of the Mind, after Bodhidharma returned to the West, the Great Master continued to propagate the profound wind [of the Dharma], extensively seeking a Dharma heir.

Later, he encountered a layman over forty years of age who did not state his name or lineage. He came and performed a ritual of greeting, then asked: "I, your disciple, am afflicted by a chronic wind-ailment;
I pray that the Master will absolve my transgressions. The Master said: "Bring forth your transgressions, and I shall absolve them for you. The layman remained silent for a long while.

The man said, "I have searched for my transgression, but it is utterly unfindable. The Master said, "I have finished repenting your transgression for you; you should now dwell in accordance with the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.

The man said, "Now that I have seen the Venerable Master, I already know what the Sangha is. I do not yet understand what is meant by 'Buddha' and 'Dharma. The Master said, "This very mind is the Buddha;
this very mind is the Dharma. The Dharma and the Buddha are non-dual; so too is the Jewel of the Sangha. The man said, "Only today do I truly know."
"The nature of sin is not within, nor without, nor in between. As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha-dharma; there is no duality.
The Master regarded him with deep esteem and immediately shaved his head, saying, "He is my treasure. He should be named Sengcan.
On the eighteenth day of the third month of that year, he received full ordination at Guangfu Temple. From then on, his illness gradually abated, and he attended upon the Master for two years.
The Master then declared: "Bodhidharma came from afar from Western India and secretly entrusted to me the Treasury of the Eye of the True Dharma along with the robe of faith.
I now transmit it to you; you must guard it and ensure that it does not come to an end.
Listen to my verse: 'Originally there was ground for conditions; based on that ground, seeds and flowers grew. Originally there were no seeds, and thus flowers have never existed.'"
He was born. Thus he became the Second Patriarch of this land. The eulogy says:
"Coming by sea, how much bitter toil! In the land of China, only one person was found— One who cannot be sought out, yet is like water that conforms to its vessel.
Transmitting the family lineage through this is the second [patriarch]."
The Biography of the Third Patriarch, Zen Master Sengcan Jingzhi:
As for the Great Master Sengcan, the Third Patriarch, it is unknown where he was from. As a layman (*baiyi*), he visited the Second Patriarch, received ordination, and was transmitted the Dharma.
He lived in seclusion at Mount Wangong in Shuzhou. It was during the reign of Emperor Wu of the Later Zhou, when the Buddha-dharma was being suppressed and destroyed, that the Master...
He traveled between Lake Tai and Mount Sikong, dwelling in no fixed place for more than ten years; at that time, none among the people were able to recognize him.
It was until the twelfth year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty that a novice monk named Daoxin, then fourteen years of age, came to pay his respects to the Patriarch, saying:
"I pray that the Master will, out of compassion, grant me the Dharma-gate of liberation. The Patriarch asked: "Who has bound you? He replied: "No one."
Huineng said, "What further liberation do you seek? Under these words, Xinxing attained great enlightenment. He served the Master with diligence for nine years.

Later, he received the full precepts in Jizhou and attended upon the Master with even greater reverence. The Master repeatedly tested him with profound and subtle mysteries; knowing that his karmic conditions were ripe, he then entrusted him with the robe and the Dharma.
The verse said: "Though the seeds of flowers depend on the earth, From the earth the flowers are grown. If no one plants the seeds,"
The Flower Land is entirely non-arising. This is the teaching of the Third Patriarch of this land. He praised [the situation] saying:
"The entire body is illness, yet one does not know its origin. Suddenly encountering the King of Physicians, one suddenly awakens to its cause.
The mind is empty and the bones are firm; now one should set out on foot. When meeting one of great strength, entrust the burden to them."
The Biography of the Thirty-first Patriarch, Master Daoyi of Daci:
The Fourth Patriarch, Master Daoyi, was surnamed Sima. His family had resided for generations in Henei, later migrating to Guangji County in Qizhou.

From birth he was exceptionally gifted; from childhood he aspired to the gates of liberation within the school of Emptiness, as if these were the result of habitual practice from previous lives. Once...
It is recorded that the Third Patriarch succeeded to the Dharma and, with his mind restrained, did not sleep for sixty years, his side never touching the mat.

In the thirteenth year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he led his disciples to Jizhou. There they encountered a band of rebels surrounding the city; after seventy days, the siege had not been lifted, and the multitude was filled with terror.
The Patriarch took pity on them and instructed them to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*. At that time, from the battlements of the city walls, the rebel host beheld [visions] as if...
There were divine soldiers who said to one another, "There must be extraordinary people within this city; it is not fit to attack. They gradually withdrew.
In the Jia-shen year of the Wu-de era of the Tang dynasty, the master returned to Qi and stayed at Mount Pòtóu during the spring. Disciples arrived there like clouds.
One day, he went to Huangmei County. On the road, he encountered a woman carrying a young boy whose skeletal features were extraordinary and refined, unlike those of ordinary children.
The Patriarch asked, "What is your surname? She replied, "I do have a surname, but it is not an ordinary one.

The Patriarch asked, "What is it? She replied, "It is Buddha-nature. The Patriarch said, "Do you have no surname? She replied, "Because nature is empty, there is none. The Patriarch [was deeply impressed].
Recognizing her as a vessel for the Dharma, he immediately dispatched an attendant to her mother’s residence to request that she allow her to leave the household life.

Because of their past karmic connection, the mother showed no sign of reluctance and eventually relinquished her to become his disciple. Upon the transmission of the Dharma and the robe, he spoke this verse:
"The nature of the lotus seed exists; Because of the ground, the lotus grows. When the great conditions unite with its nature, It gives rise to birth, yet is ultimately unborn. Thus it was.
He entrusted his disciples to him, thereby becoming the Fourth Patriarch of this land. A eulogy says:
"Leaving home in youth with faculties sharp and swift, for over sixty years his side never touched the mat.
Disciples arrive like clouds; what need is there for a mere child? Because of their prior agreement, onlookers do not recognize him."
The Biography of the Thirty-second Patriarch, Great Master Huiming (Daman) Hongren.
Great Master Hongren, the Fifth Patriarch, was a native of Huangmei in Qizhou. Formerly, he was known as Daozhe, the Pine-Planter of Mount Poutou.
He once requested of the Fourth Patriarch, saying, "May I hear the Way of the Dharma? The Patriarch replied, "You are already too old; you have [already] fallen away."
He heard that [the Master] was capable of widespread conversion. "If he should come again," he thought, "it would still be possible to wait for you.

He then went to the water's edge and saw a young woman washing clothes. He bowed to her and said, "I seek lodging here. The woman replied, "I have parents; you may go and ask them. He said, "Very well. I shall go at once.
The woman nodded her head in agreement, and he turned his horse and departed. This woman was Zhou Shi Jizi.

Every time she returned home, she became pregnant. Her parents detested her greatly and cast her out. Having nowhere to go, the girl worked as a hired spinner in the village during the day and stayed beneath a public inn at night.
Afterward, she gave birth to a son; deeming him an ill omen, she threw him into a muddy creek.
The next day, seeing him swimming upstream, his body radiant and bright, they were greatly astonished. They then took him up, and he grew to boyhood following his mother.
He begged for alms, and the villagers called him "The Child Without a Surname. He encountered a man of wisdom who sighed and said, "This boy lacks seven of the marks [of a great man];
he does not yet equal the Tathāgata. Later, he met Master Xin and attained the Dharma, succeeding him in his transformation of beings on Mount Pòtóu.
During the Xiánhé era, there was a layman named Lú Huínéng from Xīnzhōu who came to visit the Patriarch and asked: "As for you yourself—"
“Where have you come from? he asked. He replied, “From Lingnan. The Patriarch said, “What do you seek? He replied, “I seek only to become a Buddha.
The Patriarch said, “The people of Lingnan have no Buddha-nature. He replied, “People may be from the north or the south, but how could Buddha-nature have a north or a south?
The Patriarch knew he was an extraordinary man and said, “Go and work in the fodder shed. Lu entered the rice-hulling room and hulled rice with a stone tied to his waist for eight months. One day—
The Patriarch Huineng sought a successor to the Dharma and ordered the assembly to each write a verse to present as an interpretation.

The Senior Monk Shenxiu wrote a verse upon the wall, saying: "The body is the Bodhi tree; The mind is like a bright mirror’s stand. At all times diligently wipe and polish it, Lest dust and grime should gather.

The Patriarch knew that [Shenxiu] had not yet attained awakening. Lu (Huineng) then wrote a verse, saying: "Bodhi is fundamentally no tree; The bright mirror is likewise no stand. From the beginning..."
"When nothing comes, where can dust be stirred? The Patriarch, knowing this, entered the rice-pounding room himself and ordered [Huineng] to enter his quarters at the third watch.
He then bestowed upon him the robe and bowl, saying in verse: "When sentient beings come to sow seeds, The fruit grows back according to the ground.
Since insentient things have no seeds, They lack nature and thus do not grow. For this reason, the Fifth Patriarch of this land offered this praise:
His origins are obscure, yet his station is perfectly suited; One task unfinished, both houses are brought to an end.
On the road to Huangmei within Mount Toupo, He comes and goes with ease, possessing the marks of a Great Man.
The Biography of the Thirty-third Patriarch, Chan Master Dajian Huineng.

The Sixth Patriarch, Master Huineng, was of the secular surname Lu. His ancestors were from Fanyang. His father, Lu Xingtao, was transferred to serve in Xinzhou during the Wude era and subsequently registered his residence there.
The Master lost his father when he was three years old; his mother remained steadfast in her resolve to raise him.
Upon reaching adulthood, the family was impoverished, and he gathered firewood to provide for them. One day, while carrying wood into the market, he heard a guest reciting the *Jin*.

Upon reaching the passage in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, "One should give rise to the mind without abiding anywhere," he attained sudden enlightenment. He asked a guest, "What dharma is this? From whom did you obtain it?
The guest replied, "This is called the *Vajracchedikā Sūtra*; I obtained it from the Great Master Ren at Huangmei.

The Patriarch then informed his mother of his intention to seek a teacher for the sake of the Dharma. First, he traveled to Shaoshan, where he met the nun Wujin, who spoke to him of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Yi subsequently repaired Bao Lin Temple at Cao Xi and resided there. Shortly thereafter, he went to Huang Mei to visit the Great Master.

Upon their first meeting, the Master recognized him intuitively; he then transmitted the robe and the Dharma to him, instructing him to remain hidden among the ranks of hunters between Huai Ji and Si Hui for sixteen years.
In the first month of the first year of the Yifeng era, he arrived at Fa Xing Temple in Nan Hai. At that time, Yin...

Master Zong was lecturing on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Among those in the assembly were two monks who saw the wind blowing and a banner fluttering; they debated the meaning of this movement without reaching a conclusion.
The Patriarch said, "It is neither the wind nor the banner; it is the mind of the worthy ones that moves. When Master Yin Zong heard this, he knew him to be an extraordinary person.
He questioned him. The Master told him the truth and subsequently presented his robe and bowl; the entire assembly was struck with wonder and admiration.

Thereupon, he gathered the multitude to have his hair shaved beneath the Bodhi tree. Vinaya Master Zhiguang conferred the full precepts upon him, and Yinzong assembled a thousand monastics and laypeople.

He was sent back to Baolin Temple, where he opened the Dharma under Caoxi. More than thirty people attained awakening, yet among them, only the two great masters Qingyuan Xingsi and Nanyue Huairang were the preeminent leaders.
From this point on, the Way split into two lineages. One day, the Patriarch addressed the assembly, saying:
"I have had the honor of receiving the robe and Dharma from Master Huineng. I have now preached the Dharma for you all, but I shall not transmit it [to anyone here]."
[The Master] gave him his robe, saying: "I have bestowed this robe upon you because your faculty of faith is mature and you are resolute, free from doubt, and capable of undertaking the great task.

Listen to my verse: 'The ground of the mind contains all seeds; When the rain falls everywhere, they all sprout. Once the essence of the flower is suddenly realized, The fruit of Bodhi is spontaneously attained.
For this reason, he was the Sixth Patriarch of this land. He then offered this praise:
The woodcutter’s axe was just cast down when a stone fell upon his waist; the numinous root, long planted, has from this point begun to sprout its branches.
Originating at Caoxi, it flows across the great earth, reaching even until today—there is nowhere that is not [the Dharma].
This is the compilation by Zhan’an and the transmission of Master Guanding.

Dharma Master Zhang’an, whose name was Guanding, was a native of Zhang’an in Linhai. His surname was Wu. At only three months of age, he was able to recite the names of the Triple Gem following his mother.
When a monk passed by their door, he said to his mother, "This child is no ordinary person," and thus he was named accordingly.
At the age of seven, he entered the monastic life under Master Huji at Shejing Temple; he could memorize ten thousand words a day. At the age of twenty, he received the full precepts.
He was fully endowed with the precepts and possessed innate wisdom and understanding; he never forgot what he heard upon hearing it once.

At the beginning of the Zhide era of the Chen dynasty, he visited Zhiyi of Tiantai at Xuchan Temple to receive instruction in the methods of contemplation. After long and diligent study, he suddenly received the Master’s seal of approval and became his attendant.
Wherever they stayed, he was able to fully comprehend every Dharma gate taught. He followed Master Zhiyi to listen to lectures on the *Lotus Sūtra*.
In Jīnlíng Guāngzé, he received the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra) and the *Yuantun zhiguan* (Perfect and Sudden Calming and Contemplation) at Yùquán in Jiānglíng.

As for his travels to other locations, during the course of his lectures and the receiving of teachings, he compiled and recorded more than one hundred fascicles of texts from both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna traditions, transmitting them to those who had not yet heard them.
Regarding the doctrinal and contemplative systems of the Tiantai school, the Master’s contributions were immense. When Zhìzhě passed away...
Later, the Master was summoned by the Crown Prince to enter the capital to lecture on the *Fahua xuanyi* (The Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra).

He was subsequently sent back to the mountains, where he composed two fascicles of the *Niepan xuanyi* (The Profound Meaning of the Nirvāṇa Sūtra) and twenty fascicles of commentaries (*shu*). At that time, the end of the Sui dynasty had arrived; warfare broke out and bandits rose up in swarms. The Master wrote in his own preface:
"In calculating the sacred texts, a total of five years have passed. In what year have we not seen the fires of war? In what month have we not seen..."
Amidst the clamor of arms, he maintained a vegetarian diet and water fasts, using ice for his bed and snow for his blanket; such was the nature of his toil and hardship.

When the commentary was completed, he attempted to burn it with a fierce fire, but it would not catch flame. He lived to the age of seventy-two and entered parinirvāṇa. He was one of the nine patriarchs of the Tiantai school.

Previously, his fellow student Zhìxī had said at the time of his death: "I shall be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven, where I shall see the precious throne of my former teacher, Zhìzhě. Upon arriving there, he...
The rows were all already occupied, with only one seat left vacant. A celestial being said, "Six years hence, the Dharma Master Ding will come to ascend this seat.
Calculating the years and reckoning the period, Xi’s words proved not to be in error. Zàn said:
Influencing the Dharma-transformation like clouds and dragons, wind and tigers; wherever a banner is raised, there must be its corresponding ranks.
The teachings and contemplations of our family have reached their great flourishing through the Master. Entering the ocean of vast learning, the source is distant and the stream is long.

The Biography of the Dharma Master Ci’en Xuánzàng.
The Dharma Master Ci’en Xuánzàng was the son of the Chen family of Luoyang. He entered the monastic order in his youth and received full ordination.

At the age of eleven, he was already able to recite and master the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Upon reaching maturity, he carried his book-bag westward to visit Dharma Master Dàojī, from whom he received the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*.

Regarding the *Abhidharma-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, and other treatises, Ji praised him, saying: "I have frequented many lecture halls, yet I have never seen a youth of such divine insight.
In the third year of the Zhenguan era, he submitted a memorial to the imperial court requesting to travel to the Western Regions to retrieve scriptures.

The Emperor did not grant permission, so the Master secretly departed through the Jade Gate (Yumen Pass) and proceeded to the kingdoms of Gaochang and Yehe. On his journey, he traversed four [countries].
He traveled to Central India, where he encountered a Mahāyāna lay practitioner who bestowed upon him the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
He entered the city of Rājagṛha and stayed at Nālandā Monastery, where he received from the Master of Śāstras Śīlabhadra the essential tenets of the Yogācāra-Vijñaptimātra school.

He traveled throughout the Western Regions for more than ten years, visiting one hundred and thirty kingdoms. There was no land where the Tathāgata had spread his teachings or any site containing his relics that he did not reach.

In total, he obtained six hundred and fifty-seven works of the various sūtras and śāstras in their original Sanskrit, including the teachings of the five periods, the treatises of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, and the divergent tenets of the six schools and seven sects of non-Buddhist outsiders.
He was thoroughly proficient in the five sciences (*pañcavidyā*) and the six methods of interpretation (*ṣaḍvyākhyāna*). Having collected and researched them all, he mastered their texts.

In the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era, he returned from the Western Regions and arrived at the capital. When the Palace Guard, Fang Xuanling, reported his arrival in a memorial, the Emperor summoned him to the Yidian Hall.
The Emperor asked, "Why did you not inform me of your departure? The Master replied, "When I departed, I submitted three memorials [requesting leave]."

Having received his gracious consent, [the Master] proceeded to travel privately. The Emperor said, "That you, Master, are able to risk your life to seek the Dharma for the benefit of all living beings is something I deeply admire.

He issued an edict that [the Master] should reside at Hongfu Monastery to translate various sutras and śāstras, and he commanded Xiao Yu (Xuanling) to oversee the project and provide all necessary provisions from the imperial treasury.
Once the translations were completed, the Emperor composed the "Preface to the Holy Teachings of the Tripitaka of the Great Tang," and the Crown Prince...
The Master compiled the *Śāstrasaṃgraha* (or *Zhēnshèngjì*). He was granted a gold-embroidered monastic robe and a precious razor.
Later, at Cien Monastery, he constructed a great stūpa to enshrine the newly translated scriptures. Thus, he became the Second Patriarch of the Cien School. The eulogy says:
When the Great Teaching flowed eastward, its Dharma had not yet spread universally; thereupon, an Arhat risked his life to go and retrieve it.
The Prajñāpāramitā shone its light and the Abhidharma school was grandly inaugurated; as a vessel for the sea of suffering, its salvation of beings was without end.

The Vinaya Master’s name was Daoxuan. He was a native of Jingzhao and belonged to the Qian clan. He was the son of Shen, the Minister of the Board of Personnel.

His mother dreamed that a lunar disc pierced her womb before she conceived. At the time of his birth, his mother dreamed that a Buddhist monk said to her, "The one you carry is the Vinaya Master You of the Liang dynasty.
When he grew up, he left the household life and maintained himself according to the Vinaya. He moved the heavens to send him offerings, and celestial youths served as his attendants.

While the Master was practicing the Way, his mind grew weary and he fell ill. Suddenly, the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa bestowed upon him a prescription for tonifying the heart—this is the "Heart-Tonifying Pill" (Buxin Dan) used today.
Because the Master felt that the ordination platform did not conform to the Vinaya, he personally carried earth to rebuild it according to the rules.
While the Master was walking at midnight, he stumbled and fell against a stone step. A youth clad in armor appeared to protect him. The Master asked:
"Who are you? The spirit replied, "I am the disciple Zhang Qiong, the prince of the god Vatsa. Because of your teacher’s virtue in the precepts, I serve you.
The teacher asked about the events concerning the World-Honored One while he was in the world and after his parinirvāṇa; Qiong recounted them one by one.

In total, there were three thousand eight hundred matters recorded as they occurred during his inquiries, compiled as the *Gantong zhuan* (Records of Miraculous Responses). The deity further bestowed upon him a Buddha tooth that he had treasured;

such miraculous occurrences were exceedingly numerous. The Master composed the following works: the *Neidian lu* (Record of the Inner Canon), the *Gantong lu* (Records of Miraculous Responses), the *Shijia pu* (Genealogy of Śākyamuni), the *Sifen jieben* (Four-Part Code of Monastic Discipline), the *Jieshen shu* (Commentary on the Precepts), the *Xu gaoseng zhuan* (Continued Biographies of Eminent Monks), and the *Guang hongming ji* (Expanded Collection for the Propagation and Clarification [of Buddhism]). 8.
In eleven fascicles, these works have circulated throughout the world. He was the ninth patriarch of the Nanshan Vinaya School. The eulogy states:
The Tathāgata established the teachings, taking the Three Studies as his masters; That which is brought forth by concentration and wisdom takes the precepts as its foundation.
When the Great Dharma flowed eastward, these teachings had not yet flourished; A hero from the South Mountain emerged and single-handedly restored their guiding principles.

The Biography of Dharma Master Kuiji of Cien:
Dharma Master Kuiji was a native of Dai Commandery. He was the younger brother of the late General of the Right, the Duke of Zhongwu, Wei Ji Jingde, and the son of Duke Jingzong.
His mother, Lady Pei, dreamed of swallowing the moon before giving birth to him. At the age of six, his intelligence surpassed that of others; he had a [jade-like] mark upon his head.

Zhen (Zhizhen): His finger patterns were like seals. Even before reaching the age of childhood, he was already able to compose writings. Initially, when Master Xuanzang held a vegetarian feast at his residence, Zhizhen’s father, Lord Zong, ordered him to come out and pay his respects.
The Master approached the father and requested that the boy be allowed to leave the household life. Lord Zong said, "This child is fierce and violent; he is incapable of receiving instruction.

The Master replied, "The capacity and bearing of this young gentleman will not be realized except through a general, nor would they have been recognized except by me, a poor monk. Lord Zong finally granted permission.
The Emperor issued a special decree appointing the śrāmaṇera Kuiji as a full monk (bhikṣu). He entered the Great Ci’en Monastery to participate in the correct translation of the scriptures.
Whenever Kuiji read the commentaries and records, he could recite them from memory after a single reading. At that time, the Master was seventeen years old;

he received from Master Xuanzang the Yogācārabhūmi and the tenets of Vijñaptimātratā, and composed commentaries and sub-commentaries on over a hundred works. At the time, he was known as "The Hundred-Volume Master."

The Master of the *Abhidharma* School was by nature grand and luxurious. Whenever he went out, he invariably prepared three carriages for scriptures, books, and food. Consequently, people of the time called him the "Master of the Three Carriages.
Originally, the Sanskrit text of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* consisted of ten sections and one hundred fascicles; its prose was vast and its meaning profound.
The Master requested Master Xuanzang to synthesize it into ten fascicles, which has been followed and practiced to this day. He is thus the third patriarch of the Cien School. In praise, it is said:
The profound and mysterious doctrine of Consciousness-Only is deep and abstruse; only the Master has revealed it like the sun shining in the sky.
Having surely received its precepts in advance from Maitreya in Tuṣita Heaven, how could he have known its secret instructions had they not come from within?
—Recorded by the Dharma Master Xianshou Fazang.
The Dharma Master Xianxiu, whose name was Fazang, was a native of Kangju.

Having come to reside in Chang’an, at the age of sixteen he visited the Ashoka Stūpa containing relics at Siming and offered his finger in a rite of refinement, vowing to study the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*. During the reign of Empress Wu Zetian, he was registered in the imperial palace.
In the first year of the Tongtian era, by imperial decree, he expounded the essential tenets of the *Avataṃsaka* at Taiyuan Temple, whereupon a brilliant white light was perceived.

However, as soon as it issued from his mouth, it instantly formed a canopy. The multitude cheered with joy, and Empress Wu issued an edict commanding the ten Great Virtuous Ones of the capital to confer the full ordination upon him.
She bestowed upon him the title "Virtuous Head Preceptor" (Xianshou Jieshi) and issued a decree for him to enter Dabiankong Monastery.
When Śikṣānanda assisted in translating the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and subsequently lectured on the new scripture, the earth shook as they reached the "World Chapter" (*Lokadhātu-parivarta*).
Empress Wu summoned him to the Changsheng Hall and inquired about the fundamental tenets of the *Avataṃsaka*.

The Master pointed to the golden lion before the hall and expounded upon the meanings of the six characteristics, the ten mysteries, and the five teachings. Empress Wu suddenly attained realization and composed [a work] regarding them.
This is called the "Chapter on the Golden Lion. When Emperor Ruizong received the internal abdication of power, he requested that the Master confer upon him the Bodhisattva Great Precepts.

The Master wore rag robes and ate coarse food; he lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* more than thirty times. He also composed commentaries on the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Ghanavyūha*, and the *Awakening of Faith*.

In the first year of the Xiantian era, he passed away at Dajianfu Monastery and was posthumously granted the title of Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial. He is known as the Third Patriarch of the Huayan school.
The Patriarch praised him, saying:
"In the great dharma-realm net, the holy and the ordinary are arrayed; there is but one main cord, which only you, Master, can pull.
You cause the myriad streams to flow together back to the ocean of nature; the five teachings are gathered in their entirety, remaining unchanged through all eternity."

The Biography of Chan Master Fazhao:
Chan Master Fazhao received the Dharma from National Teacher Fazhao during the Dali era of the Tang dynasty. He resided at Yunfeng Temple in Hengzhou and was venerated by his contemporaries.
Once, within his alms bowl, he beheld five-colored clouds containing a Buddhist monastery, with golden script inscribed upon it that read: "The Great Sage’s Zhulin Monastery."
On another day, he again saw a pavilion within the clouds amidst the contents of his alms bowl, observing ten thousand bodhisattvas dwelling together therein.
The Master reported what he had seen to his learned associates, who said, "Based on the topography of what you have seen, it must be Mount Wutai. Thereupon, the Master vowed to travel there.
Later, while residing at Huduosi Temple in the prefecture, he established five assemblies for the recitation of the Buddha’s name, which moved the heavens so that auspicious clouds filled the sky.
He was covered by clouds, within which he beheld pavilions and towers. There he saw Amitābha Buddha and two Bodhisattvas, their bodies filling the void.

Several Brahmin masters were walking along, carrying *khakkhara* staffs. Furthermore, there was an old man who said to him, "You previously made a vow to travel to the Golden Realm (*Suvarṇabhūmi*) to pay homage and visit ten great monks;
why do you stop now? The Master then joined his companions and traveled far to Mount Wutai to seek the Buddha.
Guang Temple was exactly as he had seen it within the bowl. Upon reaching a mountain ravine, there was a stone gate. At that moment, two youths dressed in green robes led the Master through the gate.
He beheld a palace of golden and emerald hues; on a golden plaque, it was inscribed: "The Great Sage’s Zhulin Monastery.

It spanned approximately twenty *li* and contained one hundred courtyards, all with golden grounds and jeweled ponds, adorned with flower pedestals and jade trees. Entering the lecture hall, he saw...
Mañjuśrī was to the west and Samantabhadra was to the east, seated upon lion thrones and preaching the Dharma for the assembly. Ten thousand bodhisattvas surrounded them on all sides.
The Master prostrated before the two bodhisattvas and asked: "As for ordinary beings of the final age, I do not yet know what dharma-gate they should practice.
Mañjuśrī replied: "Among all those who practice cultivation, there is none like the recollection of the Buddha—namely, Amitābha Buddha."
"The power of your vows is inconceivable; you should fix your mindfulness and resolve to attain rebirth there.

At that time, the two Great Beings simultaneously extended their golden arms and touched his crown, prophesying: "By the power of your recollection of the Buddha, you shall ultimately realize unsurpassed enlightenment.
Mañjuśrī further said: "You may proceed before the various Bodhisattvas, prostrate, and receive their instructions. Thus, he visited each of the assembly one by one.
The Sage again went before Mañjuśrī, prostrated, and took his leave. Two young men in green robes escorted him to the gate, but when he looked up, they had both vanished.
Later, Emperor Daizong summoned him to the palace and conferred upon him the title of National Teacher; he is thus regarded as the Fourth Patriarch of the Pure Land school. The eulogy says:
The Great Being Mañjuśrī was about to grant him an audience; thus, in the Golden World (*Suvarṇabhāsottama-kṣetra*), [the Buddha] first appeared within his alms-bowl.
Upon entering the gate, it was as if he were returning from a familiar journey. He directly pointed out that Sukhāvatī is the place to which one should take refuge.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master of Yoga, Amoghavajra.
The Tripitaka Master Amoghavajra was a native of the Western Regions. In his youth, he followed his uncle to visit the Great Kingdom (China).

There he encountered the Venerable Master Vajrabodhi and studied the meaning of Yoga-tantra under him. Vajrabodhi bestowed upon him the Sanskrit text of the *Śabdavidyā-śāstra* (Treatise on Grammar); within ten days, he had mastered it through recitation.

Vajrabodhi marveled at this and initiated him into the Vajra-maṇḍala, where they performed the rite of casting flowers to determine spiritual affinity. [Amoghavajra] proved superior to his teacher, who then first sought...

The Dharma. In his dreams, the capital and its images all moved toward the east. Upon waking, he questioned Vajrabodhi (Ji). Vajrabodhi said, "You possess the capacity to receive the Way; why should I be parsimonious?

He immediately bestowed upon him the five sections [of the *Mahāvairocana Sūtra*] and the ritual manuals (*vidhi*) of Susiddhi. After Vajrabodhi passed away, he honored his final instructions and traveled west to India.
Arriving at the Kingdom of Siṃhala, he met Vajrabodhi (Longzhi), from whom he received the eighteen assemblies of the Vajra-empowerment and the Great Compassion [mantra].

Regarding the method for constructing the Garbhadhātu Maṇḍala, he transmitted over five hundred sections of sūtras and śāstras. In the twenty-ninth year [of the Kaiyuan era], he returned from Siṃhala (Sri Lanka) to Guangzhou.
Liu Jujì, the Commissioner for the Collection of Tribute, requested that he establish an Abhiṣeka Maṇḍala; thereupon, Mañjuśrī manifested his physical form.
In the first year of the Tiānbǎo era, Dàshíkāng of the Western Regions, who ruled over the Five Kingdoms, launched an invasion of Anxi. The Master was summoned to enter [the capital].
Inside, the Emperor personally held the incense burner while the Master recited the *Ratnaketuparivarta* (The Benevolent King’s Protection of the Nation) mantra.
Suddenly, the Emperor beheld divine soldiers clad in armor and bearing spears standing in the palace courtyard. The Master said, "This is the second son of King Vaiśravaṇa;

he has come at Your Majesty’s behest to go and rescue Anxi. Please prepare food to send him off. Shortly thereafter, a report arrived from Anxi stating that a black cloud had appeared to the northeast of the city.
In the midst of the clouds, he saw a divine being clad in golden armor, over ten feet tall. From the sky, drums and horns resounded loudly, their sound shaking heaven and earth.
Among the enemy’s tents, a golden rat gnawed through the bowstring. The five kingdoms immediately fled in disarray. A moment later, on the city tower, he beheld the form of a Heavenly King.
He carefully drew its image and presented it; upon verification, it was found to be the deity from whom he had recited mantras daily. When he arrived—

Thereafter, whenever he recited mantras, they produced miraculous efficacy. During the two reigns of the Xuanzong and Suzong emperors, he was honored as the State Preceptor of Consecration (Guanding Guoshi).
Later, his rank was increased to that of Kaifu Yitongsan Si, Duke of the State of Su, with an appanage of three thousand households.
Thus, the Yoga Tantric teachings are truly based upon his tradition. The eulogy says:
The Vairocana Empowerment is the Heart-Seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*). When the True Command is fully upheld, Buddhas and demons obey and flee;
gods and dragons submit, and a hundred monsters are silently extinguished. Therefore, the wise attain great sovereignty.
