and collated by Qian Yingjin, a gentleman of the upper class from Jiaxing.
The Biography of Chan Master Qingyuan Si:
Chan Master Xing Si of Mount Qingyuan in Jizhou was a native of the Liu clan of Ancheng in that same province. He left home to become a monk in his youth.
Whenever he sat in the assembly discussing the Way, the Master remained silent. Later, having heard of Caoxi, he went there to pay his respects. He asked, "What should I devote myself to?"

[The Master] immediately said, "I do not fall into any stage. The Patriarch asked, "What have you been doing? The Master replied, "I do not even practice the Noble Truths. The Patriarch asked, "In what stage do you then fall?
The Master replied, "Since I do not even practice the Noble Truths, what stage could there be? The Patriarch held him in high esteem and placed him at the head of the assembly.
One day, the Patriarch said to the Master, "From of old, the Dharma and the robe have been transmitted together; master and disciple..."
The robe is transmitted to signify faith; the Dharma is the seal upon the mind. Now that I have found the right person, what need is there to worry about a lack of faith?
Since I received this robe, I have encountered many hardships; how much more so will those who come after me face much contention and strife? Let the robe remain here to guard the mountain gate.
You shall go forth to transform and guide one region, ensuring that the lineage does not cease. Once the Master had received the Dharma, he returned to reside at Qingyuan. Six.
As the Patriarch was about to pass away, the śrāmaṇera Xiqian asked him, “After the Master has passed on, I do not yet know whom I should rely upon.
The Patriarch replied, “Seek it out for yourself. When the Patriarch entered nirvana, Xiqian would often sit upright in quietude, as if he had forgotten his very birth.
The Head Seat asked him, “Your teacher has already departed; what is the purpose of sitting here in vain? Xiqian replied:
"I have received his final instructions, and therefore I am investigating this matter. The Master said, "You have an elder brother, Master Si, who is currently at Jizhou.

Your karmic conditions lie there; the Master’s words were very straightforward, yet you yourself were deluded. Baizhang Qian then paid his respects at the patriarch's shrine and went directly to Qingyuan to pay his respects.
The Master asked, "From where have you come? Qian replied, "From Caoxi. The Master asked, "What have you brought back?"

Molai said, "Even before arriving at Caoxi, one does not lose it. The Master said, "If you employ it in such a manner, what would arriving at Caoxi accomplish? Qian said, "If I had not arrived at Caoxi, how could I have known that I do not lose it? After being interrogated and examined in many ways, his quick-witted eloquence was found to be spontaneous and free;

the Master thereupon certified him as a Dharma heir. He became the first generation after Caoxi. In praise, it is said: [The original Chinese text provided for this section is: 麼來。曰未到曹溪。亦不失。師曰。若恁麼用。到曹溪作甚麼。遷曰。若不到曹溪。爭知不失。詰勘多端。機辯自在。遂印為法嗣。是為曹溪下一世。贊曰。 **Translation:** Molai said, "Even before arriving at Caoxi, one does not lose it. The Master said, "If you employ it in such a manner, what would arriving at Caoxi accomplish? Qian said, "If I had not arrived at Caoxi, how could I have known that I do not lose it?

After being interrogated and examined in many ways, his quick-witted eloquence was found to be spontaneous and free; the Master thereupon certified him as a Dharma heir. He became the first generation after Caoxi. In praise, it is said:
Naturally noble and beyond all ranks, a single word that strikes the vital point is like a bee finding honey.
From this single stream of Caoxi, branches and tributaries have spread; from then on, the descendants have rolled forth like thunder and lightning.
This is the lineage transmitted by Master Nanyue Huairang.
The Zen Master Huairang of Nanyue was a native of Jinzhou. His surname was Du. At the time of his birth, a white vapor appeared in response to the celestial omens.
The Grand Astrologer divined and memorialized that he would become a vessel of the Dharma for the state. The Emperor issued an edict to the Governor of Jinzhou to personally console his family.
When he reached the age of ten, an extraordinary monk beheld him and said to his parents: "If this child leaves the household life, he will surely attain [enlightenment]."

He belonged to the Supreme Vehicle (Mahāyāna). At the age of fifteen, he took leave of his parents and entered the monastic life under Vinaya Master Hongjing at Yùquán Monastery in Jīngzhōu, where he received full ordination.
Later, he visited Master Huì'ān of Mount Sōng, who directed him to Cáoxī to study under the Sixth Patriarch.

When the Patriarch asked him, "Where have you come from? he replied, "From Mount Sōng. The Patriarch then asked, "What is it that comes like this? The Master was speechless. He remained there for eight years.
Suddenly he had an awakening. He then said to the Patriarch, "I have reached a point of understanding. The Patriarch asked, "How so?
The Master replied, "To describe it as a single thing is immediately incorrect. The Patriarch asked, "Is there still need for cultivation and realization?
The Master replied, "There is no lack of cultivation and realization, yet one must not be defiled. The Patriarch said, "This very state of non-defilement is that which all Buddhas protect."
"Be mindful," [the Master] said. "The Indian Prajñātāra prophesied that from beneath your feet would emerge a colt that would trample the people of the world to death;
this has always been in your heart. The Master attended him for fifteen years.

Later, he went to Mount Heng, where there was a śramaṇa named Dàoyī who constantly practiced seated meditation in the mountains. Knowing that he was a vessel for the Dharma, the Master took a brick...
On a stone before the hut, he was polishing it. One asked, "What are you making by polishing? The Master said, "I am making a mirror.
The one asked, "How can a brick become a mirror? The Master said, "Just as a brick cannot become a mirror by being polished, so too can sitting in meditation not make one a Buddha.
The one asked, "What then is the way? The Master said, "It is like a cow pulling a cart. If the cart does not move, you must strike the ox; you cannot strike the cart."
This was a great and total awakening. He then transmitted the Dharma to him, saying in verse: "The ground of the mind contains all seeds;
When it meets with moisture, they all sprout. The flower of samādhi is formless; What could be destroyed, and what could be formed? This was the first generation after Caoqi. Praise says:
His spirit soars to the heavens, his mind is empty and boundless. He grasped the waters of Caoxi to stir up waves and billows;
he put the foal to sleep and roused it with a single brick. Striding across with fearless tread, all who encounter him perish.
This is the biography of Chan Master Yongjia Zhenjue.
The Great Master Wuxiang of Yongjia was named Xuangjue. A native of Yongjia, his surname was Dai. He entered the monastic life at the age of seven and extensively explored the Tripiṭaka.

He mastered the profound and wondrous Dharma-gate of Tiantai *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight). Throughout the four modes of deportment, he constantly practiced meditative contemplation in accordance with the ultimate truth.
Later, inspired by the encouragement of Chan Master Zuoxi Lang, he traveled together with Chan Master Ce of Dongyang to Cao...

Xuefeng. Upon first arriving, he shook his staff and carried his alms bowl as he circumambulated the Patriarch three times. The Patriarch said, "A śramaṇa is endowed with three thousand dignified manners and eighty thousand subtle practices.
From what direction have you come, Venerable One, that you display such great arrogance? The Master replied, "The matter of birth and death is great;
impermanence is swift. The Patriarch asked, "Why do you not realize non-arising? Why do you not understand that there is no swiftness? He replied:
"The essence is itself non-arising; one realizes that it is fundamentally without speed. The Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is. At that time, the entire assembly was not without astonishment.
The Master then performed the full formalities of prostration and salutation, and after a short while, took his leave. The Patriarch asked, "Is your return too soon?

The Master replied, "Since it is fundamentally without movement from the start, how could there be speed? The Patriarch asked, "Who knows it is without movement? The Master replied, "It is you, O Benevolent One, who conceive of it as such."
[The Master] made a distinction. The Patriarch said, "You have attained a state that is utterly free of intention. The Master said, "If there is no birth, how could there be intention?

The Patriarch said, "If there is no intention, who would perform the distinction? The Master said, "Even this distinction is not intention. The Patriarch sighed in admiration and said, "Excellent! Excellent!"

He stayed for one night; at that time, he was called "One-Night Enlightenment" (Yi-suo-jue). Master Ce then detained the teacher, who descended the mountain the following day and returned to Wenjiang.
Students gathered there like the spokes of a wheel, and he was titled Zhenjue (True Enlightenment). He was posthumously honored with the title Grand Master Wuxiang (Formless).

He authored the *Chan-zong-xiu-wu-yuan-zhi* (The Perfect Meaning of Cultivating and Awakening in the Chan School), which is known as the *Yongjia Zhengdao Ge* (Song of Realizing the Way by Yongjia). This constitutes the first generation after Caoxi. The eulogy says:
Golden and tin stand solitary, giving birth to dragons and tigers; It was not until Old Lu had suffered several humiliations that he could speak.
Having been recommended before a word was spoken, he departed that very night; Even such transcendence as this remains merely the work of his descendants.
—The Biography of Chan Master Yixing.

Master Xingxiu was a native of Julu and surnamed Zhang. From his youth, he was extraordinary among his peers; he was profoundly learned and possessed a prodigious memory, such that he needed to read a text only once to master it.
Initially, he followed Chan Master Pujì of Mount Song, whereupon he realized the world’s illusory nature and subsequently took the tonsure to enter the monastic life.
Having received the full precepts, he once transmitted the Esoteric teachings from Vajrabodhi and compiled commentaries on the *Vairocanābhisaṃbodhi-sūtra*.

He ascended the altar for consecration and received the teachings of the five families of Yoga. Furthermore, he investigated the texts of *yin-yang*, *chan* (prophecy), and *wei* (astral divination), and sought out the methods of calendrical calculation from an extraordinary monk at Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai, mastering their entire depths. From this point on, his reputation grew exceedingly great.

In the third year of the Kaiyuan era, an imperial edict summoned him to the court. There, he was consulted regarding the path to transcendence as well as the methods for securing the state and governing the people; he responded accordingly.

The Emperor was pleased with his response and conferred upon him the title "Celestial Master" (Tianshi). When asked about the state, he replied, "Though the imperial carriage shall travel ten thousand li, the altars of soil and grain will ultimately meet with good fortune.
He then presented a golden casket, saying, "Open this upon reaching ten thousand li; it contains only a small amount of *danggui* (angelica)."

Later, when An Lushan rebelled, the Emperor fled to Chengdu. Upon reaching Wanli Bridge, he realized the significance of the "destined return" prophecy; his worries vanished and he felt a sense of clarity.
As for the phrase "ending in good fortune," the line of emperors ended with Emperor Zhaozong, who had once been enfeoffed as the Prince of Ji.

In the ninth year of the Kaiyuan era, because the state calendar was found to be inaccurate, the court issued an edict for the Master to revise and compose a new calendar. The Master calculated the *Dayan* (Great Expansion) calendar based on the five... [text ends].
Twelve fascicles. From the "Treatise on Calendrical Astronomy" (*Lü lì zhì*) in the *Jiu Tang shu*: Previously, there was one named Xing Hepo, a man of esoteric arts, who said to Yin Yin:
"The Monk Yixing is truly a sage. When Luo Xiahong of the Han dynasty was constructing the calendar, he said:"
"Eight hundred years are short by one day; a sage shall surely come to rectify this. When the *Dayan* calendar was produced, Hong’s words were proven true.
In the eleventh year of the Kaiyuan era, the Master completed the construction of the Water Armillary Sphere (*Shui Huntuanyiqi*), the likes of which had never existed before in antiquity.
As the Master succeeded Pujì of the Northern School and also studied the *Abhiṣeka* (Consecration), he is regarded as the fifth patriarch of the Esoteric School. The eulogy says:
The principles of the Exoteric and Esoteric schools and the significance of the *Chen* and *Wei* commentaries;

the single perfection of the *Dayan* [Great Divination] system where Yin and Yang accord with their measures—there is no dharma, whether mundane or supramundane, that he does not thoroughly master. It is through his practice of the fifth stage that we see the lineage of the Chan Master Mazu Daoyi of Jiangxi.
Chan Master Daoyi of Jiangxi was a native of Shifang County in Hanzhou. His surname was Ma. He left the household life at Luohan Temple in his home district.
His appearance was extraordinary: he had the gait of an ox and the gaze of a tiger, his tongue could extend past his nose, and his feet were marked with the sign of the wheel.
In his youth, he received full ordination from Master Tang of Zizhou. During the Kaiyuan era, he practiced meditative concentration on Mount Heng, where he met Master Rang.
He secretly transmitted the seal of the mind. Later, he opened the Dharma at Jiangxi, where scholars from the four quarters gathered like clouds.
One day, the Master said to the assembly, "All of you, believe that your own mind is the Buddha; this very mind is the Buddha-mind.
The Great Master Bodhidharma came from South India to China to transmit the supreme vehicle of the Dharma of the single mind, in order to cause you..."

Thus they are awakened. Furthermore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* uses its text to seal the minds of sentient beings, for fear that you might be deluded and lack self-confidence regarding this Dharma of the one mind, which each and every person possesses.
Therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* takes the Buddha’s words on the mind as its central tenet.
The Gateless is the Dharma-gate. Now, one who seeks the Dharma should have nothing to seek. Outside of the mind there is no separate Buddha;
outside of the Buddha there is no separate mind. Do not grasp at good, do not grasp at evil; do not rely upon either of the two extremes of purity or defilement.

Realize that the nature of offenses is empty and cannot be apprehended in every thought-moment, for they lack intrinsic nature. Therefore, the triple world is but mind; the myriad phenomena of the universe are all one.
This is the seal of the Dharma: whatever forms are perceived are all perceptions of the mind. The mind is not a mind in itself; it exists because of form.
You need only speak according to the occasion, whether in terms of phenomena or principle, and you will encounter no obstruction whatsoever. It is the same with the wondrous fruit of Bodhi:
that which arises within the mind is what is called "form. Because one knows that form is empty, its arising is non-arising. If you understand this...
This is the meaning: you may simply put on clothes and eat meals as the occasion demands, nurturing the holy embryo and passing the time spontaneously.
What further matters are there? You have received my instruction; listen to these verses of mine: "The Mind-Ground is explained according to the occasion; Bodhi is likewise only tranquility."
Phenomena and principle are both unimpeded; that which arises is itself non-arising. This was the first generation after Nanyue.
Among his disciples who attained awakening under him were over one hundred and thirty people; seventy-six of them appeared in the world [as teachers]. Thus, the Way of Chan came to the East.
From this point on, it reached its greatest prosperity. The encomium says:

The colt gallops like a dragon; his gait is that of an ox, his gaze like a tiger. One hundred and thirty men, with a single footstep upon the earth, cause the Dharma-stream to flow westward, as the hundred rivers surge eastward.
A single drop spreads and overflows, nourishing all that was withered and parched.
The Biography of Chan Master Shitou Xiqian.
Chan Master Shitou Xiqian was a native of the Chen family of Gaoyao in Duanzhou. When his mother first became pregnant, she had no desire to eat meat.

From the time he was born as an infant until he was a young child, he required no nursemaid. Once he reached adulthood, he was known for his reliability and integrity. Among the local mountain-dwelling tribespeople, he was highly esteemed.

The people feared ghosts and spirits and practiced many illicit sacrifices, killing oxen and pouring out wine as a habitual custom. Whenever the Master went to destroy these shrines, he would seize the oxen and take them back;
in a single year, there were several dozen such instances. The village elders could not restrain him. Later, he went directly to Caoxi and received ordination.
Shortly after his master’s passing, he received the final instructions to visit Qingyuan. He then adjusted his robes and followed him. One day, Qingyuan asked, "Some say there is news from Lingnan.
The Master replied, "There is someone, but they do not say there is news from Lingnan.
Qingyuan said, "If that is so, from where do the Great and Small Collections of the scriptures come? The Master replied, "They all come from right here. Qingyuan—
He did so. Having studied under his master for a long time and having received the seal of the mind, he went to Mount Heng. To the east of Nan Temple, there was a rock shaped like a platform;
he built a hut upon it and was then known as Master Shitou. While reading the *Zhao Lun*, he reached the passage: "Only the sage is able to take all things as himself.
He then struck the table and said, "The sage has no self; there is nothing that is not himself."
It does not stop there. The Dharma-body is without marks; who can speak of self and other? Within it, the perfect mirror shines with spiritual illumination.
All phenomena embody the profound mystery and manifest of themselves. Since object and wisdom are not one, who can speak of coming and going? How sublime these words! Thereupon, he closed the scroll.
He fell asleep without realizing it and dreamed that he and the Sixth Patriarch were riding upon a tortoise, swimming within a deep pool. Upon waking, he reflected deeply on this:
"The numinous shrine represents wisdom; the pool represents the ocean of nature. I and the Patriarch are together riding upon numinous wisdom."
He roamed the ocean of the nature of reality and subsequently composed the *Cantong qi* (The Mysterious Coincidence), elucidating the essential principles of the Chan school.
He was the first generation after Qingyuan. In praise, it is said:
"The Buddha-nature of this rustic man was originally possessed; Seeking a teacher once, he immediately attained its truth."
Sitting cross-legged upon a stone, the path was exceedingly slippery; even those capable of walking there would receive a "cooling kick.
This is the biography of National Teacher Qingliang (National Teacher Chengguan).
His name was Chengguan. He was a native of Shanyin and belonged to the Xiahou clan. He left the household life at Yingtian Temple.

At fourteen, he received the tonsure. He studied the Vinaya at Qixia, received the Bodhisattva precepts from Changzhao, and transmitted the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Awakening of Faith*, and the *Fajie guan huan yuan ji* at Waguan.
Later, he traveled to Dongjing, where he received the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* from Dashi.
From Jingxi, he studied the commentaries on the *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra*, the *Mohe zhiguan*, the *Lotus Sūtra*, and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*.
He visited Niutou Zhong and Jingshan Qin to seek resolution regarding the mind-seal of the Southern School. He also visited Huiyun Mingliao to clarify the profound principles of the Northern School.

Regarding the various schools of Confucianism, Mohism, Laozi, and Zhuangzi in this land, as well as the diverse doctrines of the various sects in India, the four Vedas and five sciences, and the ritual protocols of the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings—there was nothing he did not master comprehensively.

He was extensively versed in all fields of learning. He traveled to Mount Wutai to behold the auspicious manifestations and resided at the Great Huayan Temple, where he devoted himself to the practice of the Vaipulya (Fangdeng) Repentance Rite and lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

He composed new commentaries and sub-commentaries. Later, while residing in the capital, Emperor Dezong summoned him to lecture in the inner palace, remarking that the "Sublime Dharma" had cooled his heart;
he was thus granted the title Master Qingliang and appointed as Professor Monk (*upādhyāya*). He translated the *Avataṃsaka*...
He edited the *New Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. In the fifth year of the Yuanhe era, Emperor Xianzong personally presided over the translation hall.

When the Emperor inquired about the fundamental tenets of the *Avataṃsaka* Dharma-realm, the Master attained a sudden and profound realization. By imperial decree, the relevant authorities were ordered to cast a golden seal and bestow upon him the title "Great State Preceptor Qingliang.
The Master stood nine chi and four cun tall; his hands reached below his knees, his eyes emitted light at night, and he did not blink during the day. He memorized [the scriptures] daily.

He could compose ten thousand words at once, writing seven lines simultaneously; his talent required only two brushes. He ate but one meal throughout his life and never left his robes even while sleeping. He served as the preceptor to seven emperors.

Although he lived more than a hundred years after the time of Xianshou, he received his teachings from afar. His commentaries and records total over four hundred fascicles, and he lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* fifty times.
He reached the age of one hundred and two. He is thus known as the Fourth Patriarch of the Huayan school. (Praise)
It is said:
Holding the seal of great wisdom, he encompasses the Dharma-realm; entering the gate of dhāraṇī, he possesses the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge.
With a physical stature of nine chi, he dwells in the world for a hundred years; serving as the teacher to seven successive emperors, his deeds are inconceivable.
The Biography of Chan Master Tianhuang Daowu.
Chan Master Tianhuang Daowu was a native of the Zhang family of Dongyang in Wuzhou. His divine countenance was exceptionally outstanding, and he possessed innate wisdom from childhood.
At the age of fourteen, he earnestly sought to leave the household life, but his parents would not permit it; he consequently reduced his intake of food and drink to only one meal a day.

His physical form became emaciated and haggard. His parents, having no other choice, finally granted their permission. He followed a Great Virtue (Mahāsattva) in Mingzhou, where he shaved his head and received full ordination.
He practiced the Brahma-faring with such diligence that he was esteemed for his courage and vigor. Whether in wind, rain, or the darkness of night, he sat in meditation amidst burial mounds;
his body and mind remained tranquil, free from all fear. He first visited National Teacher No. 1 at Mount Jing to receive the Dharma of the Mind, serving him diligently for five years.
Later, he visited Mazu and reaffirmed his previous understanding. He remained in attendance for two summer retreats and then went to see Shitou.
He asked, "Setting aside concentration and wisdom, by what dharma do you instruct people? Shitou said, "In my place here, there are no servants;
what would there be to set aside? He asked, "How can one realize this? Shitou said, "Can you grasp empty space? He replied, "If that is so, then it does not depend on me."

Dayu departed. Baizhang asked, "I do not know at what time or from where you have come. Dayu replied, "Daowu is no one from 'that side'. Baizhang said, "I already knew where you had come from. Dayu asked, "Why does the Master frame me with false charges? Baizhang said, "Your very person is right here. Dayu said, "Even though it is so, how is it ultimately? Please show this to future generations. Baizhang said: "Baizhang said: 'The Great Way is vast and boundless; it is not something that can be measured by the intellect. It is like empty space—how could there be any coming or going? If you seek it through the mind, you will wander in confusion for ten thousand kalpas. If you wish to see its true form, you must first cease all mental activity.

When the mind is stilled and thoughts are extinguished, the original face appears before you. This is what is called 'the transmission outside of words. Baizhang then composed a verse: "The Great Way is originally complete; Do not seek it elsewhere. If you try to grasp it with the mind, You will wander in confusion for ten thousand kalpas. Cease all mental activity, And the original face will appear. This is the transmission outside of words; It is not something to be grasped by the intellect. He then instructed his disciples: "When I am gone, you must each go to a different mountain to propagate the Dharma. Do not stay together in one place. If you remain together, you will surely fall into the ways of the world.

Furthermore, when you teach others, do not speak of my virtues or my faults. Simply point directly to the truth. If you do so, you will be able to benefit sentient beings. Baizhang then passed away. His final words were: "My life has reached its end; I shall now enter nirvana. He sat upright and passed away. His remains were cremated, and his relics were enshrined in a stupa. His legacy continues to this day.
Who was this successor? The Master attained sudden enlightenment from him and fully inherited what had been transmitted by the two former masters.
Later, he resided at Tiantai Temple in Zuojun, where the Dharma path of Shitou flourished greatly. He is the second generation under Qingyuan. In praise, it is said:
Not abiding anywhere, from whence did it come? Upon seeing the stone, the eight characters were laid bare.
Showing this to people, it is valued only for knowing that it exists. Picking it up amidst inversion is like the hand of one playing with a ball.
—The Biography of Chan Master Dazhu.
Chan Master Dazhu Huihai of Yuezhou was the son of the Zhu family of Jianzhou. He received his training under Master Zhi of Dayun Temple in Yuezhou.
When he first visited Mazu, Mazu asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Dayun Temple in Yuezhou.
Mazu asked, "What do you intend to seek by coming here? He said, "I have come to seek the Buddha-dharma. Mazu said, "In my place here, there is..."
"Things do not exist. What Dharma is there to seek? Your own precious treasury—why do you disregard it and wander away from home?
He asked, "Which one is the treasure-trove of Haima? The Patriarch said, "That which is asking me right now is your treasure-trove."

Everything was fully complete; there was nothing lacking or deficient. Its functioning was sovereign—why rely on seeking from without? Upon these words, the Master recognized his own original mind for himself, not through intellectual cognition.
He leaped with joy and offered his thanks, attending upon [his teacher] for six years. Later, because his preceptor had grown old, he returned home abruptly to provide for him.

Thereupon, he concealed his traces and hid his capacities, outwardly appearing dull and mute. He then composed the *Wuwei ruzhen yaojue* (The Essential Instructions for Entering the Truth through Sudden Enlightenment).
*The Essential Gate*, one fascicle. This constitutes the second generation under Nanyue. The encomium says:
Holding the precious treasury oneself, yet seeking it elsewhere; A single word points it out—its application is free and at ease.
Beyond this is the great pearl, perfectly bright and radiating light; It shines in every direction, never falling into a fixed pattern.
The Biography of Chan Master Xiyun of Huangbo in Hongzhou:
Chan Master Xiyun of Huangbo in Hongzhou was a native of Min. In his youth, he left the household life at Mount Huangbo in his home prefecture;
a protrusion on his forehead rose like a pearl, his speech was clear and resonant, and his disposition was profound and serene. Later, he traveled to the capital, where he encountered a person...
He was inspired and went to visit Baizhang. Baizhang asked, "From where do you come, so majestic and dignified?
The Master replied, "I come from Lingnan, majestic and dignified. Baizhang asked, "Being so majestic and dignified, for what purpose have you come?

The Master replied, "Being so majestic and dignified, I have come for no other purpose," and he immediately prostrated himself. Baizhang then asked, "How do you point to the ancestral vehicle of the past masters? The Master—
After a long silence, the Master said, "I cannot allow future generations to have this lineage cut off. The Staff-bearer said, "I thought you were someone of substance.

He then rose and entered the abbot’s quarters, followed by the Master, who said, "I have come specifically for this purpose. The Staff-bearer asked, "If that is so, then hereafter you must not let me down.
One day, the Staff-bearer asked the Master, "Where have you been? The Master replied, "To the Great [Mountains]."
While at Mount Xiong, he went out to gather mushrooms. Baizhang asked, "Did you see a tiger? The Master then let out a tiger's roar.
Baizhang raised his axe and made a gesture as if to strike him; the Master immediately gave him a slap. Baizhang laughed heartily and returned to the hall, where he said:
Beneath Mount Daxiong lived a great beast. You all must watch out for this old fellow Baizhang; today he has been personally caught by its mouth.
Once, when Prime Minister Pei was governing Wanling, he invited the Master to the prefecture and presented him with a treatise on his own understanding.
The Master received it and placed it upon his seat, not deigning to open or read it. After a long while, he asked, "Do you understand? Pei [remained silent].

[Pei Xiu] said, "I have not yet fathomed it. The Master said, "If you understand it in this way, you are still somewhat close; but if it were expressed in ink and paper, what would remain of our school?
Pei then presented him with a poem containing the line, "I intend to serve you as your disciple.

Thereafter, he requested further instruction, and [the Master] explained for him the essential heart-teachings of Huangbo. From that time on, the monastic tradition of Huangbo flourished throughout the region south of the Yangtze River.
These constitute the three generations under the Southern Peak (Nanyue). The eulogy says:
Beneath Mount Daxiong dwells a great beast; With one roar, those who hear it go deaf.
The mechanism of the swift thunder and the eye of the flashing lightning— From this point on, the "Gate-Wind" of the West has become exceedingly perilous.
The Biography of Chan Master Lingyou of Mount Gui, Tanzhou:
Chan Master Lingyou of Mount Gui was a native of the Zhao clan of Changxi, Fuzhou.

At the age of fifteen, he left home to become a monk, following Vinaya Master Fachang of Jianshan Temple in his native prefecture. He received the tonsure at Longxing Temple in Hangzhou and thoroughly investigated the Mahāyāna...

The Hīnayāna teachings. Twenty-three. While traveling in Jiangxi, he visited Baizhang. Upon seeing him, Baizhang granted him entry into the inner quarters; he subsequently became the foremost among those engaged in study.
During a period of standing in attendance, Baizhang asked, "Who is your teacher? He replied, "I am such-and-such. Baizhang said, "Go stir the embers in the hearth."
"Is there fire? The Master brushed it away and said, "There is no fire. The Zen Master (Zhaozhou) rose personally and probed deeply, finding a small amount of fire.
He held it up and showed it to the Master, saying, "You say there is no 'this'—what about this? From this, the Master attained awakening; he bowed in gratitude and explained his understanding.
The Zen Master said, "This is merely a temporary crossroads. As the Sutra says: 'If you wish to know the meaning of Buddha-nature, you should observe the conditions of time and season.'"
When the proper time arrives, it is like suddenly awakening from a dream or suddenly remembering what was forgotten; one then realizes that one's own property was never obtained from another.
Thus the Patriarch said: "Awakening is the same as non-awakening; there is no mind and there are no dharmas. It is simply the absence of delusion."
The minds of ordinary beings and sages are equal; the fundamental nature of the mind is originally complete. Since you are now thus, protect and maintain it well yourself.
One day the Master ascended the hall and said: "After this old monk passes away, I shall become a water buffalo at the home of a lay donor at the foot of the mountain.
On my right flank, I will write five characters that say: 'A monk of Mt. Gui, [Name]. At such a time, if someone calls out..."
"To be a monk of Mount Gui is to be a water buffalo; to call him a water buffalo is to be a monk of Mount Gui.
Ultimately, what should he be called? Yangshan stepped forward, prostrated, and withdrew. From this point on, it was known as the Guiyang School.
There were many such karmic encounters. This constitutes the third generation under Nanyue. The eulogy says:
Bai Zhang’s cliffs stood sheer; those who came gazed upon the precipice. Only the Master entered directly, and as he pushed through the fire, his mind was opened.
Acting as an ox among the herd, he walked among the heterodox. Yangshan saw through him, and the reputation of their father-son lineage was established.
This is the biography of Chan Master Guifeng Mi.
Chan Master Guifeng, whose name was Zongmi, was a native of Guozhou and surnamed He. His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations.

In the second year of the Yuanhe era of Emperor Xianzong, while he was preparing to go to the capital to take the imperial examinations, he happened upon the Dharma seat of Chan Master Daoyuan of Suizhou and came to savor his teachings and methods.

He then sought to receive the tonsure and the full precepts (*upasampadā*). One day, while following the assembly of monks to a meal at the home of Ren Guan, a government official, he sat in the lowest seat.
As he received the scriptures in order, he came upon the twelve chapters of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (the *Yuanjue jing*). Before he had finished a single fascicle, he attained profound realization.

Upon returning, he informed Yuan [Zhao]. Yuan said, "The Buddhas have entrusted this scripture to you. You shall greatly propagate the teaching of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuantun*). You must practice it."
"Let it be so! Do not remain stagnant in one corner. Having thus taken his leave, he went to visit Chan Master Zhong of Jingnan and Chan Master Zhao of Luoyang;

both granted him their seal of approval. Upon reaching Xianghan, he encountered a sick monk who entrusted him with a commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which was composed by the Great Master Qingliang Guanzhi of the Capital.
Reading it, he said with joy: "In Chan, I have met the Southern School; in the teachings, I have encountered the *Awakening of Faith* (Yuánjué). One—
Upon hearing these words, his mind was opened and enlightened. Now, having further attained this Great Dharma, he thought, "How fortunate I am! He then proceeded to lecture upon it.
As he had not yet met Qingliang in person, he sent a letter from afar to express the etiquette due to a disciple. Qingliang’s seal of approval read:
"As for one who wanders with me through the nature-ocean of Vairocana, who could it be other than you? You may truly be likened to a son of the Turning-Wheel King."

Emperor Wenzong issued an edict for him to enter the palace and bestowed upon him purple robes. The Emperor repeatedly inquired about the essentials of the Dharma, and the court officials turned to him with devotion.

Among them, only Prime Minister Pei Xiu entered deeply into the inner sanctum of his teaching and served as a lay protector who received his instructions. The Master [Zongmi] observed that practitioners of Chan and the doctrinal schools were mutually disparaging one another.

He then composed the *Chan-yuan ch'üan* (Exposition of the Source of Dhyāna), as well as commentaries and sub-commentaries on various sutras and treatises—including the *Yuanjue*, *Avataṃsaka*, *Vajracchedikā*, *Śraddhotpāda*, and *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, along with the *Dharmadhātudarśana-prakaraṇa* and the *Caryāpraṇidhāna-parivarta*—and the *Daochang xiuzheng yi* (Ritual for Cultivation and Realization in the Practice Hall). In total, these comprise more than ninety fascicles.
He is thus known as the Fifth Patriarch of the Huayan school. The eulogy says:
To attain the rank of Marquis over ten thousand *li*, one casts aside the writing brush;

to cast oneself directly into the ocean of the nature beyond birth and death, one receives the seal of the True Son and enters the gate of the Dharma-realm—this is what is called being a "Sublime Sage.
This is the Biography of Chan Master Linji Yixuan.
Chan Master Linji Yixuan of Zhenzhou was the son of the Xing family from Caizhou. From his youth, he bore the aspiration to transcend the mundane world.
Upon shaving his head and receiving full ordination, he first visited Huangbo. He asked, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?

Before he had even finished speaking, Huangbo struck him. This occurred three times; each time he asked the same question, he received a severe beating. The Master did not attain realization and consequently took his leave.

Huangbo said, "There is no need for you to go elsewhere; simply go to the head of the rapids at Gaoyuan and consult Dayu. He will surely explain it for you. When the Master arrived at Dayu’s place, Dayu asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "I have come from Huangbo. Dayu asked, "What words did Huangbo say? The Master said, "Three times I asked about the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma, and three times I was struck with a staff. Dayu said, "Huangbo is a man of great compassion; he would rather strike you than let you go away with a mere intellectual understanding. The Master then asked, "What shall I do now? Dayu said, "Go back and ask him again. If he strikes you again, come back and tell me. I will then explain it to you. The Master returned to Huangbo and asked the same question as before. Huangbo struck him again. Upon returning, the Master told Dayu, "Huangbo struck me once more. Dayu said, "The old fellow truly has great compassion; he would rather strike you than let you go away with a mere intellectual understanding. The Master said, "Just now, when he struck me, I felt as though my body and mind were shattered into pieces. Dayu said, "If so, go wash your bowl; there is food ready to be served. At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment. He then returned to Dayu and said, "My body and mind are shattered into pieces. Dayu said, "If so, go wash your bowl; there is food ready to be served. The Master then composed a verse: "The thirty years of bitter toil / Were all for nothing; / Today I have met the true teacher / And am free from the debt of gratitude. Dayu said, "You have finally understood Huangbo’s intent. The Master then took leave of Dayu and returned to Huangbo. Huangbo asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "I have come from Dayu. Huangbo asked, "What did he say? The Master recounted everything that had occurred. Huangbo said, "That fellow is indeed a man of great compassion; he would rather strike you than let you go away with a mere intellectual understanding. The Master then bowed and withdrew. Later, when Huangbo was about to pass away, he summoned the Master and said, "When I was at Xichan Temple, I dreamed of a golden dragon coiling around my staff. Now I entrust this staff to you; you must protect it well. The Master wept and said, "I am unworthy of such a great responsibility. Huangbo said, "Do not speak of worthiness or unworthiness. Go and take it. The Master then took the staff and wept. Huangbo said, "Do not cry; you have now inherited the Dharma. The Master then bowed and withdrew. After Huangbo passed away, the Master stayed at Dayu for several days. Dayu said, "You should go see Nanquan. The Master said, "Nanquan is an old fellow who knows how to deceive people. Dayu said, "He will surely be able to help you. The Master then went to Nanquan. Nanquan asked, "Where have you come from? The Master replied, "I have come from Dayu. Nanquan said, "Did Dayu give you the seal of approval? The Master said, "Dayu is a man of great compassion; he would rather strike me than let me go away with a mere intellectual understanding. Nanquan said, "Is that so? Let me test you. What did he say? The Master recounted the story of his enlightenment. Nanquan said, "So it is! So it is! The Master then bowed and withdrew. [The Master] asked, "Does so-and-so have faults or not? Yuyou said, "Huangbo’s heart is so earnest and compassionate that he has caused you to attain thorough penetration;

yet you come here again to ask whether he has faults or not. At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment and said, "So it turns out that Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma amounts to nothing more than this.
Yuyou grabbed him and said, "You bed-wetting little devil! Just now you said..."
"Whether there was a fault or not, you now say, 'Huangbo’s Buddha-dharma is nothing more than this. What principle have you seen? Speak quickly! Speak quickly!
The Master struck Daoyu three times under the ribs. Daoyu pushed him away and said, "Your teacher is Huangbo;
it is none of my business. The Master took his leave and returned to Huangbo. Upon seeing him, Huangbo said, "This fellow has come back again!"
"Go, go! When will you ever reach the end? The Master said, "It is precisely because my compassionate heart is too earnest. Baizhang asked, "Where have you been coming from?
The Master replied, "Yesterday I received your instruction and went to consult Dayu; that is where I have come from. Baizhang asked, "What words did Dayu say?"
The Master brought up the previous conversation. Baizhang said, "That old fellow Dayu is too talkative; wait until he comes here, and I will give him a thorough beating.

The Master said, "What need is there to wait? I shall strike him right now," and immediately slapped him. Baizhang said, "This madman has come here to pull at the tiger's whiskers. The Master then shouted.
Baizhang called to his attendant, "Lead this madman away to attend to the hall duties. From [that time on].
The swift and sharp wit of this Chan school began with the Master himself. He was the fourth generation descendant of Nanyue in the Linji lineage.
In praise, it is said:
"As soon as Huangbo’s lion-like claws and fangs were revealed, Dayu’s skill was like a hawk seizing a rabbit."
Three fists under the armpits, one palm on the cheek—just now you have met his edge; this was not mere recklessness.
The Biography of Chan Master Liangjia Wuben of Dongshan in Ruizhou:
Chan Master Dongshan Jia was the son of the Yu family of Kuaiji. He left home to become a monk at a young age. From...

The master was reciting the Heart Sūtra when he reached the passage, "No eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. Suddenly, he touched his own face with his hand and asked the master, "I have eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and so forth;
why does the sūtra say there are none? The master was startled and marveled at him, saying, "I am not your teacher.
He then directed him to Mount Wuxie to pay respects to Chan Master Mo and receive the tonsure. He was twenty years old at the time.
While traveling, he first visited Mount Gui (Huishan). He brought up the story of Master Zhong’s “insentient beings preaching the Dharma” to seek further instruction.
Huishan provided an explanation, but it did not accord with his understanding. Thereupon, he was directed to visit Yunyan. The Master then took his leave and went straight to Yunyan.

He repeated the previous story and asked, "Regarding 'insentient beings preaching the Dharma,' which scriptural authority does this encompass? Yunyan said, "Have you not seen it stated in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* that the waterfowl and the forest trees..."

Everyone was recollecting the Buddha and recollecting the Dharma. At this, the Master had an awakening and composed a verse, saying: "How wondrous! How truly wondrous! The insentient preaching the Dharma is inconceivable.
If one listens with the ears, it will ultimately be difficult to understand; Only when hearing through the faculty of sight does one come to know.

After the Master had practiced for a long time, one day he took his leave of Guishan and asked: "Suppose after a hundred years someone were to ask: 'Can you still paint [your likeness]? What would you do?"
"Is this the true master? How shall I respond? Yan remained silent for a long while and said, "It is just this. The Master hesitated.
Yan said, "Dharma brother Jia, you who take up this matter must be extremely careful. The Master still harbored doubts. Later, while crossing a stream, he beheld his own reflection.
He attained great enlightenment regarding the original intent [of his teacher]. He spoke a verse, saying: "Be most careful not to seek it from another;
To do so would distance you far from me. I shall now go forth alone, And everywhere I shall encounter him. He is precisely me at this very moment, Yet I am not he.
One must understand it in this way Before one can finally accord with Suchness (tathatā). Thereafter, he flourished in the teaching at Dongshan in Gaoyang, Yuzhang. His name was Quan.
He opened up the five ranks and skillfully received the three roots; he extensively expounded the single sound and broadly propagated it for the myriad species.
Transversely drawing his jeweled sword, he cut through the dense forest of various views; wondrously harmonizing with the great penetration, he severed the myriad ends of artificial fabrication.

Furthermore, he attained Cao Shan’s profound and clear realization of the ultimate meaning, his sublime songs and excellent maxims embodying the Way through the mutual interplay of ruler and minister and the shifting of the partial and the absolute. Thus, the whole world shared in this.
He is posthumously honored as the founder of the Caodong school; he is the fourth generation descendant of Qingyuan. The eulogy says:
"The original face is seen at a single touch; The insentient preaching of Dharma seems still lacking.
Having seen Yunyan overturn the old nest, Only upon seeing one's reflection while crossing water does one finally attain thorough penetration."
The Biography of Chan Master Cao Shan Ji:
Chan Master Benji of Cao Mountain in Fuzhou was the son of the Huang family of Putian. In his youth, he studied Confucianism.

At the age of nineteen, he left home to become a monk and received full ordination. He subsequently went to visit Dongshan, who asked, "What is your name, Venerable? The Master replied, "Benji. Dongshan said:
"What about that? The Master replied, "It is not called 'original stillness'. Fushan deeply esteemed him; from then on, he entered the Master's room and remained there for several years.

Fushan secretly transmitted to him the essential principles of the Dongshan school, after which he took his leave to go to Caoxi to pay homage at the ancestral pagoda, and subsequently returned to Yihuang.

The assembly requested that he expound the Dharma. The Master’s aspiration was to emulate the Sixth Patriarch; consequently, he named his mountain residence "Cao" (after Caoxi). His dharma seat flourished greatly, and students gathered like clouds.

The lineage of Dongshan reached its peak of prosperity during the Master's time. When a monk asked about the essential principles of the Five Ranks regarding Sovereign and臣 (Minister), the Master said:
"The Correct Position is the realm of emptiness; originally there is nothing therein. The Partial Position is the realm of form; it possesses [phenomena]."

The myriad phenomena are its form. "Centered within the partial" refers to turning one's back on principle to engage with phenomena. "Partial centered within the correct" refers to relinquishing phenomena to enter into principle.

"Simultaneously encompassing both" refers to the seamless integration of principle and phenomena, responding mysteriously to all conditions without falling into any state of existence; it is neither defiled nor pure, neither correct nor partial.
Therefore, it is called the "Vast and Mysterious Great Way," the "Unattached True Teaching. The former masters of antiquity have all pointed to this single stage.
Most wondrous and most profound! One must examine and discern this with care: the Sovereign represents the position of correctness, while the Minister represents the position of partiality.

When the Minister faces the Sovereign, it is "partiality within correctness"; when the Sovereign looks upon the Minister, it is "correctness within partiality. The union of the Way of Sovereign and Minister is expressed through this "comprehensive" language. The Master further said:

"To speak in terms of the partiality and correctness of Sovereign and Minister is because one does not wish to offend the Center; thus, when a Minister addresses a Sovereign, he does not dare to name him directly."
He said, "It is so. This is the essential core of my Dharma school. He then composed a verse, saying: "The student must first recognize their own fundamental source;

Do not conflate the ultimate reality with inert emptiness. The wondrously luminous essence fully knows how to avoid injury and offense; Its power lies in meeting conditions without borrowing from the center."

When speech issues forth, it is taught that even fire cannot burn it; when practicing in secret, one must be identical to the ancients. To have affairs while lacking a body is to transcend the byways;

to lack both affairs and a body is to fall into the beginning and the end. Therefore, at the moment of responding to conditions, one must avoid speech that is "ten parts complete" (absolute certainty);
rather, one prizes ambiguity and mutual interpenetration. This is the fundamental principle of the Cao-Dong school. Being the fifth generation under Qingyuan, the eulogy says:
A capacity that transcends categories leaves no trace of fame; an eye that surpasses the mundane recognizes all at once.
The five ranks are empty and profound, their fundamental principle subtle and dense. Therefore, even to this day, they remain as black as lacquer.
This is the biography of Chan Master Niaoke Daolin.
Chan Master Daolin of Niaoke in Hangzhou was originally from Fuyang in that same prefecture. His surname was Pan and his mother’s was Zhu.
She dreamed that sunlight entered her mouth, and consequently became pregnant. At the time of his birth, a wondrous fragrance filled the room; he was thus named Xiangguang (Fragrant Light).
He left home at the age of nine and received full ordination at Guoyuan Temple in Jingzhou at twenty-one. Later, he traveled to Ximing [Temple] in Chang’an.

The Master [Zongmi] further studied with Master Fali of the temple. He studied the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Awakening of Faith*. Fali showed him verses on truth and falsehood (*tattva-mṛṣā*) and instructed him to practice *dhyāna*.
The Master asked, "How should one first contemplate? How should one apply the mind? Fali remained silent for a long time.

The Master performed three prostrations and withdrew. Later, he returned south and visited National Teacher Guoyi of Mount Jing, where he realized the ground of his own mind. Thereupon, he encountered Master Qin...
Looking toward the mountains, he saw tall pines with lush, dense foliage that curved and twisted like parasols. He subsequently took up residence upon one of them;

thus, people of the time called him Chan Master Niaoke (Nest-of-Birds). When Minister Bai Juyi was sent to govern this prefecture, he entered the mountains to visit the master and asked, "The place where the Chan Master dwells is extremely precarious.
The master replied, "Your Excellency, the danger is even greater. Bai said:

The disciple said, "When one’s position is as stable as the mountains and rivers, what danger could there be? The Master replied, "When firewood and flame intersect, the nature of consciousness does not rest;
is this not a danger? The disciple asked again, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "Commit no evil; practice all that is good.
Baizhang said, "Even a three-year-old child understands how to say that. The Master replied, "A three-year-old child..."
"Though you have attained the Way, at eighty years old you still cannot walk. Having spoken thus, he performed a prostration and withdrew.
This constitutes the eighth generation descending from the side of the Fourth Patriarch. The eulogy says:
Riding the sunlight, he comes to abide in his own nature; thus, as soon as he emerges with his head, he naturally attains wondrous enlightenment.
While those who nest among the tall pines may say it is perilous, one need only observe others without self-examination—this is the tradition of the Chan Master Xuefeng Cun.
Chan Master Yicun of Xuefeng in Fuzhou was the son of the Zeng family of Quanzhou. His family had served the Buddha for generations.
From his infancy, he loathed the consumption of meat; whenever he heard the sound of bells or chanting, or saw banners, flowers, or consecrated images, his countenance would move with emotion.
At the age of twelve, while traveling with his father to Yujian Temple in Putian, he encountered Vinaya Master Qingxuan and immediately prostrated himself before him.
He replied, "He is my teacher. He then remained there to serve him. Having shaved his head and received full ordination, he participated in numerous Zen assemblies.

He went to visit Deshan and asked, "Regarding the ancestral vehicle of our school, does a student have any share in it or not? Deshan struck him with a staff and said, "Speak! He replied, "I do not understand.
The following day, he requested further instruction. Deshan said, "In my school, there are no words or phrases; in truth, there is not a single dharma to be given to anyone."
The Master attained an awakening as a result of this. When Yantou heard of it, he said, "The old man Deshan has a backbone as hard as iron;
it cannot be bent. Nevertheless, even so, within the gate of proclaiming the Teaching, he still falls short by a small measure.
The Master studied together with Yantou and deeply benefited from their mutual砥砺 (polishing and correction). When the Master and Yantou took their leave of Deshan, Deshan asked, "What..."
“Where are you going? Tou said, “I am taking leave of the Master for a while to go down the mountain. Shan said, “What will you do after that? Tou said, “I shall not forget.
Shan said, “On what basis do you make such a statement? Tou said, “Have you not heard that one must have wisdom exceeding that of the teacher before one may transmit the teachings?
If one’s wisdom is equal to the teacher’s, it is but half the virtue of the teacher. Shan said, “So it is, so it is. You should...”
"Guard it well. The master prostrated together with him and withdrew. Later, he returned to Min Province and established the Dharma at Xuefeng.
He constantly taught his students to sit upright like a withered tree stump; thus, the hall was known as the "Withered Tree Hall.
From there, the two schools of Yunmen and Fayan emerged. This was the fifth generation under Qingyuan. The eulogy says:

That which is familiar is difficult to forget; the habitual tendencies toward vegetables and bamboo shoots remain. The sound of the bells and the chanting of the sutras intoxicate the mind of the teacher;
his staff is like a dragon’s jaw and his mouth is like iron. Therefore, he emerges from the body naturally transcendent. Appendix:
Eulogy on Chan Master Yunmen Wenyan (Dharma Heir of Xuefeng).
As soon as he saw Muzhou close the door and push him out, [Yunmen] pressed his body against him with a shove, instantly breaking one of his legs;
from that moment on, he turned himself around to cover heaven and earth. Before seeing Xuefeng, [Yunmen] had already attained a mental accord.
Chan Master Fayen Yi (who succeeded Faluo Guichen; Chen succeeded Xuansha Shibei; Bei succeeded Xuefeng) offered this eulogy.
All things are fully manifested, free from lingering hesitation; amidst the myriad phenomena, one stands forth with majestic dignity.
With a single flavor of equanimity, that which is right before one’s eyes is it. As soon as thought falls, one has already fallen into the secondary.
