The Biography of Chan Master Shou-shan Sheng-nian of Ruzhou:
Chan Master Shou-shan Sheng-nian was the son of the Di clan of Lai Prefecture. He left the household life at Nan-chen Monastery in his native prefecture.

Having received full ordination at a temple, he traveled extensively among various monastic assemblies. He constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra* in secret, so that the community came to know him as "Nian Fahua" (The One Who Recites the Lotus).
Later, while serving as the guest prefect under Fengxue, one day, as he stood in attendance, Fengxue shed tears and said to him:
"Alas, the Way of Linji is on the verge of falling to the ground through me," [Zhaozhou] said. The Master asked, "Looking at this assembly, is there no one at all?
Xuefeng replied, "There are many who are clever, but few who have seen their nature. The Master asked, "What about someone like me?"
Xue said, "Although I have long looked forward to you, I still fear that you may remain attached to this scripture and be unable to let it go.
The Master said, "That is acceptable; I wish to hear its essential point. Xue then ascended the hall and, raising his hand, said:
"When the World-Honored One, with his blue-lotus eyes, looked out upon the great assembly—right at such a moment, what could he have said? If one says he spoke without speaking..."
This was another instance of being buried [in oblivion]. The former sage said, "Tell me, what did he say? The Master then brushed his sleeves and went down.
Xue threw down his staff and returned to the abbot's quarters. The attendant followed him and asked for clarification, saying, "Why did Nian Fahua not respond to the Master?
Xue replied, "Nian Fahua understood. The next day, the Master and Zhen the garden overseer both paid their respects.
Xue asked Zhen, "What is the Buddha’s 'speaking that which is not spoken'? Zhen said, "A magpie calls from the top of a tree.
Xue said, "Why do you perform so much foolish merit? He then asked the Master, "How about you? The Master said: *Note: The Master's response is omitted in the source text provided.*

His movements and expressions revealed the ancient path; he did not fall into the trap of silent stillness. Xue said to Zhen, "Why do you not look at the recorded sayings (*xià yǔ*) from the *Lotus Sūtra*?
The Master received Wind Cave’s seal of approval, then vanished his traces and concealed his brilliance such that no one knew of him.
Later, he opened the Dharma at Shoushan, greatly reviving the Way of Linji. He was the eighth generation descendant of Nanyue. In praise, it is said:
Having held the Lotus Sutra for seven volumes for a long time, one word of letting go reveals that which is inherently present;
this unspeakable teaching appears the moment it is brought forth. To shake off one’s sleeves and walk away—how swift and convenient!
From the *Biography of Chan Master Yongming Yanshou*.
Chan Master Huiji Yongming Yanshou Zhijue of Hangzhou was the son of the Wang family of Yuhang. From his youth, he turned his heart toward the Buddha-vehicle.
Once he reached adulthood, he abstained from meat and pungent roots, eating only one meal a day. He upheld the Lotus Sūtra and was able to recite it entirely within sixty days.
At the age of twenty-eight, he served as the military commander of Huating. King Wenmu of Wuyue, recognizing the Master’s aspiration for the Way, permitted him to follow his resolve;
he thus took Cuiyan of Longce Monastery as his teacher. He devoted himself to his duties with such diligence that he forgot his own person:

his clothing was never of silk or down, and his food never of rich flavors. With wild vegetables and coarse cloth tunics, he sustained himself from day to day. Subsequently, he went to Mount Tiantai for a period of ninety days.
While he was practicing meditation, a bird nested within the folds of his robe. Later, upon visiting National Teacher Yao, he was immediately perceived as a man of great potential;

the Master bestowed upon him the profound essence of the teachings in secret and said to him, "You have a karmic affinity with the Grand Marshal; in the future, you shall greatly promote the Buddhist cause. He first resided at Xuedou.
A monk asked, "How does one tread the single path of Xuedou? The Master replied, "At every step, frosty flowers form. Thus it is said.
Regarding the phrase "thoroughly frozen," the Master had a verse that said: "The lone ape cries as the midnight moon falls; The wild guest chants until the midnight lamp is spent.
Who can find the true meaning in this state at this time? Only the meditation monk sitting deep within the white clouds. —Prince Qian Zhongyi.

He requested permission to open Lingyin Monastery. The following year, he moved to Yongming, where his assembly numbered over two thousand. He resided there for fifteen years, ordaining one thousand seven hundred disciples.

He then entered Tiantai Mountain, where he ordained approximately ten thousand people. He released living beings in numbers beyond calculation. Every day, he performed one hundred and eight kinds of skillful means;
with the remaining energy from his practice of the Way, he maintained the Lotus Sūtra. (Total count: 135 characters)

He compiled thirteen thousand fascicles and authored the *Zongjing Lu* (Record of the Mirror of the Source) in one hundred volumes. His poetry, gāthās, and prose compositions totalled several million words.
The King of Goryeo from overseas sent a letter expressing his status as a disciple; thirty-six monks from that country all received his seal of transmission.
He was the tenth generation descendant of Qingyuan. The eulogy says:
Riding the wheel of great vows, he emerged as an auspicious sign for the Dharma; The gate of *dhāraṇī* opened, and all practices were fully perfected.
Hanging the mirror of single-mindedness, he shone brightly upon the myriad things; The Buddha-sun was at its zenith in the sky, illuminating all that is obscure.
The Biography of Chan Master Ciming Yuan.
Chan Master Chiming Ciyuan of Shishuang in Tanzhou was the son of the Li family of Quanzhou. In his youth, he was a scholar;
at the age of twenty-two, he left home to become a monk at Yinjing Temple on Mount Xiang. His mother, who possessed virtuous conduct, encouraged him to travel abroad to seek the Dharma.

Having heard of Fenyang’s reputation for spiritual eminence, he went there to pay his respects. Fenyang looked at him and silently took note of him as a vessel of potential. For two years, however, he did not permit him to enter the inner sanctum.
Whenever they met, Fenyang would invariably scold and revile him, or disparage and denounce various other teachers.

Furthermore, whenever he offered instruction, it was always of a mundane and vulgar nature. One night, the student complained, saying: "Since arriving at this Dharma seat, two summers have already passed, yet I have received no guidance; I have only seen my worldly [delusions] increase."
"Worldly dust and toil! As the years and months pass in a blur, my own task remains unclarified; I have lost the benefit of leaving the household life.
Before he had finished speaking, Yang stared at him intently and scolded, "This evil teacher! How dare you try to deceive me? In a rage, Yang raised his staff to drive him away.

The Master attempted to intervene to rescue him, but Yang covered the Master’s mouth. At that moment, the Master attained great enlightenment and said, "Now I know that Linji’s Way transcends ordinary sentiment. To serve..."
After seven years, he took his leave and went to rely upon Chan Master Ming-song of Tang.

Ming-song said to him, "The Inner Secretary Yang Dainan possesses lofty insight and is steady and authentic in his entry into the Way; you must not fail to see him. Thereupon, the Master went to visit Dainan.
Their words and spiritual resonance met perfectly, and [Dainan] regretted having met him so late. At court, Dainan said to the Prince Consort Li Zunxu: "Recently I have obtained..."
A certain practitioner was truly a lion of the Western River. Li said, "I am constrained by official duties and cannot go to see you; what can be done?
Nanmo remained silent and returned home, saying to his master, "Lord Li is one among those who follow the Buddha-dharma.

Having heard that your reputation for the Way has reached afar, he harbors a desire to meet you, yet he is precisely bound by the law. Thereupon, at dawn, the Master went to visit Lord Li; upon seeing him, they were both delighted.
Qi. At this time, the Master and the two elders, Yang and Li, were considered the most intimate within the Dharma-gate. When Lord Li passed away, the Master attended his burial mound.
Upon hearing of this, Emperor Renzong praised him and issued an edict granting him an official boat for his return home.
The Master entered the world to preach the Dharma and later resided at Shishuang. He was a successor of Fenyang Zao and belonged to the tenth generation under Nanyue. The eulogy says:
Those who encounter the contrary mechanism of the West River do not recognize it; personally encountering it, they cover their mouths and lose their nostrils.
Its mechanism strikes out with such rapidity that it cannot be restrained. Those with clear eyes call him a true lion cub.
—From the Biography of Chan Master Tianyi Huai.
Chan Master Tianyi Yihuai of Yuezhou was the son of the Chen family of Leqing in Yongjia. His family had followed the occupation of fishing for generations.

His mother dreamed that a star fell upon her house and she subsequently conceived; at his birth, there were many auspicious signs. As a child, he sat at the stern of a boat when his father caught a fish and gave it to him to string.
The Master immediately threw it secretly into the river. His father became angry and beat him, yet the Master remained as serene as before.
Therefore, there was the world-transcending master Chou Shouzhi. He traveled extensively through the capital, where he became a novice monk (*śrāmaṇera*) at Jingde Temple.

Later, having passed the scriptural examinations, he received full ordination. Initially, he visited Jinluan and Shan Yue of Xian County, both of whom granted him their seal of approval. Subsequently, he went to Gusu and paid his respects to Mingjue at Cuifeng.
Mingjue asked, "What is your name? He replied, "Yihuai. Mingjue said, "Why do you not name yourself Huaiyi? He replied:
At that time, he attained realization. Huairang asked, "Who gave you this name? He replied, "I have been receiving precepts for ten years now.
Huairang said, "How many pairs of straw sandals have you worn out on your travels? He replied, "Master, do not deceive people.
Huairang said, "I too am without measure; you too are without measure. What will you do? The teacher was speechless. Huairang struck him and said, "Take off [your sandals]!"
"You empty-headed talker, get out! One day, while entering the room for instruction, Jué said, "It cannot be thus;

it cannot be not-thus; it cannot be both thus and not-thus. As the Master hesitated, Jué struck him again. This occurred several times. Subsequently, the Master served as the water-bearer. While drawing water, his carrying pole broke and he suddenly fell, whereupon he attained great enlightenment.

He then composed a verse of realization: The water is drawn from the well, The bucket is lowered and raised. When the bucket is empty, it is light; When full, it is heavy. If you wish to know the Great Way, Look at the bucket being carried back.
He said: "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Standing alone on one foot atop a ten-thousand-fathom peak, he snatches the bright pearl from the jaws of the black dragon.
With a single word, he exposes the deception of Vimalakīrti. Juewen struck the desk and praised him, saying it was excellent. Later, he sat upon the seat of enlightenment seven times.
He transformed and traveled throughout the land, and those who inherited his Dharma were very numerous. This constitutes the tenth generation under Qingyuan. The eulogy says:
His original nature is compassionate, coming to repay his karmic debts from former lives; Upon seeing the fish, he released them at once with his hand.
Having escaped the net of worldly dust, he ascended to the stage of enlightenment; The carrying pole was broken, the bucket discarded, and empty space shattered to pieces.
The Biography of Chan Master Foyin Yuan:
Chan Master Foyin’s name was Liaoyuan; his style name was Juelao. He was a native of Fuliang and belonged to the Lin clan. His family had followed the Confucian profession for generations.

When the Master was two years old, he could recite the *Analects* and various poems with clear, resonant intonation. By the age of five, he had memorized three thousand poems. Upon reaching adulthood...
He followed a teacher and studied the Five Classics, mastering their great principles. Upon reading the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he attained a profound realization;

he then cast aside all that he had previously learned and informed his parents of his desire to leave the household life. He paid homage to the śramaṇa Riyong of Baoji Temple and was tested on the *Lotus Sūtra* for ordination.
After receiving full precepts, he traveled to Mount Lu to visit the practitioner Kai-xian Xian. Xian prided himself on being a "roaming giant of the seas," looking down upon others with contempt.
Later, when Yuan was a junior monk, his responses to the Master’s questions were so swift and incisive that the Master praised him and subsequently made him his successor.
He went to visit Nianchuan (Nanquan) Yuantong, who remarked, "His skeletal structure already resembles Xuedou; he is a talent of the future. Yuan remained there to serve as the Secretary.

When the seat at Chengtian Temple in Jiangzhou became vacant, Nianchuan recommended Yuan for the appointment. At that time, Yuan was twenty-eight years old. From Chengtian, he was transferred to Dou Mountain in Huai.
In Fangzhou, there were Kaixian and Guizong; in Runzhou, Jinniu and Jiaoshan; and in Jiangxi, Dayang and Yunju.
For forty years, he transformed both the monastic and lay communities through his virtue. Among the worthy officials and scholars, many befriended him.
When Su Dongpo was exiled to Huangzhou, the Master resided at Guizong; their exchange of exquisite verses vied with the splendor of clouds and mists. At that time, Li Boshi served as...
The Master had his portrait painted. He said, "You must depict me making a laughing face. Then he composed this eulogy for himself: "Master Li is a stone qilin from the heavens;

He has transmitted the true likeness of the Cloud Dweller (Yunju Daozhe). Not for the sake of the 'Plucking the Flower' to clarify the Great Matter, Why would he casually open his mouth to laugh at anyone?
A clay ox needlessly sniffs before the wind; A withered tree brings forth spring amidst the snow. Facing the Hall."
No one in the hall recognized him. On the fourth day of the first month of the first year of the Yuánfú era, while listening to the conversation of a guest, he attained realization of the heart-mind;

with a single laugh, he passed away, just as depicted in the portrait. The eulogy says: A free-spirited man in an age of Great Peace, On the fourth day of the first month of the first year of Yuánfú, Hearing the words of a guest, his heart attained resonance; With a smile, he returned to the source—just as the likeness portrays. The eulogy says:
The habitual tendencies of words have leaked forth since birth; Speaking Zen with a reckless mouth, he never fell into a fixed pattern.
He pre-emptively painted a smile, not knowing what it was for; To pass away with a broad laugh—this alone is the lineage record of Chan Master Huanglong Nan.
Chan Master Hui-nan of Huanglong in Longxing Prefecture was the son of the Zhang family of Xinzhou.

Having left the household life, he traveled to visit various masters and relied upon Chan Master Letan, where he was assigned a seat to preach the Dharma; his reputation resounded throughout all quarters. Later, he visited Ciming.

Upon hearing that Ciming had criticized and dismantled every point from various other schools, numbering them as instances of erroneous interpretation, the Master became disheartened. He then entered Ciming’s chamber, and Ciming appointed him to oversee the administrative affairs.
The Secretary had repeatedly heard [the Master] give instructions but did not find them resonant. One day he asked directly:
"Zhaozhou said, 'The old woman of Mount Tai has been thoroughly exposed by me. Tell me, where exactly was she exposed? The Master broke into a sweat and could offer no further reply.
The next day the Secretary visited again; Ming scolded him incessantly. The Secretary said, "Is scolding the compassionate bestowal of the Dharma?"
Ming said, "Do you understand this as an insult? At these words, the Master attained great enlightenment and composed a verse, saying:
"Standing out among the groves is Zhaozhou; The old woman’s discernment leaves no room for cause. Now the four seas are as clear as a mirror; Let travelers not treat the road as an enemy.
He presented this to Ciming, who nodded in approval. Later, he established the Dharma at Tong’an, where his eloquence and discernment were unimpeded.
Once, while in his quarters, he asked a monk, "Everyone has their own karmic affinity for birth; where is the Venerable One’s affinity for birth?
At the very moment of this question and answer, he reached out his hand and said, "How does my hand compare to the Buddha’s hand?

He then asked about what the masters of various regions had attained through their practice, and extending his legs, he said, "How do my feet compare to a donkey’s feet? He continued in this manner for over thirty years.
Among the monks of his time, few were able to accord with his spiritual capacity. These are known as the "Three Barriers" (Sanguan) of Huanglong, which greatly revitalized the Way of Linji.
He was the eleventh generation descendant of Nanyue. The eulogy says:
The Patriarchal Style of the Lion Father and Son of West River: Who dares to face the blade when it is held upside down?
If the Master but once strikes, the sentiments of sage and ordinary are exhausted. Within the room, the three barriers are fully raised as the true command.
The Transmission of Chan Master Yangqi Hui.

Chan Master Fănghuì of Yángqí in Yuánzhōu was the son of the Lěng family of Yíchūn in that prefecture. From his youth, he was alert and quick-witted; upon reaching adulthood, he did not pursue the brush and inkstone.

He was registered for the tax on commercial goods, but having been repeatedly censured for dereliction of duty, he fled by night. Arriving at Jiǔfēng in Ruìzhōu, he felt as though he were visiting an old acquaintance;

filled with affection, he could not bear to leave and subsequently shaved his head. Whenever he read the sutras, his mind merged with them and his spirit attained realization. He then went to attend...
He called upon Ciming. From Nanyuan, he moved to Daowu and Shichuang, serving in both monasteries as an assistant administrator.
Although he relied upon him for a long time, he had not yet attained awakening. Whenever he came to consult, Ciming would say, "The affairs of the storehouse are many; go now.
On another day when he asked again, Ciming said, "In the future, your disciples and grand-disciples will fill the world; why be in such a hurry? One day, Ciming...
Just as he was about to go out, it suddenly began to rain. The Master scouted a small path; upon seeing him, he seized him by the collar and said, "You old fellow!
You must explain this to me today. If you do not speak, I shall beat you. The next day, the Abbot said, "The Supervisor should have known better than to involve himself in such matters; let it rest."
Before he had finished speaking, the Master attained great enlightenment. He immediately prostrated himself in the mud and asked, "What is it like when meeting on a narrow path?
Ming said, "You should step aside; where do I intend to go? The Master returned. On the following day, having prepared his full ceremonial regalia, he went to the abbot’s quarters to offer thanks.
Ming said, "Not yet. From then on, whenever Ming went out for walks in the mountains, the Master would invariably watch for him to emerge, even late into the evening.
He invariably struck the drum to assemble the multitude. Ming Ju returned in a hurry and said angrily, "In the morning you gather the assembly, and in the evening you ascend the seat;

from where did you get this rule? The Master replied, "This is the late-evening instruction of Fenyang. How can you say it is not a rule? He frequently used such occasions to stir up and exalt the fundamental tenets.
Later, when Ming Ju moved to Xinghua, the Master took his leave to return to Jiufeng. Subsequently, monastics and laypeople welcomed him to reside at Yangqi, where he greatly [prospered].
He revitalized the Way of Ciming; this constitutes the eleventh generation under Nan Yue. The eulogy states:
"Bearing the great Dharma upon his shoulders, he maintained the structural integrity of the monastic groves. Meeting on a narrow path, a single word revealed the mind.
In time, his descendants will fill the world; the source is distant and the flow long, the roots deep and the branches vast."
The Biography of Chan Master Baizhang Shouduan of Shuzhou:
Chan Master Baizhang Shouduan was a native of the Ge clan of Hengzhou. In his youth, he devoted himself to calligraphy;
in his maturity, he relied upon Chan Master Yuru of Chaling for tonsure and went to study under Yangqi. One day, Yangqi suddenly asked him, "Who is your preceptor?"
The Master said, "There was a monk, the Venerable Yuru of Chaling. Qiyun asked, 'I have heard that he had an awakening after falling while crossing a bridge;
he composed a verse that was truly extraordinary. Can you remember it? The Master recited it: 'I possess a bright pearl, Long confined by the dust of worldly toil.'
This morning, the dust was cleared and light arose, illuminating every mountain and river in vivid detail. Daokai laughed and rose from his seat; the Master was startled and remained awake all night.
At dawn, he questioned him about it. It happened to be the end of the year. Daokai said, "Did you see those who were beating the *nanshe* (exorcist puppets) yesterday?
He replied, "I saw them. Daokai said, "In this matter, you are not one step ahead of them. The Master was again struck with awe and asked, "What is the meaning of this?"

He asked, "What is it? Qi replied, "He loves being laughed at; you fear being laughed at. The Master attained great enlightenment. He served as an attendant for a long time before taking leave to travel to Mount Lu.
Chan Master Net of Yuan Tong invited him to take charge of Chengtian Monastery, where his reputation became widespread. Later, he yielded the position to another and resided at Yuan Tong.
He subsequently moved to Fahua, Longmen, Xinghua, and Haihui. Wherever he went, the assembly gathered like clouds. In every location, he ascended the hall to instruct the multitude;
his spontaneous utterances were transcendent and peerless. He was the twelfth generation descendant of Nanyue. The eulogy says:
For a long time he held the bright pearl as a secret and rare treasure; yet upon meeting a true master, a single laugh caused it to fall away.
Having seen through the very place where one laughs, he himself fell into utter laughter. Picking up whatever came to hand, everything was nothing but treasure.
—From the Biography of Chan Master Wuzu Fayan.
Chan Master Wuzu Fayan of Qizhou was the son of the Deng family from Mianzhou. At the age of thirty-five, he first left home to shave his head and receive full ordination.

He went to Chengdu to study the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* and the *Śata-dharmaka-śāstra*. There, he heard that when a Bodhisattva enters the Path of Seeing, wisdom merges with principle and the objective realm unites with the spirit;

thus, there is no distinction between the subject that realizes and the object realized. A non-Buddhist from the Western Regions once said: [...]* *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
A monk posed this difficult question: "If you do not distinguish between the capacity to realize and that which is realized, then by what means is there realization? No one could answer.
Later, when Tripitaka Master Xuanzang arrived there, he resolved the difficulty by saying, "It is like a person drinking water; whether it is cold or warm, they know it for themselves.
The Master said, "The coldness and warmth may indeed be known, but what is the matter of 'knowing for oneself'? Thereupon, the monk was struck with doubt.
The Master [Fayan] did not neglect his question, but simply said, "If you wish to clarify this, you should go to the South and seek out those who have transmitted the Buddha-mind school.
The Master then took up his book-bag and traveled to various regions; whenever he met venerable elders, he consulted them on this matter without exception, yet his doubts remained unresolved.
Later, he visited Chan Master Fushan Yuan to request further instruction. Fushan said, "I have a parable to tell you."
"You resemble someone. You look like a firewood-seller from a remote village carrying a flat pole, standing at a crossroads and asking people:
'What matters are you discussing today in the Hall of the Secretariat? The Master silently reflected.
"If it is thus, the great matter is not far off. One day he said to his teacher, "I am old; I fear I shall spend my remaining years in vain. You should go and rely upon Baiyun;
this elder will surely enable you to realize the Great Matter. The teacher took his leave and went to Baiyun.

He then brought up the story of the *maṇi* jewel asked about by a monk of Nanquan to request instruction. Baiyun rebuked him, and the teacher attained realization. He then offered [his understanding].

The verse of seizing the opportune moment says: "Before the mountain lies a stretch of vacant land; with palms joined, I earnestly question the patriarch: 'How many times have you sold it only to buy it back?
It is for pitying the pines and bamboos that draw in the pure breeze. Yun gave his seal of approval. Later, he shared the seat and preached the Dharma.
In his later years, he resided at Mount Dongshan. He was the thirteenth generation descendant of Nanyue.
The eulogy says: "Leaving the gate brings no good fortune; one merely bumps into a shoulder-pole. Encountering people, one asks questions—this only serves to blind one's own eyes.
Fortunately meeting a master, a single blow shatters it all. Only when turning the head back does one realize the talk has fallen."
The Biography of Chan Master Wuzhun Fan:
Chan Master Wuzhun of Jingshan was named Shifan. He was a native of Zizhong in Shu, surnamed Yong.
Having left the household life and received full ordination, he traveled to Hangzhou to study under Songyuan Yue at Lingyin Temple. Thereafter, he visited Chan Master Po’an Xian.
In Pingjiang, under a single word [of instruction], he suddenly awakened to the profound essence. He left the world to reside at Qingliang in Mingzhou, then moved to Jiaoshan, and later to Xuedou.
Summoned to reside at Yuwang, he was subsequently transferred to Jingshan. He was summoned to have an audience in the Xiuzheng Hall, where he was granted a golden-embroidered monastic robe.

Furthermore, an imperial edict was proclaimed at Ciming Hall, where he ascended the high seat to preach the Dharma. The Emperor listened from behind a curtain and bestowed upon him the title Chan Master Fojian. A eulogy says:
"A single word strikes the vital point, and the ten directions are permeated; The root of his tongue rolls like thunder, as monks gather like clouds."
Entering the inner court twice to lead the Ten Thousand Chariots, he relied not on external force but entirely upon the True Command.
The Dharma Master Zhili of Siming Fazhi transmitted the Dharma from Dharma Master Fashi.
His name was Zhili, his courtesy name was Yuoyan. He was the son of the Jin family of Siming; his mother was Lady Li. They were childless.
His parents prayed to the Buddha. In a dream, a divine monk led a young boy to them and said, "This is the Buddha’s son, Rāhula.
Because he had been conceived [in this manner], from his birth his spirit was pure and refined, setting him apart from the common crowd. At the age of seven, he lost his mother;

his wailing did not cease as he beseeched his father for permission to leave the household life. He subsequently renounced the world and took refuge under Master Hóngxuǎn of Tàipíng Xīngguó Temple. At fifteen...
He was granted full ordination and specialized in the Vinaya section. At that time, Dharma Master Baoyun was exclusively propagating the teachings and contemplations of Tiantai.
When the Master was twenty years old, he went to follow him. After only three days, the Head Seat said to him, "You should practice the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm).
The Master asked, "What is meant by the 'Dharma Realm'? The Head Seat replied, "It is the Great Universal-Characteristic Dharma Gate, which is perfectly interfused and unobstructed."

The Master said, "Since it is perfectly interfused and without obstruction, how could there be any sequence? Zuo was unable to respond. After one month had passed, he himself lectured on the Heart Sūtra;
those who heard him were struck by his swift realization. Five years later, his father dreamed that the Master was kneeling before Baoyun.
Yun poured water from a jar onto his mouth; from that moment, the principles of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching were fully realized upon a single reception.
He once took the place of Baoyun to lecture. When Yun passed away, the Master again dreamed that he was piercing Baoyun’s head and wearing it on his left arm as he walked.

The Master interpreted this himself, saying: "The first part signifies receiving, studying, and circulating [the teachings]; the second signifies wielding the head of the 'Wisdom of All Modes' (sarvākārajñatā) to transform [sentient beings]."
He moved through the world [teaching]. Later, accepting an invitation, he appeared in the world to preside over Qianfu Monastery.

Subsequently, he was transferred to Ba'en Yuan, where he greatly expanded its construction and established it as a center for the long-term lecturing on the Tiantai teachings and a place where practitioners from the ten directions resided. The Master was diligent in the practice of repentance and devoted himself to ascetic cultivation with a bitter resolve.
He was widely learned and possessed great erudition, excelling in composition and being skilled at articulating arguments and resolving difficult points regarding the teachings of the Tiantai school.
The practice of *guan* (contemplation) had long been submerged by the Song dynasty. Previously, Baoyun had lectured on it for twenty years, yet many held divergent views.

Upon reaching the Master, he extensively established inquiries and challenges to elucidate the principle of the three contemplations within a single mind; thus, the Tiantai school regards the Master as its restorer.
His writings are numerous and are fully recorded in a separate catalog. The encomium says:
"The Tiantai school distantly venerates Nāgārjuna; its teachings and contemplations are clear and distinct, so that many who encounter them attain awakening.
For five hundred years, its principles have not been widely propagated, until our Master truly arose to greatly revitalize its guiding principles."

The Biography of Chan Master Xueyan Qin (Supplement) Chan Master Zuqin Xueyan of Yangshan in Yuanzhou was a native of Wuzhou. He entered the monastic life at the age of five and received full ordination at sixteen.

At eighteen, he went to the assembly of Master Tiejue Yuan of Shuanglin. Initially, he took up the koan of "Mu" (No). Suddenly, he turned his gaze inward and contemplated the thought: [text continues]

At the very moment it arose, his head became as cold as ice; it was limpid and still, unmoving. A day passed like the snap of a finger, during which he did not hear the sound of bells or drums at all.
At the age of nineteen, he entered the monastic community at Lingyin Temple. There he saw the Secretary from Chuzhou, who said:

"Master Qin’s practice of meditation is like stagnant water—it will not serve the purpose. Stillness and movement are two distinct aspects; you must strike them together as one. To study Chan, you must..."
He gave rise to a state of doubt. "A small doubt leads to a small awakening; a great doubt leads to a great awakening.

The Master then told him to change his focus and contemplate a dried-up dung pellet (*śuṣka-gomaya-śalākā*). However, due to dullness and agitation, he could not achieve a moment of purity. He moved his quarters to Jingci Temple to study under Tianmu Li.
He girded himself for meditation, sealing his bedding and refusing to lie down. One day, he asked Senior Monk Xiu, "Right now, dullness and agitation persist and cannot be dispelled. Xiu—

[The Master] said, "It is simply that you yourself are not fierce enough. You must exert your entire being and merge it into a single *huatou* (critical phrase). What further room is there for dullness or distraction?
The Master followed this instruction in his practice and suddenly realized the simultaneous forgetting of both body and mind. For three days and nights he did not close his eyes.
On the afternoon of the third day, while walking in meditation beneath the main gate, Xiu asked, "What are you doing here? [The Master] replied:
While practicing the Way, Xiu asked, "What do you call 'the Way'? He was unable to answer and became increasingly bewildered and distressed. He then returned to the hall to practice *zazen*.
As soon as he sat upon his meditation mat, the space before him suddenly opened up as if the earth had collapsed.

At that moment, it was impossible to describe it to anyone. He immediately left his seat and went to find Xiu. Upon seeing him, Xiu said, "How joyful! How joyful! and took him by the hand out [of the hall].
Walking along the willow embankment before the gate, one beholds the myriad phenomena in their full array.

Those things previously loathed and discarded—ignorance and afflictions—are fundamentally nothing other than what flows forth from the wondrously luminous true nature. For more than half a month, the movement of mental states did not arise;

yet, while fast asleep in the middle of the night, they were once again split into two separate pieces. Regarding the public cases (gong'an) of the ancients, those that follow a path of conceptual meaning...
Thus, one may understand the principle; yet, when it comes to that which is like a silver mountain or an iron wall, one still does not understand.
Later, while meeting Master Wuzhun Shanfeng at Mount Jing, the Master was commissioned to compose the introductory prose for the casting of a bell. The Master composed this verse:
"The entire body is but a single mouth, Rolled forth from within the hundred-fold smelting furnace. Having sent the setting sun back into its decline, It now hastens the rising moon upward."

Lou-tai was then appointed to serve in the administrative office for ten years, yet he still did not attain thorough enlightenment. Consequently, he traveled to eastern Zhejiang and resided at both Mount Tiantong and Mount Yuyang.
One day, while walking in front of the Buddha hall, he suddenly raised his head; seeing a branch of an ancient cypress tree, it triggered a realization that struck him.
The obstruction that had been weighing upon his chest dispersed all at once, and he said to himself: "It is as if one were in a dark room..."
Emerging beneath the midday sun, he made a circuit as if in pursuit; only then did he see where the Elder of Jing Mountain stood.
He deserved thirty blows of the staff for this. Consequently, his reputation resounded through the monastic forests, and he entered the world at Longxing Temple in Tanzhou.
He moved to Daolin in Xiangxi, Furi at Nanming in Chuzhou, Husheng in Xianju, Taizhou, and Guangxiao in Huzhou;
eventually, while residing at Yangshan in Yuanzhou, his Way became widely renowned. Scholars hailed him as the second incarnation of Yangqiao.
Ascending the hall, he said: "This matter is fundamentally manifest; seek it and it cannot be seen. A white jade vessel is originally without flaw, yet polishing it creates a blemish.
To grasp it as a substantial reality is like lightning flashing in the void. To view it as something trivial is to add a red thread beneath one's feet.
If you are a student of the Way, look well at this expedient means. How so? Do not look at the immortal."
Holding his fan in hand, he spoke universally: "Time does not wait for man; in the blink of an eye, it is already the next life.
Why do you not take advantage of your current physical strength and vigor to strike through to the bottom and seek out clarity?

How fortunate it is that we are here once more in this famous mountain and great marsh, in a world of divine dragons, where we have settled our mats in the patriarchs' Dharma cave, where the monks' hall is bright and clean, and where the congee and rice are pure and refined."

This is a matter of life and death; it is a matter of immediate urgency. If you do not strike through this point thoroughly and seek a clear understanding, it is because you have abandoned yourself and surrendered to your own fate, becoming a base and deluded person.
If you are truly such a person, utterly ignorant and without knowledge, why do you not consult those who possess prior wisdom?
Whenever you encounter the five periods of formal inquiry and see the old man upon the high seat, [you must act accordingly].
He speaks of verticality; why does it not pass through the faculty of hearing? Reflect upon this repeatedly and investigate thoroughly:
what kind of principle is this ultimately? This constitutes the twentieth generation under Nanyue. The eulogy says:
If knowledge and views persist, the pivot remains obstructed; Only by shattering the ancient cypress before the crystal palace can one ascend Yangshan’s seat and transmit the lineage of Yangqi.
When the true command is fully raised, all demons lose their spirit.
The Supplement to the Biography of Chan Master Wukuan.
Chan Master Wuyong Kuan of Mount Taihu in Shuzhou received the Dharma from Jinniu Zhen. His monastic discipline was rigorous and stern.
He successively presided over the great monasteries of Jinniu Lixiang, Taiping Rushan, Taihu Liangshan, Jingjie, and Zhengjue, all of which have recorded sayings (yulu) that circulate in the world.
When Yiyuan Ning sought certification of his realization, he was just about to enter the master’s quarters when the Master rebuked him.

He shouted at him to leave. Ning bowed outside the gate and stood there with palms joined. After a long time, the Master finally permitted him to enter. The Master asked, "Where are you from? He replied, "Tongzhou.
The Master said, "How is the state of the rivers and seas these days—full or empty? He replied, "The waters submerge the sun and overflow the heavens;
not a single drop remains. The Master said, "They do not reach the grain transport channels. He said, "I beg the Master to speak. The Master then gave a shout. Ning [bowed].
He withdrew to his meditation chamber and did not sleep throughout the night. One day, he heard the Master cite Yunmen’s words, "A single thought does not arise.
Before the sound had even faded, he attained realization. He hurried into the hall, whereupon the Master struck him and ordered him to compose a verse on Zhaozhou’s "Mu" (No).
Ningliu composed it on the spot, saying: "Zhaozhou’s dog has no Buddha-nature; The myriad phenomena all beg for their lives. An open-bottomed basket."

The boy held up a dead snake and said, "Adding much or subtracting little, there is nothing left over. The Master gave a silent, solemn smile and again cited the *Zhengdao Ge* (Song of Realizing the Way), asking:
"A flash of lightning strikes—no room for the whole body to turn back. In the space of a single thought, there is no path for sage or ordinary being.
Speak quickly! Speak quickly! Ning replied, "Fire sparks fly; what room is there for deliberation? To meet the situation face-to-face is not a matter of 'is' or 'is not.'"
The Master shook his authority and let out a single shout. Yuan Ning asked, "What was that shout for? The Master said, "In front of the Melon Mountain, he swallowed a shoulder pole;
he caught the clear breeze and stripped it of its skin. Yuan Ning, taken aback, felt sweat break out over his entire body and said, "Only today do I understand the Master's application of the Dharma.
The Master said, "Shut your mouth. Yuan Ning attended at the Master’s side for three years. The Master [entrusted him] to the lineage of Duanya Yi.
He inscribed his own portrait and personally added a flower, bestowing it upon him with these words: "When you encounter a dragon, stay; when you meet a pond, dwell.
Later, he indeed established the Yuguan Xinghua Hermitage at Longchi, truly fulfilling that prophecy. As the Song Dynasty scholar Lu Xuan (Lian) said:
"Is this not the 'jingling steel' among iron? This constitutes the twentieth generation under the lineage of Nanyue. The eulogy says:
What a fine master indeed, with such an imposing air! His gate is lofty and steep; his words are free from branches and leaves.
Having flayed the skin alive, he reveals the pure breeze. Now, shut your mouth—there is not even a thread’s breadth of passage.
*The Biography of Chan Master Gaofeng Miao*
Chan Master Gaofeng of Tianmu, whose name was Yuanmiao, was a native of Wujiang. His surname was Xu, and his mother’s surname was Zhou.

She conceived after dreaming of a monk boarding a boat to stay the night. From birth, he delighted in sitting in the lotus posture; whenever he saw a monk enter a door, he would feel a deep affection and desire to follow him on his travels.
At the age of fifteen, he earnestly requested his parents’ permission to leave the household life and entered the Miaoyin Temple in Jiahe, where he took Fazu as his teacher.

Having shaved his head and received full ordination, he entered Jingci Monastery at the age of twenty. He established a three-year limit for himself to study Chan, remaining steadfast and indifferent even when his father and elder brother came searching for him.
Later, he went to visit Chan Master Xueyan Qin; as soon as he offered his greetings, the Master struck him and shut the door.
Only after going back again did he finally gain access. One day, Yanguan suddenly asked him, "Who gave you this corpse to drag along?
Before the words had even faded, Yanguan struck him. This happened countless times. Later, upon seeing the eulogy for Master Wuzu Faian, it said:
"Turn it over and over, and it is still this very man. Suddenly, his doubt regarding the "dragging of a corpse" was shattered. And when he saw...
Yan continued as before to question him. The Master gave a shout. Yan raised his staff. The Master seized it and said, "Today you may not strike me.
The following day, Yan asked, "All phenomena return to the One; where does the One return? The Master replied, "A dog licking a hot oil cauldron.
From then on, their intellectual sharpness was such that neither would yield. One day, Yan asked, "When one is fast asleep and dreaming nothing, where is the host?"
"Where? The Master remained silent. From then on, he resolved to enter Longxu, determined to achieve enlightenment.

Five years later, while staying overnight with others, his pillow fell to the floor as he pushed it aside, making a sound; at that moment, he attained great awakening. He said, "It is like a traveler returning home;
it is simply the same person from before, walking the same path as before. Later, he entered Simha Rock on Mount Tianmu.
At the most perilous and precipitous spot, he established a "Gate of Death. He did not cut his hair, used a broken jar as a cauldron, and ate but once every two days, remaining composed and at ease.

At that time, while he was staying at Dayang, [his master] called out three times but he did not rise; thereupon, the master bestowed upon him the fly-whisk as a seal of transmission. Later, he appeared in the world [as a teacher].
His Way flourished greatly, such that there were those who came from other regions and foreign lands, crossing over vast seas and traversing ten thousand mountains.
In praise, it was said:
"The perilous cliffs of Xueyan stand like walls ten thousand fathoms high; only our Master ascended them and found their shortcut."
The peril of the "Gate of Death" exceeds even that of a precipice; thus, those who gaze upon it feel as if they were ascending to heaven.

*The Supplemental Biography of Chan Master Tienshan Qiong of Nanyue* Chan Master Tienshan Qiong of Nanyue left home at the age of eighteen. At twenty-two, he shaved his head and received full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*). He first went to...
Shishuang recalled Master Xiang’s saying: "From time to time I observe the white tip of my nose; from this point on, I apply myself to the work and immediately attain purity.
However, upon reading Xueyan’s *Canticle on Zazen*, he realized his practice had not yet reached the mark.

He then went to see Xueyan at Yangshan and applied himself to the work exactly as instructed. One day, he suddenly experienced an awakening, feeling as if his body from head to toe were being split open.
It was like breaking a skull; it was as if one had been pulled out from the bottom of a ten-thousand-fathom well and placed in mid-air.
When he presented this to Yanguan, Yanguan said, "Not yet. Go back and apply yourself further to your practice. He then sought a verse of Dharma instruction, the final line of which read:

"To perpetuate the Buddhas and Patriarchs regarding matters beyond the ordinary—behind the head, there still lacks one more blow. After Yanguan passed away, the Master [Xuedou] remarked that he had left Yanguan too soon.
He visited Mōngshān again. Mōngshān asked, "To what extent have you reached in your Zen practice? Where is the point of completion? The Master was at a loss.

Mōngshān instructed him to apply the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to wash away habitual defilements. Whenever he entered the room for instruction and offered a response, Mōngshān would simply say, "It is still lacking."

One day, through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he reached the most profound and subtle depths. Upon emerging from meditation, he reported this to Master Shàn. Shàn asked, "What is that which is your original face?
Just as he was about to offer a response, Shàn closed the door. From then on, his practice progressed daily toward wondrous insights;
yet, whenever he entered the room to offer a word, he still felt it was incomplete. One day, while in meditation, he suddenly encountered the character for "incomplete" (*quàn*).
His body and mind were suddenly cleared, like a landscape of accumulated snow suddenly breaking into sunshine.
Unable to restrain his joy, he leaped down from his seat, seized Master Shan, and said, "What was I lacking? Shan struck him three times with his palms; the Master bowed three times.

Shan said, "This one move of Iron Mountain has finally reached its conclusion today after many years. Later, he resided at Mount Nanyue, where his reputation for the Way spread far and wide, even reaching Goryeo.
The King appointed him as National Preceptor; his fame resounded beyond the seas. Later, he returned to Shishuang and succeeded Xueyan.
Master Qianyan Chang appended a colophon to the Master’s instructions, stating: "Iron Mountain Worthy possesses a single, rigid backbone that cannot be bent.
Having personally received the prediction of the elder Yangshan Huilang, he became the national preceptor of the entire kingdom of Goryeo. Upon ascending [the throne],...
Entering the gate, ascending the hall—countless millions in number. This is the twenty-first generation under Nanyue. The eulogy says:
The skull is shattered by a further blow of the mallet; Originally nothing was lacking, yet how many times were we mistaken?
Fragrance fills the heavens and scorches the earth; beyond the seas, the net opens wide. The Dharma has no place of concealment; from ten thousand miles, one returns home.
The Biography of Chan Master Zhongfeng Ben:
Chan Master Zhongfeng of Tianmu was named Mingben and styled Huanzhu. He was a native of Qiantang in Hangzhou; his secular surname was Sun.
His mother was Lady Li. She dreamed that a man who had no gate through which to enter came to her home carrying a lantern. The following day, the Master was born.
His divine countenance was exceptionally extraordinary, endowed with the marks of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*). As soon as he left the swaddling clothes, he sat in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*);

as soon as he could speak, he sang praises and chanted Buddhist hymns. In all his play, he invariably performed acts of worship (*buddhakārya*). At the age of fifteen, he resolved to leave the household life and encountered a monk named Zhao.
The Master went to visit Chan Master Gaofeng of Tianmu. Gaofeng was solitary, lofty, stern, and cold, never showing a word or a hint of color to others;
yet upon seeing the Master, he was immediately joyful. He wished to shave the Master’s head, but the Master did not consent because his father had not yet granted permission.

When he reached the age of twenty-four, he received the tonsure under Gaofeng and was ordained with full precepts at Shizi Yuan. The following year, while observing flowing water, he attained realization and went to Gaofeng to seek verification.
Feng beat him and drove him out. Shortly thereafter, a rumor spread among the common people that the authorities were selecting young boys and girls.
The Master asked Feng, "If someone were to come and ask the Master for a young boy or girl, what would you do? Feng replied, "I would simply give him a bamboo staff.
At these words, the Master attained complete and clear realization. He remained submerged within the assembly, and no one recognized him. Thereupon, Gao...
Feng wrote a eulogy for Zhen and entrusted it to the Master, saying: "My own appearance is inconceivable; even Buddhas and Patriarchs cannot behold it.
I alone permit this unworthy son to see half of my nose. He further instructed his disciples to go to the Master to seek instruction, so that the assembly might thereby know where to turn.
When Gaofeng was about to pass away, he entrusted Dajue to the Master. The Master declined, recommending the First Seat to take charge instead.
The Master subsequently traveled to Mount Xuan, Mount Lu, Shaolin, and Jinling, establishing the Huanzhu Hermitage at each location. Disciples gathered there in great numbers.
While residing on a boat in Yizhen, the imperial court heard of the Master’s reputation for the Way and bestowed upon him the title of Chan Master Fuci Yuanzhao Guanghui.
At that time, among the princes, dukes, and imperial relatives, there were none who did not pay him their respects. Zhao [Chengzhi], Director of the Hanlin Academy...
Lord Mengfu treated him with the etiquette due to a teacher and frequently inquired about the essentials of the Dharma. He possessed the awakened mind of the distinct transmission;
his teaching was unimpeded, and his extensive record in thirty volumes circulates in the world. The eulogy says:
A true lion cub within the Tianmu cave—its claws and fangs barely revealed, and all beasts flee in terror.
Its solitary wind is chilling; its Dharma ocean is vast. Therefore, my teacher was hailed as the King of the Dharma.
The Biography of Chan Master Dayan Yi (Supplement).
Chan Master Duanli Liaoyi was a native of Deqing County in Huzhou. His surname was Tang. From birth he abstained from meat.
He first began to speak at the age of six, but followed his mother only in reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*; otherwise, he was ignorant and knew nothing else.
At the age of seventeen, he heard a Chan practitioner reciting the words of Gaofeng’s formal lecture: “If you wish to exhaust the view of a thousand li, climb yet another story. The Master—
Suddenly, he said, "This is a great *kalyāṇamitra*; he will surely be able to pull out nails and remove wedges for people. I wish to see him.
His mother, Lady Zhang, packed their belongings and traveled with him. They met Gaofeng at the Dead Gate on Lion Rock (*Śiṃhaśaila*).

Gaofeng instructed him to investigate the koan: "All dharmas return to One; where does the One return? Consequently, he named him Congyi (Following the One). Later, he heard Gaofeng raise the case of the Ox Passing Through...
In "Discourse at the Window Lattice," the Master was deeply perplexed. One day, while passing by Potang (Bowl Pond), he saw snow falling from the tops of pine trees and attained realization.
He immediately presented this verse: "Without asking whether it is north, south, east, or west, The great earth, mountains, and rivers are all one expanse of snow. Before his voice had even ceased—
Feng struck him so hard with his staff that he fell unconscious down the cliff. His fellow student Mingtong rushed to rescue him;
when he emerged halfway down the mountain, he was free from pain and said, "I saw Master Qin depart. Mingtong said, "Do not let the old man's staff be in vain," and pulled him back by force.

Feng then made a vow: "If I do not attain realization within seven days, I shall leave for certain. He then stood like a wall facing the cliff until dawn, yet he did not reach the end of the allotted time.
Suddenly, he attained great enlightenment. He rushed to Siguan (Dead Gate) and called out, "Old Monk! Today you can no longer deceive me! He presented this verse:
"The mountains and rivers of the great earth are a single expanse of snow; Once the sun shines upon them, they leave no trace.

From now on, I have no doubts regarding the Buddhas and Patriarchs; There is no longer north, south, east, or west. Feng then ascended the hall and said, "I spread a great net that covers the heavens..."
The Net: "To strike the phoenix and snare the dragon—today a *jiaoming* insect has flown right into it!

Thirty years hence, atop a solitary peak and at its very summit, you shall raise your voice and cry out loud. But tell me, what do you cry out? Holding up his whisk, he said, "The great earth, mountains, and rivers are all one sheet of snow.
Master Feng then seized the whisk and used it to proclaim the Dharma for the assembly. Feng marveled at his brilliance and swiftness, and changed his name.

He was called Liaoyi (One Who Has Realized the Definitive Meaning). From this point on, he shaved his head and became a monk; wherever he went, he was held in high esteem. The Master’s character was stern and severe;
if anyone happened to provoke him, his words would burst forth like rolling thunder. He did not choose his dwelling place, yet his monastic discipline was as chilling as ice and snow.

Temples such as Shizi Zhengzong and others repeatedly invited him to serve as abbot, but he declined them all. In the third year of the Taiding era, when the Master was seventy years old, he finally yielded to the requests of the assembly.
He requested [permission to stay] for one year. He then addressed the assembly, saying: "One must not give rise to a single thought of diligence;
one must not give rise to a single thought of indolence; one must not give rise to a single thought of seeking enlightenment; one must not give rise to a single thought of gain or loss.

As soon as a thought arises, you are immediately possessed by all manner of demons and malevolent spirits within your heart and viscera, causing you to become deranged, to speak nonsense, and to utter confused ravings."
They shall remain forever as members of Māra’s retinue; even a Buddha would find it difficult to save them.

On the sixth day of the first month in the second year of the Yuantong era, he went to the west of Fayun Pagoda and pointed to a vacant space, saying, "This place is better for erecting a seamless pagoda.
That evening, he said to a Zen practitioner, "I am going to Tiantai tomorrow. The practitioner replied, "I will follow my teacher. He said, "You go!"

The horse could not catch up with him. At noon the following day, he sat in the *paryaṅka* posture and passed away. His secular age was seventy-two, and his monastic seniority (*bhikṣu-varṣa*) was forty-nine.
His entire body was enshrined at Yunshen-an (Cloud-Deep Hermitage) behind Shiziyan (Lion Rock).

By imperial decree, he was posthumously granted the title Dashi Fohui Yuanming Zhengjue Pudu (Great Master Buddha-Wisdom Perfectly Enlightened Universal Deliverance). He belongs to the twenty-second generation under Nanyue. The eulogy says:
Severing the thousand precipices, he shatters the vast primordial chaos; his eyes empty the four seas, while nose and tongue are both fully realized.
Snow melts upon the pines, clouds fall from the cliffs—what would you call this great earth and its mountains and rivers?
The Biography of Chan Master Cheng Jue (Supplement)

Chan Master Jue-xue Shicheng of Banya Monastery in Hongzhou was a senior disciple who, during the era of the Great Virtues, resided at Lingyun under Tien-niu Chiding to propagate the Way of Xueyan. He once addressed the assembly, saying:
"Brothers, if you have been practicing for three or five years and still find no point of entry, do not cast aside your previous *huatou*; you simply have not traveled far enough."
To abandon one's practice midway is a great pity for all the mental effort expended thus far.

A person of true resolve, seeing that firewood is plentiful, water is convenient, and the monks' hall is warm within the assembly, should make a vow not to leave the gate for three years; they will certainly find a place of realization.

There are those who, as soon as they apply themselves to practice, find their minds pure; yet, as soon as objects appear before them, they immediately fall into the four conceptual positions (*catuṣkoṭi*).

Thinking themselves to be people of great accomplishment, they are merely quick-tongued and eloquent, thereby wasting a lifetime. When the three-inch breath ceases, with what will they sustain themselves?
Disciples of the Buddha, if you wish to transcend [suffering], you must investigate authentically and realize truly. —Later, Mount Yangshan said:
Gumei Zhengyou requested instruction and asked to reside with the Master. The Master said, "Go and see Wuyuan, Zhongfeng, and Duanya;
once you have finished with these three, come back and live with me. Later, Mei went to Xueyan and read the *Recorded Sayings* of Fachang.

Upon reaching the case regarding "driving the plow and seizing the food," he suddenly attained thorough penetration. He then composed several verses on public cases and sent them to present to the Master. The Master said, "This man..."
He had obtained the vital power of my third bamboo whisk, yet he was still lacking the "shedding of the shell.

Three years later, while Mei was passing through the hall, his bowl struck [the floor], and he finally attained great enlightenment. He is thus reckoned as the twenty-second generation in the lineage of Nanyue. The eulogy says:
Leaning on a curved wooden chair, he brandishes a long-handled whisk; using the mechanism of the iron ox, he shatters the bones of a thousand sages.
He is called the "Blind Shaveling" and also the "Ancient Buddha. When Qianyan breaks it open, this is the second moon.
Transmitted by Chan Master Qianyan Chang.
Chan Master Qianyan, whose name was Yuanzhang and courtesy name Wuming—Qianyan being his pen-name—was the son of the Huang family of Xiaoshan in Yue.

His father was Jiuding and his mother was of the He clan. The Master was born late in their lives; at the age of seven, he began his studies abroad, and whenever a book came before his eyes, he could recite it from memory.
His paternal uncle, Tanyang, had become a monk and wished to adopt him as a successor, which he did. At nineteen, he followed [the monastic path].
He shaved his head and received full ordination from Master Gan. Recognizing him as a vessel for the Dharma, one day he followed [Master Gan] to a meal at the Chancellor’s residence.
At that time, Zhongfeng was seated there; seeing the Master from afar, he immediately called out and asked, "How do you spend your daily life?

The Master replied, "I do nothing but recite the Buddha's name. Zhongfeng asked, "Where is the Buddha now? Just as the Master was about to deliberate on an answer, Zhongfeng rebuked him with a stern voice. Thereupon, the Master...

He knelt with his right knee on the ground and paid homage, requesting instruction on the essential points of the Dharma. Feng gave him the "public case" (gong'an) concerning the dog having no Buddha-nature.
From then on, the Master investigated this matter; he sat so upright that his ribs did not touch the mat for three years. Upon hearing the cry of a magpie, he attained a realization.

He immediately went to see Feng and fully described what he had awakened to. Feng again rebuked him. The Master returned home in indignation. One night, as he was about to fall asleep, a mouse suddenly—
He overturned the cat’s food bowl; it fell to the ground with a sound. He was suddenly enlightened, feeling his body leap several *zhang* into the air.
It was as if a cicada had shed its shell from amidst filth and was now floating in the profound void. Heaven and earth were instantly clear and bright.
He donned his robes and waited for dawn, then went again to consult Master Feng. Feng asked, "Why did Zhaozhou say 'no'? The Master replied, "A rat ate the cat."
Feng said, "Not yet. The Master said, "The rice vessel is broken. Feng asked, "What is it like after it is broken? The Master said, "It is reduced to scattered shards and tiles.
Feng then smiled and instructed him, saying, "You should protect and maintain this well; hide away in mountain caves. When the time arrives, the principle will manifest of itself.
Having received these instructions, the Master went into seclusion at Tianlong, where he took delight in the flavor of Chan. Later—
His reputation for both his voice and his radiance grew daily more prominent. Master Xixian Yun earnestly recommended him, and monastics from various mountains vied with one another to invite him.

Later, he arrived at Mount Wulong, where he resolved to spend the remainder of his life. He subsequently established a monastery to spread the teachings, and students flocked to him like spokes converging on a hub.
He greatly revitalized the Way of Tianmu. His recorded sayings (*yulu*) circulate in the world. The eulogy states:
Questioning where the Buddha was, he sought him but could not find him;

a rat overturned the cat’s bowl and suddenly appeared, leaping through the air like a bird and responding to sound like an echo. Had it not been for this moment, he would have nearly sunk into deluded thoughts.
This is the supplementary biography of Chan Master Wuyi Quan.
Chan Master Wuyi Quan lived during the Yuan Yanyou era. He withdrew from the world to Stone Creek (Shixi). Stone Creek and Great Cave (Dadong) face one another;
to the left of the cave is Shixiang Temple, where at that same time Yiyuan Ning resided. People called them the two "sweet dew" gates of Guangde.
The Song scholar Luo Lun frequently praised them. As for Yiyuan, he was a dharma successor of Wuyong Kuan, namely Longchi Yu.
The founder of the monastery was Chan Master Menkai. The details regarding his dharma lineage are not known. In the past, Ying’an Hu was the adopted son in the dharma gate of Dahui Zonggao;
the world refers to his two residences as the "Two Gates of Ambrosia. By analogy with this, the Master should belong to the Linji school.
Furthermore, I once saw a verse by Master Qianyan Chang declining an invitation from Shixi, which begins: "The school that transcends the world..."
Teachers by the tens of thousands, yet only Kāśyapa remains guarding his withered dhyāna. If this old monk were to follow the current, he would bring shame upon his thirty years of mountain dwelling.
Furthermore, he sent a verse for the venerable Quan: Completely failing to recognize your own Avalokiteśvara, You visit me on Mount Fulong at the deepest hour.
At the end of the third month and the beginning of the fourth, The yellow oriole calls through the green willow shade.
I suspect this must be that very man.
Zàn said: There is not one source; they are neither two nor one. The bowl and staff are fully manifest; fame and reputation overflow.
Names may be grasped, yet words cannot be heard. I contemplate his lofty attainment: the moon over the stream, the clouds upon the rocks.

The Supplement to the Biography of Chan Master Benkong Chan Master Benkong’s clan, native place, and lineage of dharma succession remain unknown. The Master manifested the great dharma-gate of pervasive integration.
He once constructed the Songyun Pavilion at Shixi, where he painted portraits of the sages and worthies of the Three Teachings and stored all their writings therein. Some have said:

Biography of Master Chan Master Hong of Lianchi:
The Master’s name was Zhuhong; his courtesy name was Fohui, and his pen-name was Lianchi. He was a native of Renhe County, Zhejiang Province, and his surname was Shen.

At the age of seventeen, he was enrolled as a student in the state schools. From an early age, he had set his mind upon the Pure Land; he once inscribed the four characters "The Matter of Birth and Death is Great" upon his desk.
Upon reading the *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch*, he sighed deeply and said, "Vast and boundless are birth and death;

how can one remain without a fundamental basis? When his parents passed away, he resolved to leave secular life. On the eve of the New Year in the year of Yichou (1525) during the Jiajing era, he ordered his second wife, Tang, to prepare tea.
When he reached the table, the cup shattered. The Master looked at him and said, "There is no principle by which karmic affinities do not eventually disperse.
On the first day of the New Year in the year Bingyin, he took his leave of Tang, leaving behind a verse of final resolution. At that time, he was thirty-two years old.

He received the tonsure from the Venerable Xingtian Li and the full precepts from the Venerable Wujing Xing. He subsequently visited Mount Wutai, where he was moved by the manifestation of Mañjuśrī’s radiance, and later traveled to Mount Funiu.
Accompanying the assembly as they subdued demons, he arrived at Longhua Temple in Beijing and visited Master Bianrong Zhen. Bianrong said, "Do not covet profit; do not seek fame;
do not cling to external conditions. The essential gateway is simply to single-mindedly cultivate the Way, sincerely upholding the precepts and reciting the Buddha’s name.
He was subsequently entrusted with the instructions on the Six Perfections and Ten Thousand Practices. He then visited Master Xiaoyan Bao at Liuchang Lane. Xiaoyan said, "You..."

The monk said, "I have come specifically here to seek the Master’s instruction. Yan said, "You have traveled from three thousand li away to teach me.

While on his alms-rounds, he arrived at Waguan Temple in Nanjing. His illness became critical, and some wished to perform the cremation immediately;

His surname was Dan and his courtesy name was Zixu. In the *Xinwei* year of the Longqing era, he went to beg for alms at Fancun in Hangzhou.

Seeing that the mountains and waters were secluded and tranquil, he resolved to spend the remainder of his life there. The mountain had formerly been the monastery of Chan Master Fuhu Zhifeng of the Song dynasty, but it had been destroyed by a great flood.

The mountains surrounding the area were infested with tigers; each year they killed dozens of people. The Master built a thatched hut of three bays and resided there, chanting sutras and offering food.

The tiger menace was immediately quelled. During a drought, the community urged the Master to go out and pray for rain. As he walked through the fields reciting the Buddha’s name, sweet rain poured down accordingly.
The community marveled at this and together assisted in the construction of a Chan monastery, where scholars could dwell in retreat; this is the present-day Yunqi Monastery.

Not long after, he returned south to Fancun due to illness. There was a bridge called Zhupiao that had repeatedly been washed away by the tides;

He stopped there. Someone doubted that it would be sufficient, but the Master said, "If the power of the mind is great, the merit will naturally be imperishable.

He used [the funds] to relieve the famine-stricken people of Shandong. On the *bingxu* day, Empress Dowager Cisheng bestowed the Tripitaka upon Donghai and commissioned the construction of a temple, granting it the name Haiyin.
Master Daguan Ke visited him there and stayed for twenty days. On the *dinghai* day, the construction of the halls and buildings was completed.

He first opened the hall and preached the precepts for the assembly. In the year Jichou (1609), he requested the Tripitaka to be brought to Bao’en Temple in Nanjing, where he was moved by the sight of the precious pagoda emitting light.
He prepared burial sites for his two parents. In the seventh month of the year Renchen (1612), he visited Master Daguan Ke at the capital.
They conversed for forty days and nights, traveling together to Seokgyeongsan Mountain to pay homage to the relics of Śākyamuni Buddha.
They paid homage to the stone scriptures at Raeyunsa Temple and visited the pagoda complex of Master Wan. In the year Gwisi (1653), Shandong suffered another famine;

the Master distributed all the provisions and offerings stored in the mountain monastery to sustain the people of the four villages on the surrounding slopes. In the winter of the year Gamu (1654), he preached the precepts in the capital.
The Master resided at Cishou Temple. In the year of Yimwei, calumnious rumors spread from a court sorcerer leading to an encroachment upon him; he was subsequently summoned to the imperial prison.

Although the investigation found no evidence of actual wrongdoing, he was sentenced for privately constructing a temple and banished to serve as a soldier at Leizhou Guard. Master Daguan Ke wished to clear his innocence.

The Master stopped him. He composed a discourse titled "On Expelling Guests" as a gift for the Master and took his leave. Traveling by way of Jiangxi, he was welcomed by Zou Zhongjie Yuanbiao at Tiefo An.
With a single word, they found mutual resonance, and Yuanbiao’s former reservations were instantly overturned.

In the spring of the Bingshen year, he entered Caoxi to pay homage to the Sixth Patriarch, then proceeded to his place of exile, staying at an ancient temple on Pogu Ting to the west of the city. Lèizhou was suffering from famine.
He buried the remains of those afflicted by the pestilence, numbering in the tens of thousands, and established the *Ullambana* assembly to preach the Precepts for the Netherworld.
It rained heavily, and the pestilence ceased accordingly. Not long after, he built Huacheng Hermitage on Kufeng Ridge to the west of Dianbai County, providing tea to aid the masses.
In the year Wuxu, he compiled the *General Gazetteer of Caoxi*. He constructed a meditation hall amidst the ruins and modeled it after that of Dahui.
Wearing a ceremonial cap and kerchief, he preached the Dharma. In the year Gengzi, he first took up residence at Caoxi.

He conferred the precepts upon the attendant Lingtong, reclaimed encroached-upon fields, and expelled those who occupied the monastery quarters. Butchers' shops and wine taverns were transformed into a flourishing monastic complex. Monastics and laypeople gathered in great numbers;

he employed both the methods of *sheluo* (restraint and subduing) to cause the Way of the Great Mirror (Huineng) to flourish once more. In the year Yisi, he crossed the Qionghai Sea to visit Su Dongpo’s *guāngláng* (practitioner’s hut).
At Longquan Hermitage, he sought the remains of Chan Master Juefan but could not find them; he was moved with deep regret.
He renovated the Changchun Hermitage at the Blue Gate in Wuyang and established the Caoxi Monastery, making offerings for the Sixth Patriarch. In the eleventh month of winter.
The Shixi Emperor ascended the throne, and by imperial decree, the military service quota was opened for recruitment. In the year *guichou*, he crossed the mountain ridges and arrived at Hudu.
He renovated the Tanhua Jingśe (Flower-Splendor Monastery) in Hengzhou and traveled to Deshan to pay homage to the Patriarch. In the summer of the year *jiayin*, Empress Dowager Cisheng passed away;

when the imperial summons arrived, the Master returned to his monastic robes. In the year *yimao*, he paid homage at Mount Nanyue, ascending directly to Zhurong Peak, before traveling to Jiuyi Mountain to spend the winter there.
At Yuxi, on the Bingchen day, I established the succession of the monastic lineage for the Flower Medicine Temple (Huayao Si). Passing through Meixuetang, I paid my respects at the tomb of Sun’an.
Reaching Wuchang, I worshipped the Great Buddha and toured Jiufeng, where I paid homage at the stupa of Master Wunian You.

Arriving at Xunyang, I visited Donglin and composed a poem on "Lamenting Antiquity. Ascending Mount Kuanglu, I paid my respects at the site of Chekong. I spent the summer heat at Jinzhuping and toured Guizong Temple.

For two years, he lay in an ancient shrine and begged for food, yet found no way of entry into the path. One day, he encountered the abbot Miaozhen and consequently studied under him.
When his mind was thoroughly penetrated by the "Ancestral Hall Examination of the Shaolin Monk" kōan concerning the monk from the Three Indias, the past and future suddenly severed.
