When Layman Guo asked, "To whom do you entrust this? the Master said, "This path has been defiled too much; today I shall cut it off completely.

He wrote a verse, saying: "Little children! Little children! On the road of birth and death, one must be carefree. At the break of dawn, bright with moonlight, frost, and ice, I drink a cup of tea and depart while sitting.
On the twenty-sixth day of the eighth month, at the hour of You (5–7 p.m.), he requested a cup of tea. One [cup].
The Master followed by chanting the line, "Snowflakes fly," and passed away while sitting upright. He was seventy-seven years of age and forty-nine years since his ordination.
His entire body was enshrined in a stupa on the front ridge of Yunmen. His collected works, including his *Recorded Sayings* and *Verses on the Pure Land*, were circulated in the world.
These were the thirty-third generation successors under the Southern Peak (Nanyue).

Among his入室 (入室) disciples—Che Ya-xie, Xing Shan-nao, Wei Yi-run, Cao Yuan-jin, Shi Tao-kai, and Shan Ming-lu—they took turns presiding over monastic seats in various forest retreats. The eulogy states:
"Yunqi’s dripping rain and Yunmen’s scattering snow; waves rising at Longchi, transcendent and peerless."
In the realm of calligraphy and painting, the "Elegant" (Yi) grade is like this; as for Zen, I consider myself to surpass even a single hill and a single valley.
— Appendix: Postscript to the Biographies and Eulogies of the Three Great Masters.
In the winter month of the Guiwei year, my late father returned from Baodi and was about to depart for Jingxian.

He then recalled his ancestral Zen lineage and took pleasure in composing biographical eulogies for the three great masters Yunqi, Zibo, and Hanshan, so as to continue the succession of the eighty-eight patriarchs.
He recorded these at the beginning of the Xiaoyuan period in the Jia Shen year. Not long after, the Elder Xueqiao further established a bond of mutual resonance with him. Before long...
When Master Xue passed away, my late father further composed a postscript to continue the lineage of the three great masters.
Not long after, my late father succumbed to grief and fell ill, eventually passing away and leaving behind his orphaned children.

This humble son of mine, unable to bear forgetting the traces of his father’s handiwork, has reflected that during the intervals of his formal studies, he once attended upon [the master] at Shuangjing with a water vessel and towel. Thus, this is our family’s ancestral tradition.
Master Sun, father and son, are both manifest within the light and shadow of all spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), appearing layer upon layer.
Therefore, with tears flowing, I bow my head in reverence and respectfully record this.
In the second month of spring in the *Xinchou* year of the Shunzhi era, Gao Youqian (Nianzu) of Xiuwater respectfully recorded this at Jiegu Hall.
— Appendix: Another Postscript.
The Great Master Hanshan of Caoxi received the tonsure in the Jiazi year of the Jiajing era;

he was only nineteen years old when, upon hearing Master Wujie lecture on the *Profound Discourse on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, he attained awakening to the principle of the perfect fusion of the Dharma-realm at the point concerning "the ocean-seal of the eternal abiding of all phenomena.
Admiring the character of Master Qingliang, he accordingly chose for himself the style name Chengyin. In the Guiyou year of the Wanli era, he traveled...
At Mount Wutai, he sought out the account of the "Cool and Clear" (Qingliang) mountain and traveled there following its traces.

Upon reaching the Northern Terrace (Beitai), he beheld the extraordinary beauty of Hanshan and silently adopted it as his monastic name, composing a poem to commemorate the event which included the lines: "Let no one follow me; I shall merely use this to still the workings of the mind.
In the year of Wuyin, he transcribed the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, using his own blood to soak gold powder as an offering, disregarding the fact that his blood was completely exhausted.
Because of this, he experienced various auspicious dreams: sometimes he dreamed of entering a Vajra Cave, where he personally received the instructions of Qingliang;
sometimes at night he ascended to Tuṣita Heaven, entered a multi-storied pavilion to pay homage to Maitreya, and listened to the great meaning of the transformation of consciousness into wisdom;
or he dreamed of paying homage to Mañjuśrī, who summoned him into a bathhouse, whereby he attained great purity from impurity. In the year of Xinsi, Empress Dowager Cisheng...

Later, [the Emperor] ordered the establishment of a prayer hall for the succession of the heir at Mount Wutai. He happened upon Dayatanyisi (Great Pagoda Courtyard Monastery), where the construction of a śarīra stūpa had recently been completed.

He immediately commissioned the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to be written in gold and enshrined it within the stūpa’s treasury. The following spring, he ascended the seat to lecture on profound discourse; the audience numbered ten thousand.

By chance, he saw the *Qingliang Shu* (Commentary by Qingliang), which mentions that among the Bodhisattva’s dwelling places is the Nalayan Cave in the Eastern Sea—this being translated as "Firm and Secure" (*jiānláo*).

This is the present-day Laoshan. In the summer of the Guiwei year, he traveled to that place and, at the ruins of the Guanyin Hermitage on the southern side of the mountain, cleared away the weeds to construct a hut for seclusion.
Eventually, because the Empress Dowager was moved by his labor in offering prayers, she provided the gold to build a temple and bestowed upon it the name Haiyin.
Yet the Master’s initial intent had already been to dwell between concealment and manifestation; in his later years, he established a late-life hut at Wuru on Mount Lu.
At the foot of the peak, he constantly reflected upon the Huayan school. Qingliang was the patriarch of its composition in this land;
yet, as many in the world feared the voluminousness and breadth of his commentaries and sub-commentaries, they followed only the *Huayan jing tanxuan ji*. How could this be right?

Consequently, he extracted the essential passages from the commentary and distilled its great principles, titling it the *Huayan gangyao* (Essentials of the Avataṃsaka). By the year Renxu of the Tianqi era, the work was completed, and he subsequently returned once more to Caoxi.

The following year, he entered parinirvāṇa. Having previously studied under the two elders Yungok and Soran, the Master transcended the academic schools of doctrine and proceeded directly toward the supreme state.
Thus, he was able to take a single drop from Caoxi and transform it into the rain of Dharma, irrigating those whose meditation had withered.

Consequently, the doctrinal and Chan traditions were mutually integrated; he constantly revealed his initial capacity, yet his realization emerged with such mastery that its beginning and end appeared as one seamless whole.
He alone was in accord with the fundamental tenets of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra;
it was just as Qingliang was the Dharma-grandson of the Sixth Patriarch, yet was ultimately titled the Fourth Patriarch of the Huayan school.

When I, Youqie, read the biographies of my late father’s three great masters, I privately felt that Yunqi resembled Yongming, Zibo resembled Juefan, and Master Han (Zhixu) was like Qingliang; furthermore, Guanzhi and Guifeng were his close friends. Externally...
My uncle, Master Tan S’o-an, nodded his head in agreement with these words and requested that they be further verified by those throughout the various quarters who possess the true eye.
In the winter of the Dingwei year of the Kangxi era, Gao Youqian (Nianzu) of Xiushui respectfully recorded this at Ba’en Temple in Jinling.
